title: Network with Positive Integer Mapping is Multigraph
theorem_text:
Let $N = \struct {V, E, w}$ be a network whose weights are all strictly positive integers.
Then $N$ can be represented as a multigraph.
Conversely, any multigraph can be expressed as a network whose weights are all strictly positive integers.
proof_text:
Network as Multigraph
Let $N = \struct {V, E, w}$ be a network, either directed or undirected.
without loss of generality, suppose $N$ is undirected, and in the following argument allow the term edge to include arcs.
Let $e \in E$ be an edge of the underlying graph $\struct {V, E}$ of $N$.
Let $e = u v$, where $u, v \in V$ are vertices of the underlying graph $\struct {V, E}$ of $N$.
Let $n = \map w e$ be the weight of $e$.
By hypothesis, $n$ is a strictly positive integer.
Let $n$ edges be identified between $u$ and $v$.
Repeat this process for all edges of $N$.
The resulting object is a multigraph.
Multigraph as Network
Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a multigraph, where each element of $E$ may occur multiple times.
Let $e = u v$ where $e \in E$ and $u, v \in V$.
Let $\map m e$ be the multiplicity of $e$.
Then $m$ can be identified with a weight function from $w: E \to \Z_{>0}$.
Thus the network $N = \struct {V, E, w}$ can be created.

title: Complete Graph is Regular
theorem_text:
Let $K_p$ be the complete graph of order $p$.
Then $K_p$ is $p-1$-regular.
proof_text:
By definition of complete graph, $K_p$ has $p$ vertices.
Also by definition of complete graph, each vertex of $K_p$ is adjacent to all the other $p - 1$ vertices of $K_p$.
As $K_p$ is a simple graph, there can be only one edge joining any pair of vertices of $K_p$.
So each vertex of $K_p$ has $p - 1$ edges to which it is incident.
So, by definition, $K_p$ is $p-1$-regular.

title: Circuit has Three Edges or More
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a simple graph.
Let $C$ be a circuit in $G$.
Then $C$ has at least $3$ edges.
proof_text:
By definition, a circuit contains at least one edge.
That is, a single vertex does not comprise a trivial degenerate circuit with no edges.
Suppose $C$ contains only one edge $e$.
As $G$ is a simple graph it contains no loops.
Therefore $e$ starts and ends at two distinct vertices.
Therefore $C$, consisting entirely of $e$ can not be a circuit.
Suppose $C$ contains exactly $2$ edges $e$ and $f$.
Let $e = u v$ where $v$ and $v$ are vertices of $G$.
Then for $C$ to be a circuit it must follow that $f = v u$.
Thus there are two edges between the same vertices $v$ and $u$.
As $G$ is an undirected graph, it must be that $e$ and $f$ are part of a multiple edge between $u$ and $v$.
But $G$ is not a multigraph, and so such a circuit can not exist.
A circuit containing $3$ edges definitely exists, though.
Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ where $V = \set {u, v, w}$ and $E = \set {\set {u, v}, \set {u, w}, \set {v, w} }$.
Then $\tuple {u, w, v, u}$ is a $3$-edge circuit.

title: Bridge divides Graph into Two Components
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a connected graph.
Let $e$ be a bridge of $G$.
Then the edge deletion $G - e$ contains exactly $2$ components.
proof_text:
Let $G$ be a connected graph and $e = u v$ be a bridge of $G$.
By definition of bridge, $G - e$ has to be of at least $2$ components.
Aiming for a contradiction, suppose that $G - e$ were of more than $2$ components.
Let $G_1, G_2, G_3$ be $3$ of those components such that $u \in G_1$ and $v \in G_2$.
Note that $u$ and $v$ cannot both be in the same component or $e$ would not be a bridge.
Now let $e$ be replaced so as to connect $G_1$ and $G_2$ again.
Then $G_3$ would still be disconnected from the rest of $G$, and $G$ itself would therefore be a disconnected graph.
From this contradiction it follows that $G - e$ can only be of two components.

title: Connected Graph with only Even Vertices has no Bridge
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a connected graph whose vertices are all even.
Then no edge of $G$ is a bridge.
proof_text:
Let the vertices of $G$ all be even.
Then by Characteristics of Eulerian Graph, $G$ is Eulerian.
By definition of Eulerian, $G$ therefore contains a Eulerian circuit.
Thus every edge of $G$ lies on a circuit of $G$.
From Condition for Edge to be Bridge, if an edge $e$ of $G$ is a bridge, then it does not lie on a circuit.
Hence no edge of $G$ is a bridge.

title: Dirac's Theorem/Proof 2
theorem_text: If a connected graph $G$ has $n \ge 3$ vertices and the degree of each vertex is at least $\dfrac n 2$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian.
proof_text:
Take any two non-adjacent vertices $u, v \in G$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \deg u + \deg v \ge \frac n 2 + \frac n 2 = n$
The result follows by a direct application of Ore's Theorem.

title: Path in Tree is Unique/Sufficient Condition
theorem_text:
Let $T$ be a graph.
Let $T$ be such that between any two vertices there is exactly one path.
Then $T$ is a tree.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be such that between any two vertices there is exactly one path.
Then for a start $T$ is by definition connected.
Suppose $T$ had a circuit, say $\left({u, u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n, v, u}\right)$.
Then there are two paths from $u$ to $v$:
$\left({u, u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n, v}\right)$
and
$\left({u, v}\right)$.
Hence, by Modus Tollendo Tollens, $T$ can have no circuits.
That is, by definition, $T$ is a tree.

title: Size of Tree is One Less than Order/Necessary Condition/Induction Step/Proof 1
theorem_text:
Let the following hold:
:A tree of order $k$ is of size $k - 1$.
Then this holds:
:A tree of order $k + 1$  is of size $k$.
proof_text:
Let $T_{k + 1}$ be an arbitrary tree with $k + 1$ nodes.
Take any node $v$ of $T_{k+1}$ of degree $1$.
Such a node exists from Finite Tree has Leaf Nodes.
Consider $T_k$, the subgraph of $T_{k + 1}$ created by removing $v$ and the edge connecting it to the rest of the tree.
By Connected Subgraph of Tree is Tree, $T_k$ is itself a tree.
The order of $T_k$ is $k$, and it has one less edge than $T_{k + 1}$ by definition.
By hypothesis, $T_k$ has $k - 1$ edges.
So $T_{k + 1}$ must have $k$ edges.

title: Size of Tree is One Less than Order/Necessary Condition/Induction Step/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let the following hold:
:For all $j \le k$, a tree of order $j$ is of size $j-1$.
Then this holds:
:A tree of order $k+1$  is of size $k$.
proof_text:
Let $T_{k + 1}$ be any tree with $k + 1$ nodes.
Remove any edge $e$ of $T_{k + 1}$.
By definition of tree $T_{k + 1}$ has no circuits
Therefore from Condition for Edge to be Bridge it follows that $e$ must be a bridge.
So removing $e$ disconnects $T_{k + 1}$ into two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$, with $k_1$ and $k_2$ nodes, where $k_1 + k_2 = k + 1$.
By hypothesis, $T_1$ and $T_2$ have $k_1 - 1$ and $k_2 - 1$ edges.
Putting the edge $e$ back again, it can be seen that $T_{k + 1}$ has $\paren {k_1 - 1} + \paren {k_2 - 1} + 1 = k$ edges.
Therefore a tree of order $k+1$  is of size $k$.

theorem_text:
Define $0$ as the only element in the set $P \setminus s \left({P}\right)$, where:
$P$ is the Peano Structure
$s \left({P}\right)$ is the image of the mapping $s$ defined in Peano structure
$\setminus$ denotes the set difference.
The theorem to be proven is:
$1 + 1 = 2$
where:
$1 := s \left({0}\right)$
$2 := s \left({1}\right) = s \left({s \left({0}\right)}\right)$
$+$ denotes addition
$=$ denotes equality
$s \left({n}\right)$ denotes the successor function as defined by Peano
proof_text:
Defining $1$ as $\map s 0$ and $2$ as $\map s {\map s 0}$, the statement to be proven becomes:
$\map s 0 + \map s 0 = \map s {\map s 0}$
By the definition of addition:
$\forall m \in P: \forall n \in P: m + \map s n = \map s {m + n}$
Letting $m = \map s 0$ and $n = 0$:
(1) $$\map s 0 + \map s 0 = \map s {\map s 0 + 0}$$
By the definition of addition:
$\forall m: m + 0 = m$
Letting $m = \map s 0$:
$\map s 0 + 0 = \map s 0$
Taking the successor of both sides:
(2) $$\map s {\map s 0 + 0} = \map s {\map s 0}$$
Applying Equality is Transitive to $(1)$ and $(2)$ we have:
$\map s 0 + \map s 0 = \map s {\map s 0}$
Hence the result.

title: Kruskal's Algorithm produces Minimum Spanning Tree
theorem_text: Kruskal's Algorithm produces a minimum spanning tree.
proof_text:
Let $N = \struct {V, E, f}$ be an undirected network.
Let $H$ be a subgraph of the underlying graph $G = \struct {V, E}$ of $N$.
Let $\displaystyle \map f H = \sum_{e \mathop \in H} \map f e$.
Let $N$ be of order $p$.
Let $T$ be a spanning tree of $N$, created using Kruskal's Algorithm.
Then from Size of Tree is One Less than Order, $T$ has $p - 1$ edges.
Let the edges of $T$ be ordered $e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_{p-1}$ according to the construction of Kruskal's Algorithm.
Then:
$\displaystyle \map f t = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{p - 1} \map f {e_i}$
Let $T_0$ be a minimum spanning tree of $N$.
Suppose that $T_0$ and $T$ are not equal.
Then $T$ has one or more edges which are not in $T_0$.
Using the ordering on the edges of $T$ created above, let $e_i$ be the first edge of $T$ not in $T_0$.
By construction, $1 \le i \le p-1$.
Let $e_i$ be added to $T_0$, to obtain the graph $G_0$.
Let $e_i = u v$ where $u, v \in V$ are vertices of $N$
Then there exists a $u-v$ path $P$ in $T_0$.
Together with $e_i$ this makes a cycle $C$ in $G_0$.
Since $T$ contains no cycles, there must be an edge $e_0$ of $C$ which is not in $T$.
Thus the edge deletion $T'_0 = G_0 - e_0$ is also a spanning tree of $N$, and:
$\map f {T'_0} = \map f {T_0} + \map f {e_i} - \map f {e_0}$
But as $T_0$ is a minimum spanning tree:
$\map f {T_0} \le \map f {T'_0}$
So:
$\map f {T_0} - \map f {T'_0} \le 0$
But since:
$\map f {T_0} - \map f {T'_0} = \map f {e_0} - \map f {e_i}$
it follows that:
$\map f {e_0} \le \map f {e_i}$
However, the manner in which $T$ was constructed, $e_i$ is an edge of smallest value which can be added to $\set {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_{i - 1} }$ without producing a cycle.
Also, if $e_0$ is added to $\set {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_{i - 1} }$, again no cycle is produced.
Therefore $\map f {e_i} = \map f {e_0}$ and so $\map f {T'_0} = \map f {T_0}$.
Thus $T'_0$ is a minimum spanning tree which has one more edge in common with $T$ than $T_0$, that is, $e_i$.
The procedure can be repeated as many times as there are edges in $T_0$ which are not in $T$.
Finally the spanning tree $T$ is arrived at, which by the above is a minimum spanning tree.
Hence the result.

title: Perimeter of Rectangle
theorem_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle whose side lengths are $a$ and $b$.
The perimeter of $ABCD$ is $2 a + 2 b$.
proof_text:
From Rectangle is Parallelogram, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
The result then follows from a direct application of Perimeter of Parallelogram.

title: Perimeter of Triangle
theorem_text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle.
Then the perimeter $P$ of $ABC$ is given by:
$P = a + b + c$
where $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides of $ABC$.
proof_text:
The perimeter of a plane geometric figure is defined as the total length of the boundary.
By definition, the boundary of a triangle comprises the three sides of that triangle.
Hence the result.

title: Perimeter of Regular Polygon
theorem_text:
Let $P$ be a regular $n$-sided polygon whose side length is $b$.
Then the perimeter $L$ of $P$ is given by:
$L = n b$
proof_text:
By definition, an $n$-sided polygon has $n$ sides.
By definition, a regular polygon has sides all the same length.
By definition, the perimeter of a polygon is the total length of all its sides.
Thus $P$ has $n$ sides all of length $b$.
Hence $L = n b$.

title: Commensurability is Transitive
theorem_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be three real numbers.
Let $a$ and $b$ be commensurable, and $b$ and $c$ be commensurable.
Then $a$ and $c$ are commensurable.
proof_text:
From the definition of commensurablility:
$\dfrac a b, \dfrac b c \in \Q$
where $\Q$ denotes the set of all rational numbers.
From Rational Multiplication is Closed:
$\dfrac a b \times \dfrac b c \in \Q$
Cancelling $b$, we have:
$\dfrac a c \in \Q$
Hence the result.

title: Image of Interval by Continuous Function is Interval/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $I$ be a real interval.
Let $f: I \to \R$ be a continuous real function.
Then the image of $f$ is a real interval.
proof_text:
As before, let $J$ be the image of $f$.
By Subset of Real Numbers is Interval iff Connected we need to show that $J$ is connected (and hence an interval).
Suppose not.
Then there exists a separation $S \mid T$ of $J$.
Define $A = f^{-1}(S)$ and $B = f^{-1}(T)$. $A$ and $B$ are both non-empty.
Because $f$ is continuous, by Continuous iff inverse image of any open set is open we must have $A$ and $B$ open.
Now, $A \cap B = f^{-1}(S) \cap f^{-1}(T) = f^{-1}(S \cap T) = \varnothing$, because $S \mid T$ is a separation.
Also, $A \cup B = f^{-1}(S) \cup f^{-1}(T) = f^{-1}(S \cup T) = f^{-1}(J) = I$ ($S \mid T$ is a separation of $J$).
Hence $A \mid B$ is a separation of $I$. $I$ can certainly not be an interval (because it is not connected).
This is a contradiction. Thus $J$ must be an interval.

title: Area of Isosceles Triangle
theorem_text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle whose apex is $A$.
Let $\theta$ be the angle of the apex $A$.
Let $r$ be the length of a leg of $\triangle ABC$.
Then the area $\mathcal A$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by:
$\mathcal A = \dfrac 1 2 r^2 \sin \theta$
proof_text:
A direct application of Area of Triangle in Terms of Two Sides and Angle:
$\mathcal A = \dfrac 1 2 a b \sin \theta$
where $a = b = r$.

title: Area of Ellipse
theorem_text:
Let $K$ be an ellipse whose major axis is of length $2 a$ and whose minor axis is of length $2 b$.
The area $\mathcal A$ of $K$ is given by:
$\mathcal A = \pi a b$
proof_text:
Let $K$ be an ellipse aligned in a cartesian plane in reduced form.
Then from Equation of Ellipse in Reduced Form:
$\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} + \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = 1$
Thus:
$y = \pm b \sqrt {1 - \dfrac {x^2} {a^2} }$
From the geometric interpretation of the definite integral:
$$\AA = b \int_{-a}^a \paren {\sqrt {1 - \dfrac {x^2} {a^2} } - \paren {-\sqrt {1 - \dfrac {x^2} {a^2} } } } \rd x$$
$$= b \int_{-a}^a 2 \sqrt {1 - \dfrac {x^2} {a^2} } \rd x$$
Let $x = a \sin \theta$ (note that we can do this because $-a \le x \le a$).
Thus:
$\theta = \map \arcsin {\dfrac x a}$
and:
$\d x = a \cos \theta \rd \theta$
Then:
$$\AA = b \int_{\map \arcsin {\frac {-a} a} }^{\map \arcsin {\frac a a} } 2 a \sqrt {1 - \frac {\paren {a \sin \theta}^2} {a^2} } \cos \theta \rd \theta$$
Integration by Substitution
$$= b \int_{-\frac {\pi} 2}^{\frac {\pi} 2} 2 a \sqrt {1 - \sin^2 \theta} \cos \theta \rd \theta$$
$$= b \int_{-\frac {\pi} 2}^{\frac {\pi} 2} 2 a \sqrt {\cos^2 \theta} \cos \theta \rd \theta$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= a b \int_{-\frac {\pi} 2}^{\frac {\pi} 2} 2 \cos^2 \theta \rd \theta$$
$$= a b \int_{-\frac {\pi} 2}^{\frac {\pi} 2} \paren {1 + \map \cos {2 \theta} } \rd \theta$$
Double Angle Formula for Cosine: Corollary 1
$$= a b \sqbrk {\theta + \frac 1 2 \map \sin {2 \theta} }_{-\frac {\pi} 2}^{\frac {\pi} 2}$$
Integration of Constant and Primitive of Cosine Function
$$= a b \paren {\frac {\pi} 2 + \frac 1 2 \map \sin {2 \cdot \frac {-\pi} 2} - \frac {-\pi} 2 - \frac 1 2 \map \sin {2 \cdot \frac {\pi} 2} }$$
$$= a b \paren {2 \cdot \frac {\pi} 2 + 2 \cdot \frac 1 2 \cdot 0}$$
$$= \pi a b$$

title: Area of Ellipse
theorem_text:
Let $K$ be an ellipse whose major axis is of length $2 a$ and whose minor axis is of length $2 b$.
The area $\mathcal A$ of $K$ is given by:
$\mathcal A = \pi a b$
proof_text:
Let $K$ be an ellipse aligned in a cartesian plane in reduced form.
Then from Equation of Ellipse in Reduced Form:
$\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} + \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = 1$
Thus:
$y = \pm \dfrac b a \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$
Consider a circle of radius $a$ whose center is at the origin.
From Equation of Circle: Cartesian: Corollary 2, its equation is given by:
$x^2 + y^2 = a^2$
and so:
$y = \pm \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$
The formulas show that each ordinate of the ellipse is $\dfrac b a$ the ordinate of the circle.
Since the same thing is true of the vertical chords:
$$\mathcal A_E = \dfrac b a \mathcal A_C$$
where $\mathcal A_E$ and $\mathcal A_C$ are the areas of the ellipse and the circle respectively
$$= \dfrac b a \paren {\pi a^2}$$
Area of Circle
$$= \pi a b$$

title: Perimeter of Ellipse
theorem_text:
Let $K$ be an ellipse whose major axis is of length $2 a$ and whose minor axis is of length $2 b$.
The perimeter $\PP$ of $K$ is given by:
$\ds \PP = 4 a \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {1 - k^2 \sin^2 \theta} \rd \theta$
where:
$k = \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a$
The definite integral:
$\displaystyle \PP = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt{1 - k^2 \sin^2 \theta} \rd \theta$
is the complete elliptic integral of the second kind.
proof_text:
Let $K$ be aligned in a cartesian plane such that:
:the major axis of $K$ is aligned with the $x$-axis
:the minor axis of $K$ is aligned with the $y$-axis.
Then from Equation of Ellipse in Reduced Form: parametric form:
$x = a \cos \theta, y = b \sin \theta$
Thus:
$$\frac {\d x} {\d \theta} = -a \sin \theta$$
Derivative of Cosine Function
$$\frac {\d y} {\d \theta} = b \cos \theta$$
Derivative of Sine Function
From Arc Length for Parametric Equations, the length of one quarter of the perimeter of $K$ is given by:
$$\frac {\PP} 4 = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {\paren {-a \sin \theta}^2 + \paren {b \cos \theta}^2} \rd \theta$$
$$= \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {a^2 \paren {1 - \cos^2 \theta} + b^2 \cos^2 \theta} \rd \theta$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {a^2 - \paren {a^2 - b^2} \cos^2 \theta} \rd \theta$$
simplifying
$$= a \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {1 - \paren {1 - \frac {b^2} {a^2} } \cos^2 \theta} \rd \theta$$
extracting $a$ as a factor
(1) $$= a \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {1 - k^2 \cos^2 \theta} \rd \theta$$
setting $k^2 = 1 - \dfrac {b^2} {a^2} = \dfrac {a^2 - b^2} {a^2}$
Since $\cos \theta = \map \sin {\dfrac \pi 2 - \theta}$ we can write for any real function $\map f x$:
$\ds \int_0^{\pi / 2} \map f {\cos \theta} \rd \theta = \int_0^{\pi / 2} \map f {\map \sin {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} } \rd \theta$
So substituting $t = \dfrac \pi 2 - \theta$ this can be converted to:
$$\int_0^{\pi / 2} \map f {\cos \theta} \rd \theta = -\int_{\pi / 2}^0 \map f {\sin t} \rd t$$
$$= \int_0^{\pi / 2} \map f {\sin t} \rd t$$
justifying the fact that $\cos$ can be replaced with $\sin$ in $(1)$ above, giving:
$\ds \PP = 4 a \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sqrt {1 - k^2 \sin^2 \theta} \rd \theta$

title: Composite of Monomorphisms is Monomorphism
theorem_text:
Let:
$\struct {S_1, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$
$\struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}$
$\struct {S_3, \oplus_1, \oplus_2, \ldots, \oplus_n}$
be algebraic structures.
Let:
$\phi: \struct {S_1, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n} \to \struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}$
$\psi: \struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n} \to \struct {S_3, \oplus_1, \oplus_2, \ldots, \oplus_n}$
be monomorphisms.
Then the composite of $\phi$ and $\psi$ is also a monomorphism.
proof_text:
From Composite of Homomorphisms on Algebraic Structure is Homomorphism, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a homomorphism.
From Composite of Injections is Injection, $\psi \circ \phi$ is an injection.
A monomorphism is an injective homorphism.
Hence $\psi \circ \phi$ is a monomorphism.

title: Composite of Epimorphisms is Epimorphism
theorem_text:
Let:
$\struct {S_1, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$
$\struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}$
$\struct {S_3, \oplus_1, \oplus_2, \ldots, \oplus_n}$
be algebraic structures.
Let:
$\phi: \struct {S_1, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n} \to \struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}$
$\psi: \struct {S_2, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n} \to \struct {S_3, \oplus_1, \oplus_2, \ldots, \oplus_n}$
be epimorphisms.
Then the composite of $\phi$ and $\psi$ is also an epimorphism.
proof_text:
From Composite of Homomorphisms on Algebraic Structure is Homomorphism, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a homomorphism.
From Composite of Surjections is Surjection, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a surjection.
An epimorphism is a surjective homomorphism.
Hence $\psi \circ \phi$ is an epimorphism.

title: Composite of Automorphisms is Automorphism
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ be an algebraic structure.
Let:
$\phi: \struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n} \to \struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$
$\psi: \struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n} \to \struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$
be automorphisms.
Then the composite of $\phi$ and $\psi$ is also an automorphism.
proof_text:
From Composite of Homomorphisms on Algebraic Structure is Homomorphism, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a homomorphism.
By the definition of a composite mapping, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a mapping from $S$ into $S$.
Hence $\psi \circ \phi$ is an automorphism.

title: Composite of Endomorphisms is Endomorphism
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right)$ be an algebraic structure.
Let:
$\phi: \left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right) \to \left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right)$
$\psi: \left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right) \to \left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right)$
be endomorphisms.
Then the composite of $\phi$ and $\psi$ is also an endomorphism.
proof_text:
From Composite of Homomorphisms on Algebraic Structure is Homomorphism, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a homomorphism.
From the definition of composition of mappings, $\psi \circ \phi$ is a mapping from $S$ into $S$.
Hence $\psi \circ \phi$ is an endomorphism.

title: Cardinality of Subset Relation on Power Set of Finite Set
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set such that:
$\card S = n$
where $\card S$ denotes the cardinality of $S$.
From Subset Relation on Power Set is Partial Ordering we have that $\struct {\powerset S, \subseteq}$ is an ordered set.
The cardinality of $\subseteq$ as a relation is $3^n$.
proof_text:
Let $X \in \powerset S$.
Since $X \subseteq S$, it follows that:
$X' \subseteq X \implies X' \in \powerset S$
because the Subset Relation is Transitive.
From Cardinality of Power Set of Finite Set, it follows that for any $X \in \powerset S$:
$\set {X' \in \powerset S: X' \subseteq X}$
has $2^{\card X}$ elements.
Therefore, the cardinality of $\subseteq$ is given by:
$\displaystyle \sum_{X \mathop \subseteq S} 2^{\card X}$
Let us split the sum over $\card X$:
$\displaystyle \sum_{X \mathop \subseteq S} 2^{\card X} = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \sum_{\substack {X \mathop \subseteq S \\ \card X \mathop = n}} 2^{\card X}$
It now follows from Cardinality of Set of Subsets that:
$\displaystyle \card \subseteq = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom n k 2^k$
From the Binomial Theorem:
$\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom n k 2^k = \paren {1 + 2}^n$
Hence:
$\card \subseteq = 3^n$

title: Order of External Direct Product
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {T, \circ_2}$ be algebraic structures.
Then the order of $\struct {S \times T, \circ}$ is $\card S \times \card T$.
proof_text:
By definition the order of $\struct {S \times T, \circ}$ is $\card S \times \card T$ is the cardinality of the underlying set $S \times T$.
The result follows directly from Cardinality of Cartesian Product.

title: Congruence (Number Theory) is Congruence Relation
theorem_text: Congruence modulo $m$ is a congruence relation on $\left({\Z, +}\right)$.
proof_text:
Suppose $a \equiv b \bmod m$ and $c \equiv d \bmod m$.
Then by the definition of congruence there exists $k, k' \in \Z$ such that:
$\left({a - b}\right) = km$
$\left({c - d}\right) = k'm$
Hence:
$\left({a - b}\right) + \left({c - d}\right) = km + k'm$
Using the properties of the integers:
$\left({a + c}\right) - \left({b + d}\right) = m \left({k + k'}\right)$
Hence $\left({a + c}\right) \equiv \left({b + d}\right) \bmod m$ and congruence modulo $m$ is a congruence relation.

title: Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
theorem_text:
Let $\theta$ be an angle such that $\cos \theta \ne 0$.
Then:
$\tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$
where $\tan$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ mean tangent, sine and cosine respectively.
proof_text:
Let a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be placed in a cartesian plane with origin $O$ such that $OP$ forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis.
Then:
$$\frac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta} = \frac {y / r} {x / r}$$
Sine of Angle in Cartesian Plane and Cosine of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$$= \frac y r \frac r x$$
$$= \frac y x$$
$$= \tan \theta$$
Tangent of Angle in Cartesian Plane
When $\cos \theta = 0$ the expression $\dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$ is not defined.

title: Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
theorem_text:
Let $\theta$ be an angle such that $\sin \theta \ne 0$.
Then:
$\cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$
where $\cot$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ mean cotangent, sine and cosine respectively.
proof_text:
Let a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be placed in a cartesian plane with origin $O$ such that $OP$ forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis.
Then:
$$\frac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta} = \frac {x / r} {y / r}$$
Cosine of Angle in Cartesian Plane and Sine of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$$= \frac x r \frac r y$$
$$= \frac x y$$
$$= \cot \theta$$
Cotangent of Angle in Cartesian Plane
When $\sin \theta = 0$ the expression $\dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$ is not defined.

title: Cotangent is Reciprocal of Tangent
theorem_text: $\cot \theta = \dfrac 1 {\tan \theta}$
proof_text:
Let a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be placed in a cartesian plane with origin $O$ such that $OP$ forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis.
Then:
$$\cot \theta = \frac x y$$
Cotangent of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$$= \frac 1 {y / x}$$
$$= \frac 1 {\tan \theta}$$
Tangent of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$\tan \theta$ is not defined when $\cos \theta = 0$, and $\cot \theta$ is not defined when $\sin \theta = 0$.

title: Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
theorem_text: $\sec \theta = \dfrac 1 {\cos \theta}$
proof_text:
Let a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be placed in a cartesian plane with origin $O$ such that $OP$ forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis.
Then:
$$\sec \theta = \frac r x$$
Secant of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$$= \frac 1 {x / r}$$
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \theta}$$
Cosine of Angle in Cartesian Plane
When $\cos \theta = 0$, $\dfrac 1 {\cos \theta}$ is not defined.

title: Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
theorem_text: $\csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$
proof_text:
Let a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be placed in a cartesian plane with origin $O$ such that $OP$ forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis.
Then:
$$\csc \theta = \frac r y$$
Cosecant of Angle in Cartesian Plane
$$= \frac 1 {y / r}$$
$$= \frac 1 {\sin \theta}$$
Sine of Angle in Cartesian Plane
When $\sin \theta = 0$, $\dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$ is not defined.

title: Half Angle Formulas/Tangent/Corollary 3
theorem_text: $\tan \dfrac \theta 2 = \csc \theta - \cot \theta$
proof_text:
$$\tan \frac \theta 2 = \frac {1 - \cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$$
Half Angle Formula for Tangent: Corollary 2
$$= \frac 1 {\sin \theta} - \frac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$$
$$= \csc \theta - \cot \theta$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine and Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
When $\theta = k \pi$, both $\cot \theta$ and $\csc \theta$ are undefined.

title: Sine of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\sin 15 \degrees = \sin \dfrac \pi {12} = \dfrac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4$
proof_text:
$$\sin 15^\circ = \sin \frac {30^\circ} 2$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {1 - \cos 30^\circ} 2}$$
Half Angle Formula for Sine: $\theta$ is in Quadrant I
$$= \sqrt {\frac {1 - \frac {\sqrt 3} 2} 2}$$
Cosine of $30^\circ$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {2 - \sqrt 3} 4}$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {8 - 4 \sqrt 3} {16} }$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {6 + 2 - 2 \sqrt 2 \sqrt 6} {16} }$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right)^2} {16} }$$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4$$
positive because $\theta$ is in the first quadrant

title: Sine of 45 Degrees
theorem_text: $\sin 45 \degrees = \sin \dfrac \pi 4 = \dfrac {\sqrt 2} 2$
proof_text:
$$\sin 45 \degrees = \map \sin {60 \degrees - 15 \degrees}$$
$$= \sin 60 \degrees \cos 15 \degrees - \cos 60 \degrees \sin 15 \degrees$$
Sine of Difference
$$= \paren {\frac {\sqrt 3} 2} \paren {\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4} - \paren {\frac 1 2} \paren {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Sine of $60 \degrees$, Cosine of $15 \degrees$, Cosine of $60 \degrees$, Sine of $15 \degrees$
$$= \frac 1 8 \paren {\sqrt 3 \paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} - \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} }$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 8 \paren {3 \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 8 \paren {3 \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 8 \paren {4 \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\sqrt 2} 2$$

title: Sine of Right Angle
theorem_text: $\sin 90^\circ = \sin \dfrac \pi 2 = 1$
proof_text:
A direct implementation of Sine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi:
$\forall n \in \Z: \sin \left({n + \dfrac 1 2}\right) \pi = \left({-1}\right)^n$
In this case, $n = 0$ and so:
$\sin \dfrac 1 2 \pi = \left({-1}\right)^0 = 1$

title: Cosine of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cos 15 \degrees = \cos \dfrac \pi {12} = \dfrac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4$
proof_text:
$$\cos 15^\circ = \cos \frac {30 \degrees} 2$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {1 + \cos 30 \degrees} 2}$$
Half Angle Formula for Cosine: $\theta$ is in Quadrant I
$$= \sqrt {\frac {1 + \frac {\sqrt 3} 2} 2}$$
Cosine of $30 \degrees$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {2 + \sqrt 3} 4}$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {8 + 4 \sqrt 3} {16} }$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {6 + 2 + 2 \sqrt 2 \sqrt 6} {16} }$$
$$= \sqrt {\frac {\paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}^2} {16} }$$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4$$
positive because $\theta$ is in the first quadrant

title: Cosine of Right Angle
theorem_text: $\cos 90^\circ = \cos \dfrac \pi 2 = 0$
proof_text:
A direct implementation of Cosine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi:
$\forall n \in \Z: \cos \left({n + \dfrac 1 2}\right) \pi = 0$
In this case, $n = 0$ and so:
$\cos \dfrac 1 2 \pi = 0$

title: Tangent of Zero
proof_text:
$$\tan 0 = \frac {\sin 0} {\cos 0}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac 0 1$$
Sine of Zero is Zero and Cosine of Zero is One
$$= 0$$

title: Tangent of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 15^\circ = \tan \dfrac {\pi} {12} = 2 - \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 15^\circ = \tan \frac {30^\circ} 2$$
$$= \frac {\sin 30^\circ} {1 + \cos 30^\circ}$$
Half Angle Formula for Tangent: Corollary 1
$$= \frac {\frac 1 2} {1 + \frac {\sqrt 3} 2}$$
Sine of $30^\circ$ and Cosine of $30^\circ$
$$= \frac {\frac 1 2} {\frac {2 + \sqrt 3} 2}$$
$$= \frac 1 {2 + \sqrt 3}$$
$$= \frac {2 - \sqrt 3} {\left({2 + \sqrt 3}\right) \left({2 - \sqrt 3}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2 - \sqrt 3$
$$= \frac {2 - \sqrt 3} {4 - 3}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= 2 - \sqrt 3$$

title: Tangent of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 15^\circ = \tan \dfrac {\pi} {12} = 2 - \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 15 \degrees = \tan \frac {30 \degrees} 2$$
$$= \frac {1 - \cos 30 \degrees} {\sin 30 \degrees}$$
Half Angle Formula for Tangent: Corollary 2
$$= \frac {1 - \frac {\sqrt 3} 2} {\frac 1 2}$$
Cosine of $30 \degrees$ and Sine of $30 \degrees$
$$= 2 - \sqrt 3$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2$

title: Tangent of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 15^\circ = \tan \dfrac {\pi} {12} = 2 - \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 15^\circ = \tan \frac {30^\circ} 2$$
$$= \frac {\sin 15^\circ} {\cos 15^\circ}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4} {\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Sine of $15^\circ$ and Cosine of $15^\circ$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right)^2} {\left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right) \left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {6 - 2 \sqrt 6 \sqrt 2 + 2 } {6 - 2}$$
multiplying out, and Difference of Two Squares
$$= \frac {8 - 4 \sqrt 3} 4$$
simplifying
$$= 2 - \sqrt 3$$
dividing top and bottom by $4$

title: Tangent of 30 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 30^\circ = \tan \dfrac \pi 6 = \dfrac {\sqrt 3} 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 30^\circ = \frac {\sin 30^\circ} {\cos 30^\circ}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac 1 2} {\frac {\sqrt 3} 2}$$
Sine of 30 Degrees and Cosine of 30 Degrees
$$= \frac 1 {\sqrt 3}$$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 3} 3$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 3$

title: Tangent of 45 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 45 \degrees = \tan \dfrac \pi 4 = 1$
proof_text:
$$\tan 45 \degrees = \frac {\sin 45 \degrees} {\cos 45 \degrees}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 2} 2} {\frac {\sqrt 2} 2}$$
Sine of $45 \degrees$ and Cosine of $45 \degrees$
$$= 1$$
dividing top and bottom by $\sqrt 2 / 2$

title: Tangent of 60 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 60^\circ = \tan \dfrac \pi 3 = \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 60^\circ = \frac {\sin 60^\circ} {\cos 60^\circ}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 3} 2} {\frac 1 2}$$
Sine of 60 Degrees and Cosine of 60 Degrees
$$= \sqrt 3$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2$

title: Tangent of 75 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 75^\circ = \tan \dfrac {5 \pi} {12} = 2 + \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\tan 75^\circ = \frac {\sin 75^\circ} {\cos 75^\circ}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4} {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Sine of 75 Degrees and Cosine of 75 Degrees
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)^2} {\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right) \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {6 + 2 \sqrt 6 \sqrt 2 + 2} {6 - 2}$$
multiplying out, and Difference of Two Squares
$$= \frac {8 + 4 \sqrt 3} 4$$
simplifying
$$= 2 + \sqrt 3$$
dividing top and bottom by $4$

title: Tangent of Complement equals Cotangent
theorem_text:
$\map \tan {\dfrac \pi 2 - \theta} = \cot \theta$ for $\theta \ne n \pi$
where $\tan$ and $\cot$ are tangent and cotangent respectively.
That is, the cotangent of an angle is the tangent of its complement.
This relation is defined wherever $\sin \theta \ne 0$.
proof_text:
$$\map \tan {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} = \frac {\map \sin {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} } {\map \cos {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} }$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$$
Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
$$= \cot \theta$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
The above is valid only where $\sin \theta \ne 0$, as otherwise $\dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$ is undefined.
From Sine of Multiple of Pi it follows that this happens when $\theta \ne n \pi$.

title: Cotangent of Complement equals Tangent
theorem_text:
$\cot \left({\dfrac \pi 2 - \theta}\right) = \tan \theta$ for $\theta \ne \left({2 n + 1}\right) \dfrac \pi 2$
where $\cot$ and $\tan$ are cotangent and tangent respectively.
That is, the tangent of an angle is the cotangent of its complement.
This relation is defined wherever $\cos \theta \ne 0$.
proof_text:
$$\cot \left({\frac \pi 2 - \theta}\right) = \frac {\cos \left({\frac \pi 2 - \theta}\right)} {\sin \left({\frac \pi 2 - \theta}\right)}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$$
Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
$$= \tan \theta$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
The above is valid only where $\cos \theta \ne 0$, as otherwise $\dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$ is undefined.
From Cosine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi it follows that this happens when $\theta \ne \left({2 n + 1}\right) \dfrac \pi 2$.

title: Tangent of Angle plus Right Angle
theorem_text: $\tan \left({x + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = -\cot x$
proof_text:
$$\tan \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right) = \frac {\sin \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)} {\cos \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\cos x} {- \sin x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Right Angle and Cosine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= -\cot x$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Cotangent of Angle plus Right Angle
theorem_text: $\cot \left({x + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = -\tan x$
proof_text:
$$\cot \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right) = \frac {\cos \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)}  {\sin \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {- \sin x} {\cos x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Right Angle and Sine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= -\tan x$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Tangent of Supplementary Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \tan {\pi - \theta} = -\tan \theta$
where $\tan$ denotes tangent.
That is, the tangent of an angle is the negative of its supplement.
proof_text:
$$\map \tan {\pi - \theta} = \frac {\map \sin {\pi - \theta} } {\map \cos {\pi - \theta} }$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\sin \theta} {-\cos \theta}$$
Sine of Supplementary Angle and Cosine of Supplementary Angle
$$= -\tan \theta$$

title: Cotangent of Supplementary Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \cot {\pi - \theta} = -\cot \theta$
where $\cot$ denotes tangent.
That is, the cotangent of an angle is the negative of its supplement.
proof_text:
$$\map \cot {\pi - \theta} = \frac {\map \cos {\pi - \theta} } {\map \sin {\pi - \theta} }$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {-\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$$
Cosine of Supplementary Angle and Sine of Supplementary Angle
$$= -\cot \theta$$

title: Tangent of Conjugate Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \tan {2 \pi - \theta} = -\tan \theta$
where $\tan$ denotes tangent.
That is, the tangent of an angle is the negative of its conjugate.
proof_text:
$$\map \tan {2 \pi - \theta} = \frac {\map \sin {2 \pi - \theta} } {\map \cos {2 \pi - \theta} }$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {-\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$$
Sine of Conjugate Angle and Cosine of Conjugate Angle
$$= -\tan \theta$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Cotangent of Conjugate Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \cot {2 \pi - \theta} = -\cot \theta$
where $\cot$ denotes cotangent.
That is, the cotangent of an angle is the negative of its conjugate.
proof_text:
$$\map \cot {2 \pi - \theta} = \frac {\map \cos {2 \pi - \theta} } {\map \sin {2 \pi - \theta} }$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\cos \theta} {-\sin \theta}$$
Cosine of Conjugate Angle and Sine of Conjugate Angle
$$= -\cot \theta$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Tangent of Right Angle
theorem_text: $\tan 90^\circ = \tan \dfrac \pi 2$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine, $\tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$.
When $\cos \theta = 0$, $\dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta}$ can be defined only if $\sin \theta = 0$.
But there are no such $\theta$ such that both $\cos \theta = 0$ and $\sin \theta = 0$.
When $\theta = \dfrac \pi 2$, $\cos \theta = 0$.
Thus $\tan \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Tangent of Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\tan 180^\circ = \tan \pi = 0$
proof_text:
$$\tan 180^\circ = \frac {\sin 180^\circ} {\cos 180^\circ}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac 0 {-1}$$
Sine of Straight Angle and Cosine of Straight Angle
$$= 0$$

title: Tangent of Three Right Angles
theorem_text: $\tan 270^\circ = \tan \dfrac {3 \pi} 2$ is undefined
proof_text:
We have:
$$\tan 270^\circ = \tan \left({360^\circ - 90^\circ}\right)$$
$$= -\tan 90^\circ$$
Tangent of Conjugate Angle
But from Tangent of Right Angle, $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined.
Hence so is $\tan 270^\circ$.

title: Cotangent of Zero
theorem_text: $\cot 0$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine:
$\cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$
When $\sin \theta = 0$, $\dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$ can be defined only if $\cos \theta = 0$.
But there are no such $\theta$ such that both $\cos \theta = 0$ and $\sin \theta = 0$.
When $\theta = 0$, $\sin \theta = 0$.
Thus $\cot \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Cotangent of 30 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cot 30^\circ = \cot \dfrac {\pi} 6 = \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\cot 30^\circ = \frac {\cos 30^\circ} {\sin 30^\circ}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac{\frac {\sqrt 3} 2} {\frac 1 2}$$
Cosine of $30^\circ$ and Sine of $30^\circ$
$$= \sqrt 3$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2$

title: Cotangent of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cot 15^\circ = \cot \dfrac {\pi} {12} = 2 + \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\cot 15^\circ = \frac {\cos 15^\circ} {\sin 15^\circ}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac{\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4} {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Cosine of 15 Degrees and Sine of 15 Degrees
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)^2} {\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right) \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {6 + 2 \sqrt 6 \sqrt 2 + 2 } {6 - 2}$$
multiplying out, and Difference of Two Squares
$$= \frac {8 + 4 \sqrt 3} 4$$
simplifying
$$= 2 + \sqrt 3$$
dividing top and bottom by $4$

title: Cotangent of 45 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cot 45 \degrees = \cot \dfrac \pi 4 = 1$
proof_text:
$$\cot 45 \degrees = \frac {\cos 45 \degrees} {\sin 45 \degrees}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 2} 2} {\frac {\sqrt 2} 2}$$
Cosine of $45 \degrees$ and Sine of $45 \degrees$
$$= 1$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\dfrac {\sqrt 2} 2$

title: Cotangent of 60 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cot 60^\circ = \cot \dfrac {\pi} 3 = \dfrac {\sqrt 3} 3$
proof_text:
$$\cot 60^\circ = \frac {\cos 60^\circ} {\sin 60^\circ}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac{\frac 1 2} {\frac {\sqrt 3} 2}$$
Cosine of $60^\circ$ and Sine of $60^\circ$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 3} 3$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2 \sqrt 3$

title: Cotangent of 75 Degrees
theorem_text: $\cot 75 \degrees = \cot \dfrac {5 \pi} {12} = 2 - \sqrt 3$
proof_text:
$$\cot 75 \degrees = \frac {\cos 75 \degrees} {\sin 75 \degrees}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4} {\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Cosine of $75 \degrees$ and Sine of $75 \degrees$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}^2} {\paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {6 - 2 \sqrt 6 \sqrt 2 + 2} {6 - 2}$$
multiplying out, and Difference of Two Squares
$$= \frac {8 - 4 \sqrt 3} 4$$
simplifying
$$= 2 - \sqrt 3$$
dividing top and bottom by $4$

title: Cotangent of Right Angle
theorem_text: $\cot 90^\circ = \cot \dfrac \pi 2 = 0$
proof_text:
$$\cot 90^\circ = \frac {\cos 90^\circ} {\sin 90^\circ}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac 0 1$$
Cosine of Right Angle and Sine of Right Angle
$$= 0$$

title: Cotangent of Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\cot 180^\circ = \cot \pi$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine:
$\cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$
When $\sin \theta = 0$, $\dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$ can be defined only if $\cos \theta = 0$.
But there are no such $\theta$ such that both $\cos \theta = 0$ and $\sin \theta = 0$.
When $\theta = \pi$, $\sin \theta = 0$.
Thus $\cot \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Cotangent of Full Angle
theorem_text: $\cot 360^\circ = \cot 2 \pi$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine:
$\cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}$
From Cosine of Full Angle:
$\cos 2 \pi = 1$
From Sine of Full Angle:
$\sin 2 \pi = 0$
Thus $\cot \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Secant of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\sec 15 \degrees = \sec \dfrac \pi {12} = \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
proof_text:
$$\sec 15 \degrees = \frac 1 {\cos 15 \degrees}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 4 {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}$$
Cosine of $15 \degrees$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} } {\paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} } {6 - 2}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$$
simplifying

title: Secant of 75 Degrees
theorem_text: $\sec 75 \degrees = \sec \dfrac {5 \pi} {12} = \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
proof_text:
$$\sec 75 \degrees = \frac 1 {\cos 75 \degrees}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Cosine of $75 \degrees$
$$= \frac 4 {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $4$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} } {\paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} \paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} } {6 - 2}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$$
simplifying

title: Secant of Right Angle
theorem_text: $\sec 90 \degrees = \sec \dfrac \pi 2$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine:
$\sec \theta = \dfrac 1 {\cos \theta}$
From Cosine of Right Angle:
$\cos \dfrac \pi 2 = 0$
Thus $\sec \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Secant of Angle plus Right Angle
theorem_text: $\sec \left({x + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = -\csc x$
proof_text:
$$\sec \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right) = \frac 1 {\cos \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {- \sin x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= -\csc x$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Cosecant of Angle plus Right Angle
theorem_text: $\csc \left({x + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = \sec x$
proof_text:
$$\csc \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right) = \frac 1 {\sin \left({x + \frac \pi 2}\right)}$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\cos x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= \sec x$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine

title: Secant of Complement equals Cosecant
theorem_text:
$\map \sec {\dfrac \pi 2 - \theta} = \csc \theta$ for $\theta \ne n \pi$
where $\sec$ and $\csc$ are secant and cosecant respectively.
That is, the cosecant of an angle is the secant of its complement.
This relation is defined wherever $\sin \theta \ne 0$.
proof_text:
$$\map \sec {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} = \frac 1 {\map \cos {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} }$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\sin \theta}$$
Cosine of Complement equals Sine
$$= \csc \theta$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
The above is valid only where $\sin \theta \ne 0$, as otherwise $\dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$ is undefined.
From Sine of Multiple of Pi it follows that this happens when $\theta \ne n \pi$.

title: Cosecant of Complement equals Secant
theorem_text:
$\map \csc {\dfrac \pi 2 - \theta} = \sec \theta$ for $\theta \ne \paren {2 n + 1} \dfrac \pi 2$
where $\csc$ and $\sec$ are cosecant and secant respectively.
That is, the secant of an angle is the cosecant of its complement.
This relation is defined wherever $\cos \theta \ne 0$.
proof_text:
$$\map \csc {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} = \frac 1 {\map \sin {\frac \pi 2 - \theta} }$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \theta}$$
Sine of Complement equals Cosine
$$= \sec \theta$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
The above is valid only where $\cos \theta \ne 0$, as otherwise $\dfrac 1 {\cos \theta}$ is undefined.
From Cosine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi it follows that this happens when $\theta \ne \paren {2 n + 1} \dfrac \pi 2$.

title: Cosecant of Conjugate Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \csc {2 \pi - \theta} = -\csc \theta$
where $\csc$ denotes cosecant.
That is, the cosecant of an angle is the negative of its conjugate.
proof_text:
$$\map \csc {2 \pi - \theta} = \frac 1 {\map \sin {2 \pi - \theta} }$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {-\sin \theta}$$
Cosine of Conjugate Angle and Sine of Conjugate Angle
$$= -\csc \theta$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Cosecant of Zero
theorem_text: $\csc 0$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine:
$\csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$
From Sine of Zero is Zero:
$\sin 0 = 0$
Thus $\csc \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Cosecant of 15 Degrees
theorem_text: $\csc 15^\circ = \csc \dfrac \pi {12} = \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
proof_text:
$$\csc 15^\circ = \frac 1 {\sin 15^\circ}$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\frac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Sine of 15 Degrees
$$= \frac 4 {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $4$
$$= \frac {4 \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)} {\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right) \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {4 \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right)} {6 - 2}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2$$
simplifying

title: Cosecant of 75 Degrees
theorem_text: $\csc 75 \degrees = \csc \dfrac {5 \pi} {12} = \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
proof_text:
$$\csc 75^\circ = \frac 1 {\sin 75 \degrees}$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\frac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4}$$
Sine of $75 \degrees$
$$= \frac 4 {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $4$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} } {\paren {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {4 \paren {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} } {6 - 2}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2$$
simplifying

title: Cosecant of Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\csc 180^\circ = \csc \pi$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine:
$\csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$
From Sine of Straight Angle:
$\sin \pi = 0$
Thus $\csc \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Cosecant of Full Angle
theorem_text: $\csc 360 \degrees = \csc 2 \pi$ is undefined
proof_text:
From Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine:
$\csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}$
From Sine of Full Angle:
$\sin 360 \degrees = 0$
Thus $\csc \theta$ is undefined at this value.

title: Cotangent Function is Odd
theorem_text:
$\map \cot {-x} = -\cot x$
That is, the cotangent function is odd.
proof_text:
$$\map \cot {-x} = \frac {\map \cos {-x} } {\map \sin {-x} }$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {-\sin x} {\cos x}$$
Cosine Function is Even and Sine Function is Odd
$$= -\cot x$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Tangent of Angle plus Full Angle
theorem_text: $\tan \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \tan x$
proof_text:
$$\tan \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \frac {\sin \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)} {\cos \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\sin x} {\cos x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Full Angle and Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle
$$= \tan x$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Tangent of Angle plus Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\tan \left({x + \pi}\right) = \tan x$
proof_text:
$$\tan \left({x + \pi}\right) = \frac {\sin \left({x + \pi}\right)} {\cos \left({x + \pi}\right)}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {-\sin x} {-\cos x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Straight Angle and Cosine of Angle plus Straight Angle
$$= \tan x$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Cotangent of Angle plus Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\map \cot {x + \pi} = \cot x$
proof_text:
$$\map \cot {x + \pi} = \frac {\map \cos {x + \pi} } {\map \sin {x + \pi} }$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {-\cos x} {-\sin x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Straight Angle and Sine of Angle plus Straight Angle
$$= \cot x$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Secant of Angle plus Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\map \sec {x + \pi} = -\sec x$
proof_text:
$$\map \sec {x + \pi} = \frac 1 {\map \cos {x + \pi} }$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {-\cos x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Straight Angle
$$= -\sec x$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine

title: Cosecant of Angle plus Straight Angle
theorem_text: $\map \csc {x + \pi} = -\csc x$
proof_text:
$$\map \csc {x + \pi} = \frac 1 {\map \sin {x + \pi} }$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {-\sin x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Straight Angle
$$= -\csc x$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Cotangent of Angle plus Full Angle
theorem_text: $\cot \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \cot x$
proof_text:
$$\cot \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \frac {\cos \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)} {\sin \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)}$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\cos x} {\sin x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle and Sine of Angle plus Full Angle
$$= \cot x$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Secant of Angle plus Full Angle
theorem_text: $\sec \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \sec x$
proof_text:
$$\sec \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \frac 1 {\cos \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\cos x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle
$$= \sec x$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine

title: Cosecant of Angle plus Full Angle
theorem_text: $\csc \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \csc x$
proof_text:
$$\csc \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \frac 1 {\sin \left({x + 2 \pi}\right)}$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\sin x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Straight Angle
$$= \csc x$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Tangent of Angle plus Three Right Angles
theorem_text: $\map \tan {x + \dfrac {3 \pi} 2} = -\cot x$
proof_text:
$$\map \tan {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} = \frac {\map \sin {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} } {\map \cos {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} }$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {-\cos x} {\sin x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Three Right Angles and Cosine of Angle plus Three Right Angles
$$= -\cot x$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine

title: Cotangent of Angle plus Three Right Angles
theorem_text: $\map \cot {x + \dfrac {3 \pi} 2} = -\tan x$
proof_text:
$$\map \cot {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} = \frac {\map \cos {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} } {\map \sin {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} }$$
Cotangent is Cosine divided by Sine
$$= \frac {\sin x} {-\cos x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Right Angle and Sine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= -\tan x$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Secant of Angle plus Three Right Angles
theorem_text: $\map \sec {x + \dfrac {3 \pi} 2} = \csc x$
proof_text:
$$\map \sec {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} = \frac 1 {\map \cos {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} }$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\sin x}$$
Cosine of Angle plus Three Right Angles
$$= \csc x$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Cosecant of Angle plus Three Right Angles
theorem_text: $\map \csc {x + \dfrac {3 \pi} 2} = -\sec x$
proof_text:
$$\map \csc {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} = \frac 1 {\map \sin {x + \frac {3 \pi} 2} }$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {-\cos x}$$
Sine of Angle plus Three Right Angles
$$= -\sec x$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine

title: Secant of Three Right Angles less Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \sec {\dfrac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} = -\csc \theta$
where $\sec$ and $\csc$ are secant and cosecant respectively.
proof_text:
$$\map \sec {\frac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} = \frac 1 {\map \cos {\frac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} }$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {-\sin \theta}$$
Cosine of Three Right Angles less Angle
$$= -\csc \theta$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine

title: Cosecant of Three Right Angles less Angle
theorem_text:
$\map \csc {\dfrac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} = -\sec \theta$
where $\csc$ and $\sec$ are cosecant and secant respectively.
proof_text:
$$\map \csc {\frac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} = \frac 1 {\map \sin {\frac {3 \pi} 2 - \theta} }$$
Cosecant is Reciprocal of Sine
$$= \frac 1 {-\cos \theta}$$
Sine of Three Right Angles less Angle
$$= -\sec \theta$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine

title: Quadruple Angle Formulas/Tangent
theorem_text: $\tan 4 \theta = \dfrac {4 \tan \theta - 4 \tan^3 \theta} {1 - 6 \tan^2 \theta + \tan^4 \theta}$
proof_text:
$$\tan 4 \theta = \frac {\sin 4 \theta} {\cos 4 \theta}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {4 \sin \theta \cos \theta - 8 \sin^3 \theta \cos \theta} {8 \cos^4 \theta - 8 \cos^2 \theta + 1}$$
Quadruple Angle Formula for Sine and Quadruple Angle Formula for Cosine
$$= \frac {4 \frac {\tan \theta} {\cos^2 \theta} - 8 \tan^3 \theta} {8 - \frac 8 {\cos^2 \theta} + \frac 1 {\cos^4 \theta} }$$
dividing top and bottom by $\cos^4 \theta$
$$= \frac {4 \tan \theta \sec^2 \theta - 8 \tan^3 \theta} {8 - 8 \sec^2 \theta + \sec^4 \theta}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac {4 \tan \theta \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta} - 8 \tan^3 \theta} {8 - 8 \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta} + \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta}^2}$$
Difference of Squares of Secant and Tangent
$$= \frac {4 \tan \theta - 4 \tan^3 \theta} {1 - 6 \tan^2 \theta + \tan^4 \theta}$$
multiplying out and gathering terms

title: Quintuple Angle Formulas/Tangent
theorem_text: $\tan 5 \theta = \dfrac {\tan^5 \theta - 10 \tan^3 \theta + 5 \tan \theta} {1 - 10 \tan^2 \theta + 5 \tan^4 \theta}$
proof_text:
$$\tan 5 \theta = \frac {\sin 5 \theta} {\cos 5 \theta}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {5 \sin \theta - 20 \sin^3 \theta + 16 \sin^5 \theta} {16 \cos^5 \theta - 20 \cos^3 \theta + 5 \cos \theta}$$
Quintuple Angle Formulas
$$= \frac {5 \frac {\tan \theta} {\cos^4 \theta} - 20 \frac {\tan^3 \theta} {\cos^2 \theta} + 16 \tan^5 \theta} {16 \cos \theta - \frac {20} {\cos^2 \theta} + \frac 5 {\cos^4 \theta} }$$
dividing top and bottom by $\cos^5 \theta$
$$= \frac {5 \tan \theta \sec^4 \theta - 20 \tan^3 \theta \sec^2 \theta + 16 \tan^5 \theta} {16 - 20 \sec^2 \theta + 5 \sec^4 \theta}$$
Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine
$$= \frac {5 \tan \theta \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta}^2 - 20 \tan^3 \theta \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta} + 16 \tan^5 \theta} {16 - 20 \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta} + 5 \paren {1 + \tan^2 \theta}^2}$$
Difference of Squares of Secant and Tangent
$$= \frac {\tan^5 \theta - 10 \tan^3 \theta + 5 \tan \theta} {1 - 10 \tan^2 \theta + 5 \tan^4 \theta}$$
multiplying out and gathering terms

title: Power Reduction Formulas/Tangent Squared
theorem_text: $\tan^2x = \dfrac {1 - \cos2x} {1 + \cos2x}$
proof_text:
$$\tan^2 x = \frac {\sin^2 x} {\cos^2 x}$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine
$$= \frac {\frac {1 - \cos 2 x} 2} {\frac {\cos 2 x + 1} 2}$$
Square of Sine and Square of Cosine
$$= \frac {1 - \cos 2 x} {1 + \cos 2 x}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2$

title: Orthocomplement of Subset of Orthocomplement is Superset
theorem_text:
Let $H$ be a Hilbert space.
Let $A, B \subseteq H$ be subsets of $H$ such that $B \subseteq A^\perp$, where $A^\perp$ is the orthocomplement of $A$.
Then $A \subseteq B^\perp$.
proof_text:
Let $B \subseteq A^\perp$.
Then by Orthocomplement Reverses Subset:
$A^{\perp\perp} \subseteq B^\perp$
By Double Orthocomplement is Closed Linear Span and the definition of closed linear span:
$A \subseteq A^{\perp\perp}$
Hence, by Subset Relation is Transitive:
$A \subseteq B^\perp$

title: Cosine to Power of Odd Integer
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \cos^{2n+1} \theta = \frac 1 {2^{2n}} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom {2n+1} k \cos \left({2n - 2k + 1}\right) \theta$
proof_text:
$$\cos^{2 n + 1} \theta = \paren {\frac {e^{i \theta} + e^{-i \theta} } 2}^{2 n + 1}$$
Cosine Exponential Formulation
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \paren {e^{i \theta} + e^{-i \theta} }^{2 n + 1}$$
Exponent Combination Laws: Power of Product
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \sum^{2 n + 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{k i \theta} e^{-\paren {2 n - k + 1} i \theta}$$
Binomial Theorem
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \sum^{2 n + 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta}$$
Exponential of Sum
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \paren {\sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta} + \sum^{2 n + 1}_{k \mathop = n + 1} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta} }$$
Partitioning the sum
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \paren {\sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta} + \sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} {2 n + 1 - k} e^{\paren {2 \paren {2 n - k + 1} - 2 n - 1} i \theta} }$$
$k \mapsto 2 n + 1 - k$
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n + 1} } \paren {\sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta} + \sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k e^{\paren {2 n - 2 k + 1} i \theta} }$$
Symmetry Rule for Binomial Coefficients
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \sum^n_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n + 1} k \, \map \cos {2 n - 2 k + 1} \theta$$
Cosine Exponential Formulation

title: Cosine to Power of Even Integer
theorem_text:
$$\cos^{2 n} \theta = \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n - 1} } \paren {\cos 2 n \theta + \binom {2 n} 1 \map \cos {2 n - 2} \theta + \cdots + \binom {2 n} {n - 1} \cos 2 \theta}$$
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n - 1} } \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom {2 n} k \map \cos {2 n - 2 k} \theta$$
proof_text:
$$\cos^{2 n} \theta = \paren {\frac {e^{i \theta} + e^{-i \theta} } 2}^{2 n}$$
Cosine Exponential Formulation
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \paren {e^{i \theta} + e^{-i \theta} }^{2 n}$$
Exponent Combination Laws: Power of Product
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \sum^{2 n}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom{2 n} k e^{k i \theta} e^{-\paren {2 n - k} i \theta}$$
Binomial Theorem
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \sum^{2 n}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom{2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta}$$
Exponential of Sum
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \paren {\sum^{n \mathop - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} + \binom {2 n} n e^{\paren {2 n - 2 n} i \theta} + \sum^{2 n}_{k \mathop = n + 1} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} }$$
partitioning the sum
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \paren {\sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} + \sum^{2 n}_{k \mathop = n + 1} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} }$$
Exponential of Zero
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \paren {\sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} + \sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} {2 n - k} e^{\paren {2 \paren {2 n - k} - 2 n} i \theta} }$$
$k \mapsto 2 n - k$
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \paren {\sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k e^{-\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} + \sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k e^{\paren {2 n - 2 k} i \theta} }$$
Symmetry Rule for Binomial Coefficients
$$= \frac 1 {2^{2 n} } \binom {2 n} n + \frac 1 {2^{2 n - 1} } \sum^{n - 1}_{k \mathop = 0} \binom {2 n} k \map \cos {2 n - 2 k} \theta$$
Cosine Exponential Formulation

title: Sum of Arctangent and Arccotangent
theorem_text:
Let $x \in \R$ be a real number.
Then:
$\arctan x + \operatorname{arccot} x = \dfrac \pi 2$
where $\arctan$ and $\operatorname{arccot}$ denote arctangent and arccotangent respectively.
proof_text:
Let $y \in \R$ such that:
$\exists x \in \R: x = \cot \left({y + \dfrac \pi 2}\right)$
Then:
$$x = \cot \left({y + \frac \pi 2}\right)$$
$$= -\tan y$$
Cotangent of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= \tan \left({-y}\right)$$
Tangent Function is Odd
Suppose $-\dfrac \pi 2 \le y \le \dfrac \pi 2$.
Then we can write $-y = \arctan x$.
But then $\cot \left({y + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = x$.
Now since $-\dfrac \pi 2 \le y \le \dfrac \pi 2$ it follows that $0 \le y + \dfrac \pi 2 \le \pi$.
Hence $y + \dfrac \pi 2 = \operatorname{arccot} x$.
That is, $\dfrac \pi 2 = \operatorname{arccot} x + \arctan x$.

title: Sine of Angle of Triangle by Semiperimeter
theorem_text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides $a, b, c$ are such that $a$ is opposite $A$, $b$ is opposite $B$ and $c$ is opposite $C$.
Then:
$\sin A = \dfrac 2 {b c} \sqrt {s \paren {s - a} \paren {s - b} \paren {s - c} }$
where $\sin$ denotes sine and $s$ is the semiperimeter: $s = \dfrac {a + b + c} 2$.
proof_text:
Let $Q$ be the area of $\triangle ABC$.
From Area of Triangle in Terms of Two Sides and Angle:
$Q = \dfrac {b c \sin A} 2$
From Heron's Formula:
$Q = \sqrt {s \paren {s - a} \paren {s - b} \paren {s - c} }$
Equating the two:
$\dfrac {b c \sin A} 2 = \sqrt {s \paren {s - a} \paren {s - b} \paren {s - c} }$
from which follows the result.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/Negation and Disjunction
theorem_text: $\set {\neg, \lor}$: Not and Or
proof_text:
From Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Conjunction, $\set {
eg, \land}$ is functionally complete.
That is: any expression can be expressed in terms of $
eg$ and $\land$.
From De Morgan's laws: Conjunction, we have that:
$p \land q \dashv \vdash 
eg \paren {
eg p \lor 
eg q}$
Thus all occurrences of $\land$ can be replaced by $\lor$ and $
eg$.
Thus any expression can be expressed in terms of $
eg$ and $\lor$.
That is: $\set {
eg, \lor}$ is functionally complete.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/Negation and Conjunction
theorem_text: $\set {\neg, \land}$: Not and And
proof_text:
From Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation, Conjunction, Disjunction and Implication, all sixteen of the binary truth functions can be expressed in terms of $
eg, \land, \lor, \implies$.
From Conjunction and Implication, we have that:
$p \implies q \dashv \vdash 
eg \paren {p \land 
eg q}$
From De Morgan's laws: Disjunction, we have that:
$p \lor q \dashv \vdash 
eg \paren {
eg p \land 
eg q}$
So any instance of either $\implies$ or $\lor$ can be replaced identically with one using just $
eg$ and $\land$.
It follows that $\set {
eg, \land}$ is functionally complete.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/Negation and Conditional
theorem_text: $\set {\neg, \implies}$: Not and Implies
proof_text:
From Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Conjunction, we can represent any boolean expression in terms of $\land$ and $
eg$.
From Conjunction and Implication, we have that:
$p \land q \dashv \vdash 
eg \paren {p \implies 
eg q}$
So it follows that we can replace all occurrences of $\land$ by $\implies$ and $
eg$.
Thus $\set {
eg, \implies}$ is functionally complete.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/Conjunction, Negation and Disjunction
theorem_text: $\set {\neg, \land, \lor}$: Not, And and Or
proof_text:
From the stronger results:
:Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Disjunction:
::the set of logical connectives: $\set {\neg, \lor}$ is functionally complete
:Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Conjunction:
::the set of logical connectives: $\set {\neg, \land}$ is functionally complete
it follows directly that $\set {\neg, \land, \lor}$ is likewise functionally complete.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/NAND
theorem_text: $\set {\uparrow}$: NAND
proof_text:
From Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Conjunction, any boolean expression can be expressed in terms of $\land$ and $\neg$.
From NAND with Equal Arguments:
$\neg p \dashv \vdash p \uparrow p$
From Conjunction in terms of NAND:
$p \land q \dashv \vdash \paren {p \uparrow q} \uparrow \paren {p \uparrow q}$
demonstrating that $p \land q$ is expressed solely in terms of $\uparrow$.
Thus any boolean expression can be represented solely in terms of $\uparrow$.
That is, $\set {\uparrow}$ is functionally complete.

title: Functionally Complete Logical Connectives/NOR
theorem_text: $\set {\downarrow}$: NOR
proof_text:
From Functionally Complete Logical Connectives: Negation and Disjunction, any boolean expression can be expressed in terms of $\lor$ and $\neg$.
From NOR with Equal Arguments:
$\neg p \dashv \vdash p \downarrow p$
From Disjunction in terms of NOR:
$p \lor q \dashv \vdash \paren {p \downarrow q} \downarrow \paren {p \downarrow q}$
demonstrating that $p \lor q$ can be represented solely in terms of $\downarrow$.
That is, $\set {\downarrow}$ is functionally complete.

title: NOR with Equal Arguments/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $\downarrow$ signify the NOR operation.
Then for any proposition $p$:
$p \downarrow p \dashv \vdash \neg p$
That is, the NOR of a proposition with itself corresponds to the negation operator.
proof_text:
Apply the Method of Truth Tables:
$\begin{array}{|ccc||cc|} \hline
p & \downarrow & p & \neg & p \\
\hline
F & T & F & T & F \\
T & F & T & F & T \\
\hline
\end{array}$
As can be seen by inspection, the truth values under the main connectives match for all boolean interpretations.

title: NAND with Equal Arguments/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $\uparrow$ signify the NAND operation.
Then, for any proposition $p$:
$p \uparrow p \dashv \vdash \neg p$
That is, the NAND of a proposition with itself corresponds to the negation operation.
proof_text:
We apply the Method of Truth Tables:
$\begin{array}{|ccc||cc|} \hline
p & \uparrow & p & \neg & p \\
\hline
F & T & F & T & F \\
T & F & T & F & T \\
\hline
\end{array}$
As can be seen by inspection, the truth values under the main connectives match for all boolean interpretations.

title: Conditional and Converse are not Equivalent
theorem_text:
A conditional statement:
$p \implies q$
is not logically equivalent to its converse:
$q \implies p$
proof_text:
We apply the Method of Truth Tables to the proposition:
$\paren {p \implies q} \iff \paren {q \implies p}$
$\begin{array}{|ccc|c|ccc|} \hline
p & \implies & q) & \iff & (q & \implies & p) \\
\hline
F & T & F & T & F & T & F \\
F & T & T & F & T & F & F \\
T & F & F & F & F & T & T \\
T & T & T & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
\end{array}$
As can be seen by inspection, the truth values under the main connectives do not match for all boolean interpretations.

title: NOR is Commutative/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $\downarrow$ signify the NOR operation.
Then, for any two propositions $p$ and $q$:
$p \downarrow q \dashv \vdash q \downarrow p$
That is, NOR is commutative.
proof_text:
Apply the Method of Truth Tables:
$\begin{array}{|ccc||ccc|} \hline
p & \downarrow & q & q & \downarrow & p \\
\hline
F & T & F & F & T & F \\
F & F & T & T & F & F \\
T & F & F & F & F & T \\
T & F & T & T & F & T \\
\hline
\end{array}$
As can be seen by inspection, the truth values under the main connectives match for all boolean interpretations.

title: NOR is not Associative/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $\downarrow$ signify the NOR operation.
Then there exist propositions $p, q, r$ such that:
$p \downarrow \paren {q \downarrow r} \not \vdash \paren {p \downarrow q} \downarrow r$
That is, NOR is not associative.
proof_text:
Apply the Method of Truth Tables:
$\begin{array}{|ccccc||ccccc|} \hline
p & \downarrow & (q & \downarrow & r) & (p & \downarrow & q) & \downarrow & r \\
\hline
F & F & F & T & F & F & T & F & F & F \\
F & T & F & F & T & F & T & F & F & T \\
F & T & T & F & F & F & F & T & T & F \\
F & T & T & F & T & F & F & T & F & T \\
T & F & F & T & F & T & F & F & T & F \\
T & F & F & F & T & T & F & F & F & T \\
T & F & T & F & F & T & F & T & T & F \\
T & F & T & F & T & T & F & T & F & T \\
\hline
\end{array}$
As can be seen by inspection, the truth values under the main connectives do not match for all boolean interpretations.

title: Implication in terms of NAND
theorem_text: $p \implies q \dashv \vdash p \uparrow \paren {q \uparrow q}$
proof_text:
$$p \implies q \dashv \vdash \neg \paren {p \land \neg q}$$
Implication Equivalent to Negation of Conjunction with Negative
$$\dashv \vdash p \uparrow \neg q$$
Definition of NAND
$$\dashv \vdash p \uparrow \paren {q \uparrow q}$$
NAND with Equal Arguments

title: Implication in terms of NAND
theorem_text: $p \implies q \dashv \vdash p \uparrow \paren {q \uparrow q}$
proof_text:
$$p \implies q \dashv \vdash \neg p \lor q$$
Rule of Material Implication
$$\dashv \vdash \neg p \lor \neg \neg q$$
Double Negation Introduction
$$\dashv \vdash p \uparrow \neg q$$
NAND as Disjunction of Negations
$$\dashv \vdash p \uparrow \left({q \uparrow q}\right)$$
NAND with Equal Arguments

title: Condition for Composite Mapping to be Identity
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ and $g: T \to S$ be mappings such that:
$g \circ f = I_S$
where $I_S$ is the identity mapping on $S$.
Then $f$ is an injection and $g$ is a surjection.
proof_text:
From Identity Mapping is Bijection, $I_S$ is a bijection.
From Identity Mapping is Injection, $I_S$ is an injection.
From Injection if Composite is Injection it follows that $f$ is an injection.
From Identity Mapping is Surjection, $I_S$ is a surjection.
From Surjection if Composite is Surjection it follows that $g$ is a surjection.

title: Surjection iff Right Inverse/Non-Uniqueness
theorem_text:
A right inverse of $f$ is in general not unique.
Uniqueness occurs if and only if $f$ is a bijection.
proof_text:
If $f$ is not an injection then:
$\exists y \in T: \exists x_1, x_2 \in S: \map f {x_1} = y = \map f {x_2}$
Hence we have more than one choice in $\map {f^{-1} } {\set y}$ for how to map $\map g y$.
That is, $\map g y$ is not unique.
This does not happen if and only if $f$ is an injection.
Hence the result.

title: Bernoulli's Inequality
theorem_text:
Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > -1$.
Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.
Then:
$\paren {1 + x}^n \ge 1 + n x$
proof_text:
Proof by induction:
For all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\paren {1 + x}^n \ge 1 + nx$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 0$ is the case:
$\paren {1 + x}^0 \ge 1$
so $\map P 0$ holds.
This is our basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 0$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
$\left({1 + x}\right)^k \ge 1 + kx$
We need to show that:
$\paren {1 + x}^{k + 1} \ge 1 + \paren {k + 1} x$
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
$$\paren {1 + x}^{k + 1} = \paren {1 + x}^k \paren {1 + x}$$
$$\ge \paren {1 + k x} \paren {1 + x}$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= 1 + \paren {k + 1} x + k x^2$$
$$\ge 1 + \paren {k + 1} x$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.

title: Bernoulli's Inequality
theorem_text:
Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > -1$.
Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.
Then:
$\paren {1 + x}^n \ge 1 + n x$
proof_text:
Let $y = 1 + x$.
Then $y \ge 0$, and:
$\paren {1 + x}^n = 1 + \paren {y^n - 1}$
If $y \ge 1$, then by Sum of Geometric Sequence:
$\displaystyle y^n - 1 = \paren {y - 1} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} y^k \ge n \paren {y - 1} = n x$
If $y < 1$, then by Sum of Geometric Sequence:
$\displaystyle y^n - 1 = -\paren {1 - y} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} y^k \ge -n \paren {1 - y} = n x$
Hence the result.

title: Categories of Elements of Ring
theorem_text:
Let $\left({R, +, \circ}\right)$ be a ring.
The elements of $R$ are partitioned into three classes:
$(1): \quad$ the zero
$(2): \quad$ the units
$(3): \quad$ the proper elements.
proof_text:
By definition, a proper element is a non-zero element which has no product inverse.
Also by definition, a unit is an element which does have a product inverse.
Because $0 \circ x = 0$ there can be no $x \in R$ such that $0 \times x = 1$, and so $0$ is not a unit.
Hence the result.

title: Multiple of Ring Product
theorem_text:
Let $\left({R, +, \circ}\right)$ be a ring.
Let $x, y \in \left({R, +, \circ}\right)$.
Then:
$\forall n \in \Z_{> 0}: \left({n \cdot x} \right) \circ y = n \cdot \left({x \circ y}\right) = x \circ \left({n \cdot y}\right)$
where $n \cdot x$ denotes the $n$th multiple of $x$.
proof_text:
By definition:
$\displaystyle n \cdot x := \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x$
Thus:
$$\left({n \cdot x} \right) \circ y = \left({\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x} \right) \circ y$$
by definition of integral multiple
(1) $$= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \left({x \circ y} \right)$$
General Distributivity Theorem
$$= n \cdot \left({x \circ y}\right)$$
by definition of integral multiple
$$= x \circ \left({\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n y} \right)$$
General Distributivity Theorem from $(1)$
$$= x \circ \left({n \cdot y}\right)$$
by definition of integral multiple

title: Power Set of Finite Set is Finite
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a finite set.
Then the power set of $S$ is likewise finite.
proof_text:
Let $S$ be a finite set.
Then by definition:
$\exists n \in \N: \card S = n$
where $\card S$ denotes the cardinality of $S$.
From Cardinality of Power Set of Finite Set:
$\card {\powerset S} = 2^n$
where $\powerset S$ denotes the power set of $S$.
As $n \in \N$ it follows that $2^n \in \N$ and so $\powerset S$ is also by definition a finite set.

title: Divisor Divides Multiple
theorem_text:
Let $a, b$ be integers.
Let:
$a \divides b$
where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Then:
$\forall c \in \Z: a \divides b c$
proof_text:
We have that Integers form Integral Domain.
The result then follows from Multiple of Divisor in Integral Domain Divides Multiple.

title: Divisor Divides Multiple
theorem_text:
Let $a, b$ be integers.
Let:
$a \divides b$
where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Then:
$\forall c \in \Z: a \divides b c$
proof_text:
By definition, if $a \divides b$ then $\exists d \in \Z: a d = b$.
Then:
$\paren {a d} c = b c$
that is:
$\paren {a c} d = b c$
which follows because Integer Multiplication is Commutative and Integer Multiplication is Associative.
Hence the result.

title: Divisor Divides Multiple
theorem_text:
Let $a, b$ be integers.
Let:
$a \divides b$
where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Then:
$\forall c \in \Z: a \divides b c$
proof_text:
Let $a \divides b$.
From Integer Divides Zero:
$a \divides 0$
Thus $a$ is a common divisor of $b$ and $0$.
From Common Divisor Divides Integer Combination:
$\forall p, q \in \Z: a \divides \paren {p \cdot b + q \cdot 0}$
Putting $p = c$ and $q = 1$ (for example):
$a \divides \paren {c b + 0}$
Hence the result.

title: Non-Zero Integer has Unique Positive Integer Associate
theorem_text:
Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \ne 0$.
Then $a$ has a unique associate $b \in \Z_{>0}$.
proof_text:
Let $a \in \Z_{\ne 0}$.
By Integer Divides its Absolute Value:
$a \divides \size a$ and $\size a \divides a$
Hence $\size a$ is an associate of $a$.
Now we prove its uniqueness.
Let $b, c \in \Z_{\ne 0}$ such that $b > 0$ and $c > 0$.
Let $a \sim b$ and $a \sim c$ where $\sim$ denotes the relation of associatehood.
By definition of associatehood:
$a \divides b$ and $b \divides a$
and:
$a \divides c$ and $c \divides a$
From Divisor Relation is Antisymmetric/Corollary/Proof 2:
$a = \pm b$
and
$a = \pm c$
That is:
$\pm b = \pm c$
which means:
$b = c$ or $b = -c$
But as both $b > 0$ and $c > 0$:
$b = c$
Hence the result.

title: Initial Part of String is Substring
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a string, and let $T$ be an initial part of $S$.
Then $T$ is a substring of $S$.
proof_text:
By definition of substring, there exists a string $T'$ such that:
$S = TT'$
Hence $S$ is the concatenation of the null string, $T$, and $T'$.
Thus by definition of substring, $T$ is a substring of $S$.

title: Prime iff Coprime to all Smaller Positive Integers
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number
Then:
$\forall x \in \Z, 0 < x < p: x \perp p$
That is, $p$ is relatively prime to all smaller (strictly) positive integers.
proof_text:
From Prime not Divisor implies Coprime, if $p$ does not divide an integer $x$, it is relatively prime to $x$.
From Absolute Value of Integer is not less than Divisors: Corollary, $p$ does not divide an integer smaller than $p$.
It follows that $p$ is relatively prime to all smaller (strictly) positive integers.
The special case when $x = 0$ is excluded as from Integers Coprime to Zero, $p$ is not relatively prime to $0$.

title: Division Theorem/Positive Divisor/Existence/Proof 2
theorem_text:
For every pair of integers $a, b$ where $b > 0$, there exist integers $q, r$ such that $a = q b + r$ and $0 \le r < b$:
$\forall a, b \in \Z, b > 0: \exists q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < b$
proof_text:
Let:
$q = \floor {\dfrac a b}, t = \dfrac a b - \floor {\dfrac a b}$
where $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function.
Thus $q \in \Z$ and $t \in \hointr 0 1$.
So:
$\dfrac a b = q + t$
and so:
$(1): \quad a = q b + r$
where $r = t d$.
Since $a, q, b \in \Z$, it follows from $(1)$ that:
$r = a - q b$
and so $r \in \Z$ also.
Since $0 \le t < 1$ and $b > 0$, it follows that:
$0 \le t b < b$
that is:
$0 \le r < b$

title: Division Theorem/Positive Divisor/Uniqueness/Proof 2
theorem_text:
For every pair of integers $a, b$ where $b > 0$, the integers $q, r$ such that $a = q b + r$ and $0 \le r < b$ are unique:
$\forall a, b \in \Z, b > 0: \exists! q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < b$
proof_text:
It is given by Division Theorem: Positive Divisor: Existence that such $q$ and $r$ exist.
Let $a = q b + r$ where $q, r \in \Z$ and $0 \le r < b$.
Thus:
$\dfrac a b = q + \dfrac r b$
and:
$0 \le \dfrac r b \le \dfrac {b - 1} b < 1$
So:
$q = \floor {\dfrac a b}$
and so:
$r = a - b \floor {\dfrac a b}$
Thus, given $a$ and $b$, the numbers $q$ and $r$ are unique determined.

title: Division Theorem/Positive Divisor/Existence/Proof 3
theorem_text:
For every pair of integers $a, b$ where $b > 0$, there exist integers $q, r$ such that $a = q b + r$ and $0 \le r < b$:
