$$= \frac 1 2 \int \map \cosh {a + p} x \rd x + \frac 1 2 \int \map \cosh {a - p} x \rd x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \frac {\map \sinh {a + p} x} {a + p} + \frac 1 2 \frac {\map \sinh {a - p} x} {a - p} + C$$
Primitive of $\cosh a x$
$$= \frac {\map \sinh {a + p} x} {2 \paren {a + p} } + \frac {\map \sinh {a - p} x} {2 \paren {a - p} } + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Sine of p x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \cosh a x \sin p x - p \sinh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \int \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{- a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int e^{a x} \sin p x \ \mathrm d x - \frac 1 2 \int e^{- a x} \sin p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{a x} \left({a \sin p x - p \cos p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) - \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{-a x} \left({-a \sin p x - p \cos p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + C$$
Primitive of $e^{a x} \sin b x$
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x - p \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x}\right) + C$$
factoring
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \cosh a x \sin p x - p \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \cosh a x \sin p x - p \sinh a x \cos p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac {a \cosh a x \sin p x - p \sinh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Cosine of p x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \cosh a x \cos p x + p \sinh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \int \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{- a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int e^{a x} \cos p x \ \mathrm d x - \frac 1 2 \int e^{- a x} \cos p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{a x} \left({a \cos p x + p \sin p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) - \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{-a x} \left({-a \cos p x + p \sin p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + C$$
Primitive of $e^{a x} \cos b x$
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x + p \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x}\right) + C$$
factoring
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \cosh a x \cos p x + p \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \cosh a x \cos p x + p \sinh a x \sin p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac {a \cosh a x \cos p x + p \sinh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x by Sine of p x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \cosh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \sinh a x \sin p x - p \cosh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \cosh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \int \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{- a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int e^{a x} \sin p x \ \mathrm d x + \frac 1 2 \int e^{- a x} \sin p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{a x} \left({a \sin p x - p \cos p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{-a x} \left({-a \sin p x - p \cos p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + C$$
Primitive of $e^{a x} \sin b x$
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x - p \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x}\right) + C$$
factoring
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \sinh a x \sin p x - p \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \sinh a x \sin p x - p \cosh a x \cos p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac {a \sinh a x \sin p x - p \cosh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x by Cosine of p x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \cosh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \sinh a x \cos p x + p \cosh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \cosh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \int \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{- a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int e^{a x} \cos p x \ \mathrm d x + \frac 1 2 \int e^{- a x} \cos p x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{a x} \left({a \cos p x + p \sin p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + \frac 1 2 \left({\frac {e^{-a x} \left({-a \cos p x + p \sin p x}\right)} {a^2 + p^2} }\right) + C$$
Primitive of $e^{a x} \cos b x$
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \left({\frac {e^{a x} - e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \cos p x + p \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x}\right) + C$$
factoring
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \sinh a x \cos p x + p \left({\frac {e^{a x} + e^{-a x} } 2}\right) \sin p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 {\left({a^2 + p^2}\right)} \left({a \sinh a x \cos p x + p \cosh a x \sin p x}\right) + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac {a \sinh a x \cos p x + p \cosh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of q plus p by Hyperbolic Secant of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x} = \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \cosh a x} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x} = \frac 1 q \int \frac {q \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $q$
$$= \frac 1 q \int \frac {\left({q + p \operatorname{sech} a x - p \operatorname{sech} a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x}$$
$$= \frac 1 q \int \frac {\left({q + p \operatorname{sech} a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x} - \frac p q \int \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 q \int \mathrm d x - \frac p q \int \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x} + C$$
Primitive of Constant
$$= \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\frac q {\operatorname{sech} a x} + p} + C$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\dfrac 1 {\operatorname{sech} a x}$
$$= \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \cosh a x} + C$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Secant

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x plus 1
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\left({\cosh a x + 1}\right)^2} = \frac 1 {2 a} \tanh \frac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 {6 a} \tanh^3 \frac {a x} 2 + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\left({\cosh a x + 1}\right)^2} = \int \left({\frac 1 2 \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac {a x} 2}\right)^2 \ \mathrm d x$$
Reciprocal of One Plus Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 4 \int \operatorname{sech}^4 \frac {a x} 2 \ \mathrm d x$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 4 \left({\frac{\operatorname{sech}^2 \dfrac {a x} 2 \tanh \dfrac {a x} 2} {\dfrac {3 a} 2} + \frac 2 3 \int \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac {a x} 2 \ \mathrm d x}\right) + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{sech}^n a x$
$$= \frac 1 {6 a} \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac {a x} 2 \tanh \dfrac {a x} 2 + \frac 1 6 \int \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac {a x} 2 \ \mathrm d x + C$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 {6 a} \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac {a x} 2 \tanh \dfrac {a x} 2 + \frac 1 6 \left({\frac 2 a \tanh \frac {a x} 2}\right) + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{sech}^2 a x$
$$= \frac 1 {6 a} \left({1 - \tanh^2 \frac {a x} 2}\right) \tan \dfrac {a x} 2 + \frac 2 {6 a} \tanh \frac {a x} 2 + C$$
Sum of Squares of Hyperbolic Secant and Tangent
$$= \frac 1 {2 a} \tanh \frac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 {6 a} \tanh^3 \frac {a x} 2 + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x minus 1
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\d x} {\paren {\cosh a x - 1}^2} = \frac 1 {2 a} \coth \frac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 {6 a} \coth^3 \frac {a x} 2 + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\d x} {\paren {\cosh a x - 1}^2} = \int \paren {\frac 1 2 \csch^2 \frac {a x} 2}^2 \rd x$$
Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Cosine Minus One
$$= \frac 1 4 \int \csch^4 \frac {a x} 2 \rd x$$
simplifying
$$= \frac 1 4 \paren {\frac {-\csch^2 \dfrac {a x} 2 \coth \dfrac {a x} 2} {\dfrac {3 a} 2} - \frac 2 3 \int \csch^2 \frac {a x} 2 \rd x} + C$$
Primitive of $\csch^n a x$
$$= \frac {-1} {6 a} \csch^2 \frac {a x} 2 \coth \dfrac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 6 \int \csch^2 \frac {a x} 2 \rd x + C$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {-1} {6 a} \csch^2 \frac {a x} 2 \coth \dfrac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 6 \paren {\frac {-2} a \coth \frac {a x} 2} + C$$
Primitive of $\csch^2 a x$
$$= \frac {-1} {6 a} \paren {\coth^2 \frac {a x} 2 - 1} \coth \dfrac {a x} 2 + \frac 2 {6 a} \coth \frac {a x} 2 + C$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cotangent and Cosecant
$$= \frac 1 {2 a} \coth \frac {a x} 2 - \frac 1 {6 a} \coth^3 \frac {a x} 2 + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh a x \cosh a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh a x \cosh a x \rd x = \int \frac {\sinh 2 a x} 2 \rd x$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int \sinh 2 a x \rd x$$
Primitive of Constant Multiple of Function
$$= \frac 1 2 \paren {\frac {\cosh 2 a x} {2 a} } + C$$
Primitive of $\sinh a x$
$$= \frac 1 2 \paren {\frac {1 + 2 \sinh^2 a x} {2 a} } + C$$
Corollary to Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + \frac 1 {4 a} + C$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
subsuming $\dfrac 1 {4 a}$ into arbitrary constant

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh a x \cosh a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh a x \cosh a x \rd x = \int \cosh a x \sinh a x \rd x$$
$$= \frac {\cosh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\cosh^n a x \sinh a x$ using $n = 1$
$$= \frac {1 + \sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine
$$= \frac 1 {2 a} + \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\sinh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
subsuming $\dfrac 1 {2 a}$ into arbitrary constant

title: Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of p x by Hyperbolic Cosine of q x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh p x \cosh q x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\cosh \left({p + q}\right) x} {2 \left({p + q}\right)} + \frac {\cosh \left({p - q}\right) x} {2 \left({p - q}\right)} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh p x \cosh q x \ \mathrm d x = \int \left({\frac {\sinh \left({p x + q x}\right) + \sinh \left({p x - q x}\right)} 2}\right) \ \mathrm d x$$
Simpson's Formula for Hyperbolic Sine by Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \frac 1 2 \int \sinh \left({p + q}\right) x \ \mathrm d x + \frac 1 2 \int \sinh \left({p - q}\right) x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 2 \frac {\cosh \left({p + q}\right) x} {p + q} + \frac 1 2 \frac {\cosh \left({p - q}\right) x} {p - q} + C$$
Primitive of $\sinh a x$
$$= \frac {\cosh \left({p + q}\right) x} {2 \left({p + q}\right)} + \frac {\cosh \left({p - q}\right) x} {2 \left({p - q}\right)} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \sinh^2 a x \cosh^2 a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh 4 a x} {32 a} - \frac x 8 + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \sinh^2 a x \cosh^2 a x \rd x = \int \paren {\sinh a x \cosh a x}^2 \rd x$$
$$= \int \paren {\frac {\sinh 2 a x} 2}^2 \rd x$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \frac 1 4 \int \sinh^2 2 a x \rd x$$
Primitive of Constant Multiple of Function
$$= \frac 1 4 \paren {\frac {\sinh 2 \paren {2 a x} } {4 \paren {2 a} } - \frac x 2} + C$$
Primitive of $\sinh^2 a x$
$$= \frac {\sinh 4 a x} {32 a} - \frac x 8 + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh a x} = \frac 1 a \ln \left\vert{\tanh a x}\right\vert + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh a x} = \int \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x}$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Secant
$$= \int \frac {\operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \operatorname{sech} a x}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\operatorname{sech} a x$
$$= \int \frac {\operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\frac {\sinh a x} {\cosh a x} }$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Secant
$$= \int \frac {\operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\tanh a x}$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Tangent
$$= \frac 1 a \ln \left\vert{\tanh a x}\right\vert + C$$
Primitive of $\dfrac {\operatorname{sech}^2 a x} {\tanh a x}$

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh^2 a x} = \frac 1 a \ln \left\vert{\tanh \frac {a x} 2}\right\vert + \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x} a + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh^2 a x \cosh a x} = \int \frac {\left({\cosh^2 a x - \sinh^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh^2 a x}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine
$$= \int \frac {\cosh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh^2 a x} - \int \frac {\sinh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x \cosh^2 a x}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh a x} - \int \frac {\sinh a x \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh^2 a x}$$
simplifying
$$= \int \operatorname{csch} a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \frac {\sinh a x \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh^2 a x}$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosecant
$$= \int \operatorname{csch} a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \frac {\tanh a x \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh a x}$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Tangent
$$= \int \operatorname{csch} a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \operatorname{sech} a x \tanh a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Secant
$$= \int \operatorname{csch} a x \ \mathrm d x - \frac {-\operatorname{sech} a x} a + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{sech}^n a x \tanh a x$ for $n = 1$
$$= \frac 1 a \ln \left\vert {\tanh \frac {a x} 2} \right\vert + \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x} a + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{csch} a x$

title: Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh^2 a x \cosh^2 a x} = \frac {-2 \coth 2 a x} a + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh^2 a x \cosh^2 a x} = \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\left({\sinh a x \cosh a x}\right)^2}$$
$$= \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\left({\dfrac {\sinh^2 2 a x} 2}\right)^2}$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Sine
$$= 4 \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh^2 2 a x}$$
Primitive of Constant Multiple of Function
$$= 4 \int \operatorname{csch}^2 2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Cosecant
$$= 4 \frac {-\coth 2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{csch}^2 a x$
$$= \frac {-2 \coth 2 a x} a + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x over Hyperbolic Cosine of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\sinh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh a x} = \frac {\sinh a x} a - \frac 1 a \arctan \left({\sinh a x}\right) + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\sinh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh a x} = \int \frac {\left({\cosh^2 a x - 1}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh a x}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine
$$= \int \frac {\left({\cosh^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\cosh a x} - \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\cosh a x}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \int \cosh a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Definition of Hyperbolic Secant
$$= \frac {\sinh a x} a - \int \operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Primitive of $\cosh a x$
$$= \frac {\sinh a x} a - \frac 1 a \arctan \left({\sinh a x}\right) + C$$
Primitive of $\operatorname{sech} a x$

title: Primitive of Cube of Hyperbolic Tangent of a x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \tanh^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\tanh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \tanh^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \int \tanh a x \tanh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \tanh a x \left({1 - \operatorname{sech}^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x$$
Sum of Squares of Hyperbolic Secant and Tangent
$$= \int \tanh a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \tanh a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \int \tanh a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Primitive of $\tanh a x$
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\tanh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\tanh^n a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x$: $n = 1$

title: Primitive of Cube of Hyperbolic Tangent of a x/Proof 1
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \tanh^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\tanh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \tanh^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \int \tanh a x \tanh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \tanh a x \left({1 - \operatorname{sech}^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x$$
Sum of Squares of Hyperbolic Secant and Tangent
$$= \int \tanh a x \ \mathrm d x - \int \tanh a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \int \tanh a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Primitive of $\tanh a x$
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\tanh^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\tanh^n a x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x$: $n = 1$

title: Primitive of Cube of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x
theorem_text: $\ds \int \coth^3 a x \rd x = \frac {\ln \size {\sinh a x} } a - \frac {\coth^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \coth^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \int \coth a x \coth^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \coth a x \left({1 + \operatorname{csch}^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cotangent and Cosecant
$$= \int \coth a x \ \mathrm d x + \int \coth a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a + \int \coth a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Primitive of $\tanh a x$
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\coth^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\coth^n a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x$: $n = 1$

title: Primitive of Cube of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x/Proof 1
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \coth^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\coth^2 a x} {2 a} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \coth^3 a x \ \mathrm d x = \int \coth a x \coth^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \coth a x \left({1 + \operatorname{csch}^2 a x}\right) \ \mathrm d x$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cotangent and Cosecant
$$= \int \coth a x \ \mathrm d x + \int \coth a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a + \int \coth a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x$$
Primitive of $\tanh a x$
$$= \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a - \frac {\coth^2 a x} {2 a} + C$$
Primitive of $\coth^n a x \operatorname{csch}^2 a x$: $n = 1$

title: Derivative of Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine of x over a
theorem_text:
$\dfrac {\map \d {\map {\cosh^{-1} } {\frac x a} } } {\d x} = \dfrac 1 {\sqrt {x^2 - a^2} }$
where $x > a$.
proof_text:
Let $x > a$.
Then $\dfrac x a > 1$ and so:
$$\frac {\map \d {\map {\cosh^{-1} } {\frac x a} } } {\d x} = \frac 1 a \frac 1 {\sqrt {\paren {\frac x a}^2} - 1}$$
Derivative of $\cosh^{-1}$ and Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
$$= \frac 1 a \frac 1 {\sqrt {\frac {x^2 - a^2} {a^2} } }$$
$$= \frac 1 a \frac a {\sqrt {x^2 - a^2} }$$
$$= \frac 1 {\sqrt {x^2 - a^2} }$$
$\cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a$ is not defined when $x \le a$.
When $x = a$ we have that $\sqrt {x^2 - a^2} = 0$ and so $\dfrac 1 {\sqrt {x^2 - a^2} }$ is not defined.
Hence the restriction on the domain.

title: Derivative of Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent of x over a
theorem_text:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\map {\tanh^{-1} } {\dfrac x a} } = \dfrac a {a^2 - x^2}$
where $-a < x < a$.
proof_text:
Let $-a < x < a$.
Then $-1 < \dfrac x a < 1$ and so:
$$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\map {\tanh^{-1} } {\dfrac x a} } = \frac 1 a \frac 1 {1 - \paren {\frac x a}^2}$$
Derivative of $\tanh^{-1}$ and Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
$$= \frac 1 a \frac 1 {\frac {a^2 - x^2} {a^2} }$$
$$= \frac 1 a \frac {a^2} {a^2 - x^2}$$
$$= \frac a {a^2 - x^2}$$
$\tanh^{-1} \dfrac x a$ is not defined when either $x \le -a$ or $x \ge a$.

title: Derivative of Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent of x over a
theorem_text:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\map {\coth^{-1} } {\dfrac x a} } = \dfrac {-a} {x^2 - a^2}$
where $x^2 > a^2$.
proof_text:
Let $x^2 > a^2$.
Then either $\dfrac x a < -1$ or $\dfrac x a > 1$ and so:
$$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\map {\coth^{-1} } {\dfrac x a} } = \frac 1 a \frac 1 {1 - \paren {\frac x a}^2}$$
Derivative of $\coth^{-1}$ and Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
$$= \frac 1 a \frac 1 {\frac {a^2 - x^2} {a^2} }$$
$$= -\frac 1 a \frac {a^2} {x^2 - a^2}$$
$$= \frac {-a} {x^2 - a^2}$$
$\coth^{-1} \dfrac x a$ is not defined when $x^2 \le a^2$.

title: Derivative of Inverse Hyperbolic Secant of x over a
theorem_text:
$\dfrac {\mathrm d \left({\operatorname{sech}^{-1} \left({\frac x a}\right)}\right)} {\mathrm d x} = \dfrac {-a} {x \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} }$
where $0 < x < a$.
proof_text:
Let $0 < x < a$.
Then $0 < \dfrac x a < 1$ and so:
$$\frac {\mathrm d \left({\operatorname{sech}^{-1} \frac x a}\right)} {\mathrm d x} = \frac 1 a \frac {-1} {\frac x a \sqrt{1 - \left({\frac x a}\right)^2} }$$
Derivative of $\operatorname{sech}^{-1}$ and Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
$$= \frac 1 a \frac {-a} {x \sqrt{\frac {a^2 - x^2} {a^2} } }$$
$$= \frac {-a} {x \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} }$$
$\operatorname{sech}^{-1} \dfrac x a$ is not defined when $x \le 0$ or $x \ge a$.

title: Derivative of Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant of x over a
theorem_text:
$\dfrac {\map \d {\csch^{-1} } {\frac x a} } {\d x} = \dfrac {-a} {\size x \sqrt {a^2 + x^2} }$
where $x \ne 0$.
proof_text:
Let $0 < x < a$.
Then $0 < \dfrac x a < 1$ and so:
$$\frac {\map \d {\csch^{-1} } {\frac x a} } {\d x} = \frac 1 a \dfrac {-1} {\size {\frac x a} \sqrt {1 + \paren {\frac x a}^2} }$$
Derivative of $\csch^{-1}$ and Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
$$= \frac 1 a \frac {-a} {\size x \sqrt {\frac {a^2 + x^2} {a^2} } }$$
$$= \frac {-a} {\size x \sqrt{a^2 + x^2} }$$
$\csch^{-1} \dfrac x a$ is not defined when $x = 0$.

title: Primitive of x squared over x squared minus a squared/Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent Form
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int \frac {x^2 \ \mathrm d x} {x^2 - a^2} = x - a \coth^{-1} \frac x a + C$
for $x^2 > a^2$.
proof_text:
Let:
$$\int \frac {x^2 \ \mathrm d x} {x^2 - a^2} = \int \frac {x^2 - a^2 + a^2} {x^2 - a^2} \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \frac {x^2 - a^2} {x^2 - a^2} \ \mathrm d x + \int \frac {a^2} {x^2 - a^2} \ \mathrm d x$$
$$= \int \mathrm d x + a^2 \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {x^2 - a^2}$$
Primitive of Constant Multiple of Function
$$= x + a^2 \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {x^2 - a^2} + C$$
Primitive of Constant
$$= x + a^2 \left({-\frac 1 a \coth^{-1} {\frac x a} }\right) + C$$
Primitive of Reciprocal of $x^2 - a^2$: $\coth^{-1}$ form
$$= x - a \coth^{-1} {\frac x a} + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of x squared over a squared minus x squared/Logarithm Form
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int \frac {x^2 \rd x} {a^2 - x^2} = -x + \frac a 2 \map \ln {\frac {a + x} {a - x} } + C$
for $x^2 < a^2$.
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {x^2 \rd x} {a^2 - x^2} = \int \frac {x^2 - a^2 + a^2} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x$$
$$= \int \frac {- \left({a^2 - x^2}\right)} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x + \int \frac {a^2} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= - \int \d x + a^2 \int \frac {\d x} {a^2 - x^2}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= -x + a^2 \int \frac {\d x} {a^2 - x^2} + C$$
Primitive of Constant
$$= -x + a^2 \paren {\frac 1 {2 a} \map \ln {\frac {a + x} {a - x} } } + C$$
Primitive of $\dfrac 1 {a^2 - x^2}$: Logarithm Form
$$= -x + \frac a 2 \map \ln {\frac {a + x} {a - x} } + C$$
simplifying

title: Primitive of x squared over a squared minus x squared/Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent Form
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int \frac {x^2 \rd x} {a^2 - x^2} = -x + a \tanh^{-1} \frac x a + C$
for $x^2 < a^2$.
proof_text:
Let:
$$\int \frac {x^2 \rd x} {a^2 - x^2} = \int \frac {x^2 - a^2 + a^2} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x$$
$$= \int \frac {- \left({a^2 - x^2}\right)} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x + \int \frac {a^2} {a^2 - x^2} \rd x$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= - \int \rd x + a^2 \int \frac {\rd x} {a^2 - x^2}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= -x + a^2 \int \frac {\rd x} {a^2 - x^2} + C$$
Primitive of Constant
$$= -x + a^2 \left({\frac 1 a \tanh^{-1} \frac x a}\right) + C$$
Primitive of Reciprocal of $a^2 - x^2$: $\tanh^{-1}$ form
$$= -x + a \tanh^{-1} \frac x a + C$$
simplifying

title: Reciprocal of One Plus Cosine
theorem_text: $\dfrac 1 {1 + \cos x} = \dfrac 1 2 \sec^2 \dfrac x 2$
proof_text:
$$\frac 1 {1 + \cos x} = \frac 1 {1 + \frac {1- \tan^2 \frac x 2} {1 + \tan^2 \frac x 2} }$$
Tangent Half-Angle Substitution for Cosine
$$= \frac {1 + \tan^2 \frac x 2} 2$$
multiplying through $\frac {1 + \tan^2 \frac x 2} {1 + \tan^2 \frac x 2}$
$$= \frac 1 2 \sec^2 \frac x 2$$
Difference of Squares of Secant and Tangent

title: Tangent of 22.5 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 22.5^\circ = \tan \dfrac \pi 8 = \sqrt 2 - 1$
proof_text:
$$\tan 22.5^\circ = \tan \frac {45^\circ} 2$$
$$= \frac {1 - \cos 45^\circ} {\sin 45^\circ}$$
Half Angle Formulas/Tangent/Corollary 2
$$= \frac {1 - \frac {\sqrt 2} 2} {\frac {\sqrt 2} 2}$$
Cosine of 45 Degrees and Sine of 45 Degrees
$$= \sqrt 2 - 1$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt 2$

title: Tangent of 67.5 Degrees
theorem_text: $\tan 67.5 \degrees = \tan \dfrac {3 \pi} 8 = \sqrt 2 + 1$
proof_text:
$$\tan 67.5 \degrees = \map \tan {45 \degrees + 22.5 \degrees}$$
$$= \frac {\tan 45 \degrees + \tan 22.5 \degrees} {1 - \tan 45 \degrees \tan 22.5 \degrees}$$
Tangent of Sum
$$= \frac {1 + \paren {\sqrt 2 - 1} } {1 - 1 \times \paren {\sqrt 2 - 1} }$$
Tangent of $45 \degrees$ and Tangent of $22.5 \degrees$
$$= \frac {\sqrt 2} {2 - \sqrt 2}$$
simplifying
$$= \frac {\sqrt 2 \paren {2 + \sqrt 2} } {\paren {2 - \sqrt 2} \paren {2 + \sqrt 2} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2 + \sqrt 2$
$$= \frac {2 \sqrt 2 + 2} {4 - 2}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt 2 + 1$$
simplifying

title: Sine of x minus Cosine of x/Cosine Form
theorem_text: $\sin x - \cos x = \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {x - \dfrac {3 \pi} 4}$
proof_text:
$$\sin x - \cos x = \sqrt 2 \, \map \sin {x - \dfrac \pi 4}$$
Sine of x minus Cosine of x: Sine Form
$$= \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {\frac \pi 2 - \paren {x - \dfrac \pi 4} }$$
Cosine of Complement equals Sine
$$= \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {\frac \pi 2 - x + \dfrac \pi 4}$$
simplifying
$$= \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {\frac {3 \pi} 4 - x}$$
simplifying
$$= \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {x - \frac {3 \pi} 4}$$
Cosine Function is Even

title: Primitive of Cosine of a x over Sine of a x plus phi
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\cos a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } = \frac {\ln \size {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } } {a \cos \phi} + \tan \phi \int \frac {\sin a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } + C$
proof_text:
First note that:
(1) $$\map {\frac \d {\d x} } {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } = a \, \map \cos {a x + \phi}$$
Derivative of $\sin a x$ etc.
Then:
$$\int \frac {\cos a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } = \int \frac {\cos a x \cos \phi \rd x} {\cos \phi \, \map \sin {a x + \phi} }$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\cos \phi$
$$= \int \frac {\paren {\cos a x \cos \phi - \sin a x \sin \phi + \sin a x \sin \phi} \rd x} {\cos \phi \, \map \sin {a x + \phi} }$$
$$= \int \frac {\paren {\map \cos {a x + \phi} + \sin a x \sin \phi} \rd x} {\cos \phi \, \map \sin {a x + \phi} }$$
Cosine of Sum
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\map \cos {a x + \phi} \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } + \frac {\sin \phi} {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\sin a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} }$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \ln \size {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } + \frac {\sin \phi} {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\sin a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} }$$
Primitive of Function under its Derivative and $(1)$
$$= \frac {\ln \size {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } } {a \cos \phi} + \tan \phi \int \frac {\sin a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } + C$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Primitive of Sine of a x over Sine of a x plus phi
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \frac {\sin a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} = \frac x {\cos \phi} - \tan \phi \int \frac {\cos a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} + C$
proof_text:
$$\int \frac {\sin a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} = \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\sin a x \cos \phi \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $\cos \phi$
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\left({\sin a x \cos \phi + \cos a x \sin \phi - \cos a x \sin \phi}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)}$$
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\left({\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right) - \cos a x \sin \phi}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)}$$
Sine of Sum
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\left({\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right) - \cos a x \sin \phi}\right) \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)}$$
Sine of Sum
$$= \frac 1 {\cos \phi} \int \mathrm d x  - \frac {\sin \phi} {\cos \phi} \int \frac {\cos a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)}$$
Linear Combination of Integrals
$$= \frac x {\cos \phi} - \tan \phi \int \frac {\cos a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} + C$$
Tangent is Sine divided by Cosine

title: Triangle Right-Angle-Hypotenuse-Side Equality
theorem_text:
If two triangles have:
: one right angle each
: the sides opposite to the right angle equal
: another two respective sides equal
they will also have:
: their third sides equal
: the remaining two angles equal to their respective remaining angles.
proof_text:
Let $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ be two triangles having sides $AB = DE$ and $AC = DF$, and with $\angle ABC = \angle DEF = 90^\circ$.
By Pythagoras' Theorem:
$BC = \sqrt {AB^2 + AC^2}$
and:
$EF = \sqrt {DE^2 + DF^2}$
$\therefore BC = \sqrt {AB^2 + AC^2} = \sqrt {DE^2 + DF^2} = EF$
The part that the remaining two angles are equal to their respective remaining angles follows from Triangle Side-Side-Side Equality.

title: Internal Angles of Regular Polygon
theorem_text:
The size $A$ of each internal angle of a regular $n$-gon is given by:
$A = \dfrac {\paren {n - 2} 180 \degrees} n$
proof_text:
From Sum of Internal Angles of Polygon, we have that the sum $S$ of all internal angles of a $n$-gon is:
$S = \paren {n - 2} 180 \degrees$
From the definition of a regular polygon, all the internal angles of a regular polygon are equal.
Therefore, the size $A$ of each internal angle of a regular polygon with $n$ sides is:
$A = \dfrac {\paren {n - 2} 180 \degrees} n$

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Straight Angle
theorem_text: The measurement of a straight angle is $\dfrac{360^\circ} 2 = 180^\circ$ or $\dfrac {2 \pi} 2 = \pi$.
proof_text:
From $2 \pi$ radians, a full rotation is defined to be $360^\circ$ or $2 \pi$ radians.
Since lines are straight, it therefore follows that from any point on a line, the angle between one side of the line and the other is one half of a full rotation.
Therefore, the measurement of a straight angle is:
$\dfrac{360^\circ} 2 = 180^\circ$
or:
$\dfrac {2 \pi} 2 = \pi$

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Right Angle
theorem_text: The measurement of a right angle is $\dfrac {180 \degrees} 2 = 90 \degrees$ or $\dfrac \pi 2$.
proof_text:
A right angle is equal to one half of a straight angle.
From Measurement of Straight Angle it follows that the measurement of a right angle is $\dfrac {180 \degrees} 2 = 90 \degrees$ or $\dfrac \pi 2$.

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Full Angle
theorem_text: A full angle is equal to one full rotation.
proof_text:
From Full Rotation measures $2 \pi$ Radians, a full rotation is $2 \pi$ radians.
By definition of degree of angle, a full rotation is $360^\circ$.
Therefore, a full angle is $360^\circ$ or $2 \pi$.

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Acute Angle
theorem_text:
An acute angle measures $\theta$, where:
$0 \degrees < \theta < 90 \degrees$
or:
$0 < \theta < \dfrac \pi 2$
proof_text:
An acute angle is defined to be an angle whose measure is between that of a zero angle and a right angle.
A zero angle measures $0$ by definition, and a right angle measures $90 \degrees$ or $\dfrac \pi 2$.
Hence the result.

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Obtuse Angle
theorem_text:
An obtuse angle measures $\theta$, where:
$90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$
or:
$\dfrac \pi 2 < \theta < \pi$
proof_text:
An obtuse angle is defined to be an angle whose measure is between that of a right angle and a straight angle.
A right angle measures $90^\circ$ or $\dfrac \pi 2$ and a straight angle measures $180^\circ$ or $\pi$.
Hence the result.

title: Measurements of Common Angles/Reflex Angle
theorem_text:
A reflex angle measures $\theta$, where:
$180^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ$
or:
$\pi < \theta < 2 \pi$
proof_text:
A reflex angle is defined to be an angle whose measure is between that of a straight angle and a full angle.
A straight angle measures $180^\circ$ or $\pi$ and a full angle measures $360^\circ$ or $2 \pi$.
Hence the result.

title: Proportion is Transitive
theorem_text:
Proportion is a transitive relation.
That is:
$\forall x,y,z \in \R: x \propto y \land y \propto z \implies x \propto z$
proof_text:
Let $x, y, z$ be arbitrary.
Let $x$ be proportional to $y$ and $y$ to $z$:
$x \propto y \land y \propto z$
Then by definition:
$\exists j, k \ne 0: x = j \times y \land y = k \times z$
Substituting $k \times z$ for $y$:
$x = \left({j \times k}\right) \times z$
so $j \times k$ is the desired constant of proportion.
The result follows from the definition of transitivity and proportion.

title: Proportion is Equivalence Relation
theorem_text: Proportion is an equivalence relation.
proof_text:
* Proportion is Reflexive: $\forall x \in \R: x \propto x$
* Proportion is Symmetric: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto y \implies y \propto x$
* Proportion is Transitive: $\forall x, y, z \in \R: x \propto y \land y \propto z \implies x \propto z$
The result follows from the definition of an equivalence relation.

title: Sine of 18 Degrees
theorem_text:
$\sin 18 \degrees = \sin \dfrac \pi {10} = \dfrac {\sqrt 5 - 1} 4$
where $\sin$ denotes the sine function.
proof_text:
From Sine of $90 \degrees$:
$\sin \paren {5 \times 18 \degrees} = \sin 90 \degrees = 1$.
Consider the equation:
$\sin 5x = 1$
where $x = 18 \degrees$ is one of the solutions.
From Quintuple Angle Formula of Sine:
$16 \sin^5 \theta - 20 \sin^3 \theta + 5 \sin \theta = 1$
Let $s = \sin \theta$:
$16 s^5 - 20 s^3 + 5s - 1 = 0$
That is:
$\paren {s - 1} \paren {4 s^2 + 2 s - 1}^2 = 0$
Therefore, either:
$s = 1$
or by the Quadratic Formula:
$s = \dfrac 1 4 \paren {\pm \sqrt 5 - 1}$
Since $0 < \sin 18 \degrees < 1$:
$\sin 18^\circ = \dfrac {\sqrt 5 - 1} 4$

title: Cosine of 3 Degrees
theorem_text:
$\cos 3^\circ = \cos \dfrac {\pi} {60} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2 + 2 \sqrt{15 + 3 \sqrt 5} + 2 \sqrt{5 + \sqrt 5} } {16}$
where $\cos$ denotes the cosine function.
proof_text:
$$\cos 3^\circ = \cos \left({75^\circ - 72^\circ}\right)$$
$$= \cos 75^\circ \cos 72^\circ + \sin 75^\circ \sin 72^\circ$$
Cosine of Difference
$$= \dfrac {\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2} 4 \times \dfrac {\sqrt 5 - 1} 4 + \dfrac {\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2} 4 \times \dfrac {\sqrt {10 + 2 \sqrt5 } } 4$$
Cosine of 75 Degrees, Cosine of 72 Degrees, Sine of 75 Degrees, Sine of 72 Degrees
$$= \dfrac 1 {16} \times \left[{\left({\sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2}\right) \times \left({\sqrt 5 - 1}\right) + \left({\sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right) \times \left({\sqrt {10 + 2 \sqrt 5} }\right) }\right]$$
$$= \dfrac 1 {16} \times \left[{\left({\sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2}\right) + \left({\sqrt{60 + 12 \sqrt 5} + \sqrt{20 + 4 \sqrt 5} }\right) }\right]$$
$$= \dfrac 1 {16} \times \left({\sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2 + \sqrt{60 + 12 \sqrt 5} + \sqrt{20 + 4 \sqrt 5} }\right)$$
$$= \dfrac 1 {16} \times \left({\sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2 + 2 \sqrt{15 + 3 \sqrt 5} + 2 \sqrt{5 + \sqrt 5} }\right)$$
$$= \dfrac{\sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2 + 2 \sqrt{15 + 3 \sqrt 5} + 2 \sqrt{5 + \sqrt 5} }{16}$$

title: Square Root of Sum as Sum of Square Roots
theorem_text:
Let $a, b \in \R, a \ge b$.
Then:
$\sqrt {a + b} = \sqrt {\dfrac a 2 + \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2} + \sqrt {\dfrac a 2 - \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2}$
proof_text:
From Sum of Square Roots as Square Root of Sum:
$\sqrt p + \sqrt q = \sqrt {p + q + \sqrt {4pq}}$
Let
$p = \dfrac a 2 + \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2$,
$q = \dfrac a 2 - \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2$.
Then
$$p + q = \frac a 2 + \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } 2 + \frac a 2 - \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } 2$$
$$= a$$
$$\sqrt {4pq} = \sqrt {4 \paren {\frac a 2 + \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } 2} \paren {\frac a 2 - \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } 2} }$$
$$= \sqrt {\paren {a + \sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } \paren {a - \sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } }$$
Real Multiplication Distributes over Addition
$$= \sqrt {a^2 - \paren {a^2 - b^2} }$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \sqrt {b^2}$$
$$= b$$
Therefore:
$\sqrt {\dfrac a 2 + \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2} + \sqrt {\dfrac a 2 - \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} 2} = \sqrt {a + b}$

title: Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 1
theorem_text: $\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \min \set {\chi_A + \chi_B, 1}$
proof_text:
By Characteristic Function Determined by 1-Fiber, it suffices to show:
$\min \set {\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s, 1} = 1 \iff s \in A \cup B$
By the nature of the min operation, this amounts to showing that:
$\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s \ge 1 \iff s \in A \cup B$
As $\chi_A, \chi_B$ are characteristic functions, the left-hand side amounts to:
$s \in A \lor s \in B$
which is precisely the definition of $s \in A \cup B$.

title: Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 2
theorem_text: $\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \chi_A + \chi_B - \chi_{A \mathop \cap B}$
proof_text:
From Subset of Union:
$A, B \subseteq A \cup B$
From Intersection is Subset of Union:
$A \cap B \subseteq A \cup B$
Thus from Characteristic Function of Subset:
$\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0 \implies \map {\chi_A} s = \map {\chi_B} s = \map {\chi_{A \mathop \cap B} } s = 0$
Now suppose that $\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s - \map {\chi_{A \mathop \cap B} } s = 0$.
That is:
$\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s = \map {\chi_{A \mathop \cap B} } s$
Suppose the latter equals $1$, that is $s \in A \cap B$.
Then both $s \in A$ and $s \in B$, so by definition of characteristic function:
$\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s = 1 + 1 = 2$
Since $2 \ne 1$, it follows that $\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cap B} } s \ne 1$, that is it equals $0$.
Thence, it follows that:
$\map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s = 0$.
This only happens when $\map {\chi_A} s = \map {\chi_B} s = 0$.
Thus, $s \notin A$ and $s \notin B$, so $s \notin A \cup B$.
It finally follows that $\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0$.
It is now established that:
$\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0 \iff \map {\chi_A} s + \map {\chi_B} s - \map {\chi_{A \mathop \cap B} } s = 0$
and from Characteristic Function Determined by 0-Fiber, the result follows.

title: Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 3
theorem_text: $\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \max \set {\chi_A, \chi_B}$
proof_text:
Suppose $\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0$.
Then $s \notin A \cup B$, so $s \notin A$ and $s \notin B$.
Hence:
$\map {\chi_A} s = \map {\chi_B} s = 0$
and by definition of max operation:
$\max \set {\map {\chi_A} s, \map {\chi_B} s} = 0$
Conversely, suppose:
$\max \set {\map {\chi_A} s, \map {\chi_B} s} = 0$
Then it follows that:
$\map {\chi_A} s = \map {\chi_B} s = 0$
because characteristic functions are $0$ or $1$.
Hence $s \notin A$ and $s \notin B$, so $s \notin A \cup B$.
That is:
$\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0$
Above considerations give:
$\map {\chi_{A \mathop \cup B} } s = 0 \iff \max \set {\map {\chi_A} s, \map {\chi_B} s} = 0$
and applying Characteristic Function Determined by 0-Fiber, the result follows.

title: Characteristic Function of Intersection/Variant 1
theorem_text: $\chi_{A \cap B} = \chi_A \chi_B$
proof_text:
By Characteristic Function Determined by 1-Fiber, it suffices to show that:
$\map {\chi_A} s \, \map {\chi_B} s = 1 \iff s \in A \cap B$
Now, both $\chi_A$ and $\chi_B$ are characteristic functions.
It follows that, for any $s \in S$:
$\map {\chi_A} s \, \map {\chi_B} s = 1 \iff \map {\chi_A} s = \map {\chi_B} s = 1$
By definition of $\chi_A$ and $\chi_B$, this is equivalent to the statement that both $s \in A$ and $s \in B$.
That is, $s \in A \cap B$, by definition of set intersection.

title: Negative of Real Function that Increases Without Bound
theorem_text:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function.
Then:
$(1): \quad \displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} -\map f x = -\infty$
$(2): \quad \displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} -\map f x = -\infty$
proof_text:
Suppose $\displaystyle  \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty$.
Then by the definition of infinite limits at infinity:
$\forall M > 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \map f x > M$
But $M > 0 \iff -M < 0$.
Likewise $\map f x > M \iff -\map f x < -M$.
Putting $M' = -M$:
$\forall M' < 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies -\map f x < M'$
The result then follows from the definition of negative infinite limit at infinity.
The proof for $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty$ is analagous.

title: Negative of Real Function that Decreases Without Bound
theorem_text:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function.
Then:
$(1): \quad \displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} -\map f x = +\infty$
$(2): \quad \displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} -\map f x = +\infty$
proof_text:
Suppose $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty$.
Then by the definition of negative infinite limit at infinity:
$\forall M < 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \map f x < M$
But $M < 0 \iff -M > 0$.
Likewise $\map f x < M \iff -\map f x > -M$.
Putting $M' = -M$:
$\forall M' > 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies -\map f x > M'$
The result then follows from the definition of infinite limit at infinity.
The proof for $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty$ is analogous.

title: Scaled Real Function that Increases Without Bound
theorem_text:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function.
Let $\lambda \in \R_{\ne 0}$ be a nonzero constant.
Then:
For $\lambda > 0$:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = +\infty$
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \lambda \map f x = + \infty$
For $\lambda < 0$:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = -\infty$
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \lambda \map f x = -\infty$
proof_text:
Let $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty$.
From the definition of infinite limit at infinity, this means that:
$\forall M > 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \map f x > M$.
Suppose $\lambda > 0$.
Then $M > 0 \iff \lambda^{-1} M > 0$.
Also, $\map f x > \lambda^{-1} M \iff \lambda f\map f x > M$.
So:
$\forall M > 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \lambda \map f x > M$
From the definition of infinite limit at infinity:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = +\infty$.
The proof for $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty$ is analogous.
Now, suppose $\lambda < 0$.
Then $-\lambda f > 0$, and so $-\lambda f \to + \infty$, from above.
Write $\lambda f = -\paren {-\lambda f}$ and the result follows from Negative of Real Function that Increases Without Bound.

title: Scaled Real Function that Decreases Without Bound
theorem_text:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function.
Let $\lambda \in \R_{\ne 0}$ be a nonzero constant.
Then:
For $\lambda > 0$:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = -\infty$
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \lambda \map f x = -\infty$
For $\lambda < 0$:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = +\infty$
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \lambda \map f x = +\infty$
proof_text:
Let $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty$.
From the definition of infinite limits at infinity, this means that:
$\forall M < 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \map f x < M$
Suppose $\lambda > 0$.
Then $M < 0 \iff \lambda^{-1}M < 0$.
Also, $\map f x < \lambda^{-1}M \iff \lambda \map f x < M$
So:
$\forall M < 0: \exists N > 0: x > N \implies \lambda \map f x < M$
From the definition of infinite limits at infinity:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \lambda \map f x = -\infty$
The proof for $\displaystyle  \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty$ is analogous.
Now, suppose $\lambda < 0$.
Then $-\lambda f < 0$, and so $-\lambda f \to -\infty$, from above.
Write $\lambda f = -\paren {-\lambda f}$ and the result follows from Negative of Real Function that Decreases Without Bound.

title: Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous/Topological Spaces
theorem_text:
Let $T_1 = \left({S_1, \tau_1}\right)$ and $T_2 = \left({S_2, \tau_2}\right)$ be topological spaces.
Let $M_1 \subseteq S_1$ be a subset of $S_1$.
Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping which is continuous.
Let $M_2 \subseteq S_2$ be a subset of $S_2$ such that $f\left[{M_1}\right] \subseteq M_2$.
Let $f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2}}: M_1 \to M_2$ be the restriction of $f$ to $M_1 \times M_2$.
Then $f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2}}$ is continuous, where $M_1$ and $M_2$ are equipped with the respective subspace topologies.
proof_text:
Let $V \subseteq M_2$ be an open set with respect to the subspace topology of $M_2$.
By definition of the subspace topology, $V = U \cap M_2$ for an open set $U \in \tau_2$.
We have that:
$$\left({f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2} } }\right)^{-1} \left[{V}\right] = \left\{ {x \in M_1 : f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2} } \left({x}\right) \in V} \right\}$$
Definition of Preimage
$$= \left\{ {x \in M_1 : f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2} } \left({x}\right) \in U}\right\}$$
$f \left({M_1}\right) \subseteq M_2$
$$= \left\{ {x \in M_1 : f \left({x}\right) \in U}\right\}$$
Definition of Restriction of Mapping
$$= \left\{ {x \in S_1 : f \left({x}\right) \in U}\right\} \cap M_1$$
Definition of Set Intersection
$$= f^{-1} \left[{U}\right] \cap M_1$$
Definition of Preimage
By definition of continuous mapping, $f^{-1} \left[{U}\right]$ is open in $T_1$.
By definition of subspace topology, $f^{-1} \left[{U}\right] \cap M_1$ is open with respect to the subspace topology of $M_1$.
As $f^{-1} \left[{U}\right] \cap M_1 = {f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2}}}^{-1} \left[{V}\right]$ it follows that ${f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2}}}^{-1} \left[{V}\right]$ is open with respect to the subspace topology of $M_1$.
Since $V \subseteq M_2$ was an arbitrary open set, $f$ is continuous.

title: Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous/Metric Spaces
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces.
Let $S \subseteq M_1$ be a subset of $M_1$.
Let $f: M_1 \to M_2$ be a mapping which is continuous at a point $\alpha \in S$.
Let $f \restriction_S = g: S \to M_2$ be the restriction of $f$ to $S$.
Then $g$ is continuous at $\alpha$.
proof_text:
Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $S$ such that:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} z_n = \alpha$
Since $\sequence {z_n}$ and $\alpha$ both lie in $S$:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map f {z_n} \to \alpha$
But:
$\forall n \in \N: \map g {z_n} = \map f {z_n}$
and also:
$\map g \alpha = \map f \alpha$
The result follows from Limit of Function by Convergent Sequences.

title: Restriction of Inverse is Inverse of Restriction
theorem_text:
Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be sets.
Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a bijection.
Let $S \subseteq S_1$ be a subset of $S_1$.
Let $f^{-1}$ be the inverse of $f$.
Let $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ be the restriction of $f$ to $S \times f\left[{S}\right]$.
Let $f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$ be the restriction of $f^{-1}$ to $f \left[{S}\right] \times S$.
Then:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ is a bijection
and:
${\left({f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} }\right)}^{-1} = f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$
proof_text:
Let $y \in f \left[{S}\right]$.
By the definition of image:
$\exists z \in S : f \left({z}\right) = y$
Since $f$ is a bijection, $f^{-1}$ is a mapping.
Let $x = f^{-1} \left({y}\right)$.
Suppose that $x \notin S$.
Suppose that $x = z$.
Then $x \in S$.
Thus $x \ne z$.
By the definition of inverse mapping:
$f\left({x}\right) = y$
By Equality is Transitive:
$f \left({x}\right) = f \left({z}\right)$
Thus, $f$ is not an injection.
Thus, $f$ is not a bijection.
This contradicts the assumption.
Therefore, $x \in S$.
By the definition of restriction of mapping:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} \left({x}\right) = f\left({x}\right)$
By Equality is Transitive:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} \left({x}\right) = y$
Suppose that there exists a $w \in S$ such that $w \ne x$ and $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} \left({w}\right) = y$.
By the definition of restriction of mapping:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} \left({w}\right) = f\left({w}\right)$
By Equality is Transitive:
$f \left({w}\right) = y$
By Equality is Transitive:
$f \left({w}\right) = f\left({x}\right)$
Thus, $f$ is not an injection.
Thus, $f$ is not a bijection.
This contradicts the assumption.
Therefore, there exists a unique $x \in S$ such that:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f\left[{S}\right]}} \left({x}\right) = y$
Since $y \in f\left[{S}\right]$ was arbitrary, $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ is a bijection.
Thus, ${\left(f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}\right)}^{-1}$ is a mapping.
Let $x' = {\left(f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}\right)}^{-1}\left({y}\right)$.
By the definition of inverse mapping:
$f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}} \left({x'}\right) = y$
By the definition of restriction of mapping, we have $f \left({x'}\right) = y$.
Suppose that $x' \ne x$.
By Equality is Transitive:
$f\left({x'}\right) = f\left({x}\right)$
Thus, $f$ is not an injection.
Thus, $f$ is not a bijection.
This contradicts the assumption.
Therefore, $x' = x$.
By Equality is Transitive:
$f^{-1}\left({y}\right) = (f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}})^{-1} \left({y}\right)$
By the definition of restriction of mapping:
$f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}} \left({y}\right) = f^{-1} \left({y}\right)$
By Equality is Transitive:
${\left(f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}\right)}^{-1} \left({y}\right) = f^{-1} {\restriction_{f\left[{S}\right] \times S}} \left({y}\right)$
Since $y \in f\left[{S}\right]$ was arbitrary:
${\left(f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}\right)}^{-1} = f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$

title: Restriction of Homeomorphism is Homeomorphism
theorem_text:
Let $T_1 = \left({S_1, \tau_1}\right)$, $T_2 = \left({S_2, \tau_2}\right)$ be topological spaces.
Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a homeomorphism between $T_1$ and $T_2$.
Let $S$ be a subset of $S_1$.
Let $f {\restriction_{S \times f\left[{S}\right]}} : S \to f \left[{S}\right]$ be the restriction of $f$ to $S \times f \left[{S}\right]$.
Let $S$ and $f \left[{S}\right]$ bear their respective subspace topologies.
Then $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ is a homeomorphism.
proof_text:
By Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous, $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ is continuous.
By Restriction of Inverse is Inverse of Restriction, $\left({f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}}\right)^{-1}$ is well-defined and equal to $f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$.
By Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous, $f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$ is continuous.
Since $\left({f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}}\right)^{-1} = f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S}}$, $\left({f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}}\right)^{-1}$ is continuous.
Hence, $f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right]}}$ is a homeomorphism.

title: Theorem of Even Perfect Numbers/Necessary Condition
theorem_text:
Let $a \in \N$ be an even perfect number.
Then $a$ is in the form:
$2^{n - 1} \paren {2^n - 1}$
where $2^n - 1$ is prime.
proof_text:
Let $a \in \N$ be an even perfect number.
We can extract the highest power of $2$ out of $a$ that we can, and write $a$ in the form:
$a = m 2^{n-1}$
where $n \ge 2$ and $m$ is odd.
Since $a$ is perfect and therefore $\map \sigma a = 2 a$:
$$m 2^n = 2 a$$
$$= \map \sigma a$$
$$= \map \sigma {m 2^{n - 1} }$$
$$= \map \sigma m \map \sigma {2^{n - 1} }$$
Sigma Function is Multiplicative
$$= \map \sigma m {2^n - 1}$$
Sigma Function of Power of Prime
So:
$\map \sigma m = \dfrac {m 2^n} {2^n - 1}$
But $\map \sigma m$ is an integer and so $2^n - 1$ divides $m 2^n$.
From Consecutive Integers are Coprime, $2^n$ and $2^n - 1$ are coprime.
So from Euclid's Lemma $2^n - 1$ divides $m$.
Thus $\dfrac m {2^n - 1}$ divides $m$.
Since $2^n - 1 \ge 3$ it follows that:
$\dfrac m {2^n - 1} < m$
Now we can express $\map \sigma m$ as:
$\map \sigma m = \dfrac {m 2^n} {2^n - 1} = m + \dfrac m {2^n - 1}$
This means that the sum of all the divisors of $m$ is equal to $m$ itself plus one other divisor of $m$.
Hence $m$ must have exactly two divisors, so it must be prime by definition.
This means that the other divisor of $m$, apart from $m$ itself, must be $1$.
That is:
$\dfrac m {2^n - 1} = 1$
Hence the result.

title: Common Ratio in Rational Geometric Sequence is Rational
theorem_text:
Let $\sequence {a_k}$ be a geometric sequence whose terms are rational.
Then the common ratio of $\sequence {a_k}$ is rational.
proof_text:
Let $r$ be the common ratio of $\sequence {a_k}$.
Let $p, q$ be consecutive terms of $r$.
By hypothesis $p, q \in \Q$.
Then, by definition of geometric sequence:
$q = r p$
It follows that:
$r = \dfrac q p$
From Rational Numbers form Field, $\Q$ is closed under division.
Thus $r \in \Q$ and hence the result.

title: Common Ratio in Integer Geometric Sequence is Rational
theorem_text:
Let $\sequence {a_k}$ be a geometric sequence whose terms are all integers.
Then the common ratio of $\sequence {a_k}$ is rational.
proof_text:
From Integers form Subdomain of Rationals it follows that $a_k \in \Q$ for all $0 \le k \le n$.
The result follows from Common Ratio in Rational Geometric Sequence is Rational.

title: Form of Geometric Sequence of Integers
theorem_text:
Let $P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n}$ be a geometric sequence of length $n + 1$ consisting of integers only.
Then the $j$th term of $P$ is given by:
$a_j = k p^{n - j} q^j$
where:
: the common ratio of $P$ expressed in canonical form is $\dfrac q p$
$k$ is an integer.
proof_text:
Let $r$ be the common ratio of $P$.
From Common Ratio in Integer Geometric Sequence is Rational, $r$ is a rational number.
Let $r = \dfrac q p$ be in canonical form.
Thus, by definition:
$p \perp q$
Let $a$ be the first term of $P$.
Then the sequence $P$ is:
$P = \paren {a, a \dfrac q p, a \dfrac {q^2} {p^2}, \ldots, a \dfrac {q^n} {p^n} }$
All the elements of $P$ are integers, so, in particular:
$a \dfrac {q^n} {p^n} \in \Z$
We have that:
$p \perp q$
From Powers of Coprime Numbers are Coprime:
$q^n \perp p^n$
and so from Euclid's Lemma:
$p^n \divides a$
Thus:
$a = k p^n$
for some $k \in \Z$, and so:
$P = \paren {k p^n, k q p^{n - 1}, k q^2 p^{n - 2}, \ldots, k q^{n - 1} p, k q^n}$

title: Integers are Coprime iff Powers are Coprime
theorem_text:
Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers.
Then:
$a \perp b \iff \forall n \in \N: a^n \perp b^n$
That is, two integers are coprime if and only if all their positive integer powers are coprime.
proof_text:
The forward implication is shown in Powers of Coprime Numbers are Coprime.
The reverse implication is shown by substituting $n = 1$.

title: Open Real Interval is Subset of Closed Real Interval
theorem_text:
Let $a, b \in \R$ be real numbers.
Then:
$\openint a b \subseteq \closedint a b$
where:
$\openint a b$ is the open interval between $a$ and $b$
$\closedint a b$ is the closed interval between $a$ and $b$.
proof_text:
Let $x \in \openint a b$.
Then by definition of open interval:
$a < x < b$
Thus:
$a \le x \le b$
and so by definition of closed interval:
$x \in \closedint a b$

title: Set Union Preserves Subsets/General Result
theorem_text:
Let $\mathbb S, \mathbb T$ be sets of sets.
Suppose that for each $S \in \mathbb S$ there exists a $T \in \mathbb T$ such that $S \subseteq T$.
Then $\bigcup \mathbb S \subseteq \bigcup \mathbb T$.
proof_text:
Let $x \in \bigcup \mathbb S$.
By the definition of union, there exists an $S \in \mathbb S$ such that $x \in S$.
By the premise, there exists a $T \in \mathbb T$ such that $S \subseteq T$.
By the definition of Subset:
$x \in T$
Thus by the definition of union:
$x \in \bigcup \mathbb T$

title: Subset of Cartesian Product not necessarily Cartesian Product of Subsets
theorem_text:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets.
Let $A$ and $B$ both have at least two distinct elements.
Then there exists $W \subseteq A \times B$ such that $W$ is not the cartesian product of a subset of $A$ and a subset of $B$.
proof_text:
Let $a \in A, b \in A, c \in B, d \in B$ be arbitrary elements of $A$ and $B$.
Let:
$W = \set {\tuple {a, c}, \tuple {a, d}, \tuple {b, d} }$
Then $W \subseteq A \times B$.
Suppose $W = X \times Y$ such that $X \subseteq A, Y \subseteq B$.
Then $a, b \in X$ and $c, d \in Y$.
But $X \times Y$ also contains $\tuple {b, c}$ which is not in $W$.
Hence the result.

title: Binomial Coefficient is Integer
theorem_text:
Let $\dbinom n k$ be a binomial coefficient.
Then $\dbinom n k$ is an integer.
proof_text:
If it is not the case that $0 \le k \le n$, then the result holds trivially.
So let $0 \le k \le n$.
By the definition of binomial coefficients:
$$\binom n k = \frac {n!} {k!\left({n - k}\right)!}$$
$$= \frac {n \left({n - 1}\right) \left({n - 2}\right) \ldots \left({n - k + 1}\right)} {k!}$$
The numerator is a product of $k$ successive integers.
From Factorial Divides Product of Successive Numbers, $k!$ divides it.

title: Inverse Mapping is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ and $g: T \to S$ be inverse mappings of each other.
Then $f$ and $g$ are bijections.
proof_text:
From Inverse is Mapping implies Mapping is Injection and Surjection:
$f$ is both an injection and a surjection.
Again from Inverse is Mapping implies Mapping is Injection and Surjection:
$g$ is both an injection and a surjection.
The result follows by definition of bijection.

title: Cardinality of Set of Restrictions of Mapping
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let the cardinality of $S$ be $n$.
Let $F$ be the set of restrictions of $f$ to a subset of $S$.
Then there are $2^n$ elements of $F$.
proof_text:
Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.
Let $g: A \to T$ be the restriction of $f$ to $A$.
By definition of restriction of mapping:
$\forall x \in A: \map g x = \map f x$
and hence there is one mapping $g: A \to T$ such that $g$ is a restriction of $f$.
Therefore for each subset of $S$ there exists a unique restriction of $f$ to that subset.
Therefore there are as many restriction of $f$ as there are subsets of $S$.
That is, by definition of power set, the same as the number of elements of the power set of $S$.
From Cardinality of Power Set of Finite Set, that is $2^n$.

title: Projection is Surjection/Family of Sets
theorem_text:
Let $\family {S_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I}$ be a family of sets.
Let $\displaystyle \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha$ be the Cartesian product of $\family {S_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I}$.
Let each of $S_\alpha$ be non-empty.
For each $\beta \in I$, let $\displaystyle \pr_\beta: \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha \to S_\beta$ be the $\beta$th projection on $\displaystyle S = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha$.
Then $\pr_\beta$ is a surjection.
proof_text:
Consider the $\beta$th projection.
Let $x_\beta \in S_\beta$.
Let $\map x \beta = x_\beta$
Suppose $\gamma \in I: \gamma \ne \beta$.
As $S_\gamma \ne \O$ it is possible to use the axiom of choice to choose $\map x \gamma \in S_\gamma$.
Then:
$\displaystyle x \in \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha$
and:
$\map {\pr_\beta} x = \map x \beta$
Hence the result.

title: Taxicab Metric on Real Vector Space is Metric
theorem_text: The taxicab metric on the real vector space $\R^n$ is a metric.
proof_text:
This is an instance of the taxicab metric on the cartesian product of $A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}$.
This is proved in Taxicab Metric is Metric.

title: Chebyshev Distance on Real Vector Space is Metric
theorem_text:
The Chebyshev distance on $\R^n$:
$\displaystyle \forall x, y \in \R^n: d_\infty \left({x, y}\right):= \max_{i \mathop = 1}^n {\left\vert{x_i - y_i}\right\vert}$
is a metric.
proof_text:
This is an instance of the Chebyshev distance on the cartesian product of metric spaces $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_3$.
This is proved in Chebyshev Distance is Metric.

title: Taxicab Metric is Topologically Equivalent to Chebyshev Distance on Real Vector Space
theorem_text:
For $n \in \N$, let $\R^n$ be a real vector space.
Let $d_1$ be the taxicab metric on $\R^n$.
Let $d_\infty$ be the Chebyshev distance on $\R^n$.
Then
$\forall x, y \in \R^n: d_\infty \left({x, y}\right) \le d_1 \left({x, y}\right) \le n \cdot d_\infty \left({x, y}\right)$
It follows that $d_1$ and $d_\infty$ are Lipschitz equivalent.
proof_text:
By definition of the Chebyshev distance on $\R^n$, we have:
$\displaystyle d_\infty \left({x, y}\right) = \max_{i \mathop = 1}^n {\left\vert{x_i - y_i}\right\vert}$
where $x = \left({x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}\right)$ and $y = \left({y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n}\right)$.
Let $j$ be chosen so that:
$\displaystyle \left\vert{x_j - y_j}\right\vert = \max_{i \mathop = 1}^n {\left\vert{x_i - y_i}\right\vert}$
Then:
$$d_\infty \left({x, y}\right) = \left\vert{x_j - y_j}\right\vert$$
Definition of Chebyshev distance
$$\le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \left\vert{x_i - y_i}\right\vert$$
$$= d_1 \left({x, y}\right)$$
$$\le n \left\vert{x_j - y_j}\right\vert$$
$$= n \cdot d_\infty \left({x, y}\right)$$

title: Euclidean Metric is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $M_{1'} = \left({A_{1'}, d_{1'}}\right), M_{2'} = \left({A_{2'}, d_{2'}}\right), \ldots, M_{n'} = \left({A_{n'}, d_{n'}}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $\displaystyle \mathcal A = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}$.
The Euclidean metric on $\mathcal A$ is a metric.
proof_text:
The Euclidean metric on $\mathcal A$ is a special case of the $p$-product metric.
The result follows from $p$-Product Metric is Metric.

title: Number of Multiples less than Given Number
theorem_text:
Let $m, n \in \N_{\ge 1}$.
The number of multiples of $m$ not greater than $n$ is given by:
$q = \floor {\dfrac n m}$
where $\floor {\cdot}$ denotes the floor function
proof_text:
By the Division Theorem:
$(1): \quad n = q m + r$
where $0 \le r < q$.
As $r < q$, it follows that the greatest multiple of $m$ up to $n$ is $q m$.
So all the multiples of $m$ up to $n$ are:
$m, 2 m, 3 m, \ldots, q m$
Dividing both sides of $(1)$ by $q$:
$(2): \quad \dfrac n m = q + \dfrac r m$
Taking the floor of $(2)$:
$\floor {\dfrac n m} = \floor {q + \dfrac r m}$
But as $0 \le \dfrac r m < 1$:
$\floor {q + \dfrac r m} = q$
Recall that all the multiples of $m$ up to $n$ are $m, 2 m, 3 m, \ldots, q m$.
It follows that the number of multiples of $m$ up to $n$ is:
$q = \floor {\dfrac n m}$

title: Restriction of Non-Continuous Mapping on Metric Space to Subspace may be Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$ be a metric spaces.
Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping.
Let $Y \subseteq A_1$.
Let $f {\restriction_Y}: Y \to A_2$ be the restriction of $f$ to $Y$.
Let $f {\restriction_Y}$ be $\left({d_Y, d_2}\right)$-continuous.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $f$ is also $\left({d_1, d_2}\right)$-continuous.
proof_text:
Proof by Counterexample:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be given by:
$f \left({x}\right) = \begin{cases}
0 & : x \in \Q \\
1 & : x \in \R
\end{cases}$
where $\Q$ is the set of rational numbers.
Then $f {\restriction_\Q}: \Q \to \R$ is the constant function $f_0$ with value $0$.
By Constant Mapping is Continuous, $f {\restriction_\Q}$ is continuous at every point.
However, $f$ is not continuous at any point on $\R$.

title: Supremum Metric on Bounded Real Functions on Closed Interval is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval.
Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$.
Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
The interval is an instance of a set.
Hence Supremum Metric on Bounded Real-Valued Functions is Metric can be directly applied.

title: Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Subspace of Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval.
Let $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$.
Let $\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right)$ be the set of all bounded real functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$.
Let $d$ be the supremum metric on $\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right)$.
Then $\left({\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], d_{\mathscr C} }\right)$ is a subspace of $\left({\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right), d}\right)$.
proof_text:
Let $f \in \mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$.
Then by Image of Closed Real Interval is Bounded, $f$ is bounded on $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$.
Thus $f \in \mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right)$ and the result follows.

title: Convergence of Square of Linear Combination of Sequences whose Squares Converge
theorem_text:
Let $\sequence {x_i}$ and $\sequence {y_i}$ be real sequences such that the series $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ and $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} y_i^2$ are convergent.
Let $\lambda, \mu \in \R$ be real numbers.
Then $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2$ is convergent.
proof_text:
Let $n \in \N$.
Then:
$\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2 = \lambda^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2 + \mu^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2 + 2 \lambda \mu \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i y_i$
By Cauchy's Inequality:
$\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i y_i \le \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2}^{\frac 1 2}$
Hence:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2 \le \lambda^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2 + \mu^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2 + 2 \size {\lambda \mu} \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i y_i$$
$$\le \lambda^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2 + \mu^2 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2 + 2 \size {\lambda \mu} \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2}^{\frac 1 2}$$
$$= \paren {\size \lambda \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} + \size \mu \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n y_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} }^2$$
$$\le \paren {\size \lambda \paren {\sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} + \size \mu \paren {\sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} y_i^2}^{\frac 1 2} }^2$$
Thus the sequence of partial sums $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2$ is bounded above.
We also have that $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2$ is also increasing.
So by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2$ is convergent.

title: Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \left({A, d_2}\right)$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then $\ell^2$ is a metric space.
proof_text:
$\ell^2$ is a particular instance of the general $p$-sequence space $\ell^p$.
Hence $p$-Sequence Space of Real Sequences is Metric Space can be applied directly.

title: Supremum Metric on Bounded Real-Valued Functions is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $X$ be a set.
Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real-valued functions $f: X \to \R$.
Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
We have that the supremum metric on $A \times A$ is defined as:
$\displaystyle \forall f, g \in A: d \left({f, g}\right) := \sup_{x \mathop \in X} \left\vert{f \left({x}\right) - g \left({x}\right)}\right\vert$
where $f$ and $g$ are bounded real-valued functions.
From Real Number Line is Metric Space, the real numbers $\R$ together with the absolute value function form a metric space.
The result follows by Supremum Metric is Metric.

title: Supremum Metric on Bounded Real Sequences is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real sequences.
Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
By definition, a real sequence is a mapping from the natural numbers $\N$ to the real numbers $\R$.
Thus a bounded real sequence is a bounded real-valued function.
The result follows from Supremum Metric on Bounded Real-Valued Functions is Metric.

title: Supremum Metric on Bounded Continuous Mappings is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $A$ be the set of all continuous mappings $f: M_1 \to M_2$ which are also bounded.
Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
The set $A$ is a subset of the set $A'$ of all bounded mappings $f: M_1 \to M_2$.
Let $d': A' \times A' \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A'$.
From Supremum Metric is Metric, $\left({A', d'}\right)$ is a metric space.
By definition, $A$ is a metric subspace of $A'$.
Hence the result.

title: Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval.
Let $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$.
Let $d$ be the supremum metric on  $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
Let $\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right)$ be the set of all bounded real functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$.
From Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Subspace of Bounded, $\left({\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], d_{\mathscr C} }\right)$ is a (metric) subspace of $\left({\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right), d}\right)$.
The result follows from Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space.

title: Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval.
Let $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$.
Let $d$ be the supremum metric on  $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$.
Then $d$ is a metric.
proof_text:
Let $A := \mathscr D^r \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R$ which are of differentiability class $r$.
Let $d_r: A \times A \to \R$ be the supremum metric on $A$, defined as:
$\displaystyle \forall f, g \in A: d \left({f, g}\right) := \sup_{\substack {x \mathop \in \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \\ i \mathop \in \left\{ {0, 1, 2, \ldots, r}\right\} } } \left\vert{f^{\left({i}\right)} \left({x}\right) - g^{\left({i}\right)} \left({x}\right)}\right\vert$
where:
$f$ and $g$ are continuous functions on $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ which are $r$ times differentiable
$r \in \N$ is a natural number.
From Supremum Metric on Differentiability Class is Metric, $d_r$ is a metric on $A$.
By definition, real functions which are continuous on $\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ are of differentiability class $0$.
Thus setting $r = 0$ it follows that $\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ is $\mathscr D^0 \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$.
The result follows.

title: Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $M = \left({A, d}\right)$ be a metric space.
Let $H \subseteq A$.
Let $d_H: H \times H \to \R$ be the restriction $d \restriction_{H \times H}$ of $d$ to $H$.
Let $\left({H, d_H}\right)$ be a metric subspace of $\left({A, d}\right)$.
Then $d_H$ is a metric on $H$.
proof_text:
By definition of restriction:
$\forall x, y \in H: d_H \left({x, y}\right) = d \left({x, y}\right)$
As $d$ is a metric, the metric space axioms are all fulfilled by all $x, y \in A$ under $d$.
As $H \subseteq A$, by definition of subset, all $x, y \in H$ are also elements of $A$.
Therefore the metric space axioms are all fulfilled by all $x, y \in H$ under $d_H$.

title: P-adic Metric is Metric
theorem_text:
Let $p \in \N$ be a prime.
Let $\norm{\,\cdot\,}_p: \Q \to \R_{\ge 0}$ be the $p$-adic norm on $\Q$.
Let $d_p$ be the $p$-adic metric on $\Q$:
$\forall x, y \in \Q: \map {d_p} {x, y} = \norm{x - y}_p$
Then $d_p$ is a metric.
proof_text:
The $p$-adic metric on $\Q$ is defined as the metric induced by the $p$-adic norm on $\Q$.
It follows from Metric Induced by Norm is Metric that $d_p$ is a metric.

title: Constant Function is Continuous/Metric Space/Proof 2
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $f_c: A_1 \to A_2$ be the constant mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$:
$\exists c \in A_2: \forall a \in A_1: f_c \left({a}\right) = c$
That is, every point in $A_1$ maps to the same point $c$ in $A_2$.
Then $f_c$ is continuous throughout $A_1$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_2$.
proof_text:
Let $f_c: A_1 \to A_2$ be the constant mapping between two metric spaces $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$.
Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$.
Let $x \in A_1$.
Pick any $\delta \in \R_{>0}$.
Let $y \in A_1$ such that $d_1 \left({x, y}\right) < \delta$.
Now we have:
$f_c \left({x}\right) = c = f_c \left({y}\right)$
Hence:
$d_2 \left({f_c \left({x}\right), f_c \left({y}\right)}\right) = d_2 \left({c, c}\right)$
By definition of a metric:
$d_2 \left({c, c}\right) = 0 < \epsilon$
Thus we have that:
$\forall \epsilon > 0: \forall x \in A_1: \exists \delta \in \R: d_1 \left({x, y}\right) < \delta \implies d_2 \left({f_c \left({x}\right), f_c \left({y}\right)}\right) < \epsilon$
Hence by definition of continuity on a metric space, $f_c$ is continuous throughout $A_1$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_2$.

title: Constant Function is Continuous/Metric Space/Proof 1
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $f_c: A_1 \to A_2$ be the constant mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$:
$\exists c \in A_2: \forall a \in A_1: f_c \left({a}\right) = c$
That is, every point in $A_1$ maps to the same point $c$ in $A_2$.
Then $f_c$ is continuous throughout $A_1$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_2$.
proof_text:
Let $f_c: A_1 \to A_2$ be the constant mapping between two metric spaces $M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right)$ and $M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right)$.
From Constant Function is Uniformly Continuous, $f_c$ is uniformly continuous throughout $A_1$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_2$.
The result follows from Uniformly Continuous Function is Continuous.

title: Identity Mapping on Real Vector Space from Chebyshev to Euclidean Metric is Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space.
Let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on $\R^n$.
Let $d_\infty$ be the Chebyshev distance on $\R^n$.
Let $I: \R^n \to \R^n$ be the identity mapping from $\R^n$ to itself.
Then the mapping:
$I: \struct {\R^n, d_\infty} \to \struct {\R^n, d_2}$
is $\tuple {d_\infty, d_2}$-continuous.
proof_text:
Let $a = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in \R^n$.
Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$.
Let $\delta = \dfrac {\epsilon} {\sqrt n}$.
Let $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be such that $\map {d_\infty} {x, a} < \delta$.
That is:
$\ds \max_{i \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \set {\size {a_i - x_i} } < \delta$
Then:
$$\map {d_2} {x, a} = \sqrt {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {a_i - x_i} }$$
$$\le \sqrt {n \max_{i \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \set {\size {a_i - x_i} } }$$
$$< \sqrt {n \delta^2}$$
$$= \sqrt {\epsilon^2}$$
$$= \epsilon$$
The result follows by definition of $\tuple {d_\infty, d_2}$-continuity.

title: Composite of Continuous Mappings at Point between Metric Spaces is Continuous at Point
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({X_1, d_1}\right), M_2 = \left({X_2, d_2}\right), M_3 = \left({X_3, d_3}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $f: M_1 \to M_2$ be continuous at $a \in X_1$.
Let $g: M_2 \to M_3$ be continuous at $f \left({a}\right) \in X_2$.
Then their composite $g \circ f: M_1 \to M_3$ is continuous at $a \in X_1$.
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$.
The strategy is to find a $\delta \in \R_{>0}$ such that:
$d_1 \left({x, a}\right) < \delta \implies d_3 \left({g \left({f \left({x}\right)}\right), g \left({f \left({a}\right)}\right)}\right) < \epsilon$
As $g$ is continuous at $f \left({a}\right)$:
$\exists \eta \in \R_{>0}: \forall y \in X_2: d_2 \left({y, f \left({a}\right)}\right) < \eta \implies d_3 \left({g \left({y}\right), g \left({f \left({a}\right)}\right)}\right) < \epsilon$
As $f$ is continuous at $a$:
$\forall \eta \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in X_1: d_1 \left({x, a}\right) < \delta \implies d_2 \left({f \left({x}\right), f \left({a}\right)}\right) < \eta$
Hence:
$d_3 \left({g \left({f \left({x}\right)}\right), g \left({f \left({a}\right)}\right)}\right) < \epsilon$

title: Composite of Continuous Mappings between Metric Spaces is Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $M_1 = \left({X_1, d_1}\right), M_2 = \left({X_2, d_2}\right), M_3 = \left({X_3, d_3}\right)$ be metric spaces.
Let $f: M_1 \to M_2$ and $g: M_2 \to M_3$ be continuous mappings.
Then their composite $g \circ f: M_1 \to M_3$ is continuous.
proof_text:
From Metric Induces Topology, the metric spaces described are topological spaces.
The result follows from Composite of Continuous Mappings is Continuous.
