title: Zeroes of Infinite Product of Analytic Functions
theorem_text:
Let $D \subset \C$ be an open connected set.
Let $\left\langle{f_n}\right\rangle$ be a sequence of analytic functions $f_n: D \to \C$.
Let $\displaystyle \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converge locally uniformly to $f$.
Let $z_0\in D$.
Then:
$(1): \quad$ $f$ is identically zero if and only if some $f_n$ is identically zero
$(2): \quad$ $f_n \left({z_0}\right) = 0$ for finitely many $n \in \N$
$(3): \quad$ If $f$ is not identically zero, $\operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({f}\right) = \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \operatorname{mult}_{z_0} \left({f_n}\right)$
where $\operatorname{mult}$ denotes multiplicity.
proof_text:
Note that by Infinite Product of Analytic Functions is Analytic, $f$ is analytic.
Let $n_0 \in \N$ and $U\subset D$ an open neighborhood of $z_0$ such that $\displaystyle \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty f_n \left({z}\right) \ne 0$ for $z\in U$.
Let $f$ be identically zero on $U$.
Then $\displaystyle \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^{n_0-1} f_n \left({z}\right)$ is identically zero on $U$.
Then some $f_k$ with $k<n_0$ is identically zero on $U$.
By Uniqueness of Analytic Continuation, $f_k$ is identically zero on $D$.
Now let $f$ be not identically zero on $U$.
We have:
$$\operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({f}\right) = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^{n_0} \operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({f_n}\right) + \operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({\prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty f_n}\right)$$
Multiplicity of Product of Analytic Functions
$$= \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^{n_0} \operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({f_n}\right)$$
$\displaystyle \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty f_n \left({z_0}\right) \ne 0$
$$= \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \operatorname {mult}_{z_0} \left({f_n}\right)$$
$f_n \left({z_0}\right) \ne 0$ for $n \ge n_0$

title: Bounds for Complex Exponential
theorem_text:
Let $\exp$ denote the complex exponential.
Let $z \in \C$ with $\cmod z \le \dfrac 1 2$.
Then
$\dfrac 1 2 \cmod z \le \cmod {\exp z - 1} \le \dfrac 3 2 \cmod z$
proof_text:
By definition of complex exponential:
$\exp z = \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {z^n} {n!}$
Thus
$$\cmod {\exp z - 1 - z} = \cmod {\sum_{n \mathop = 2}^\infty \frac {z^n} {n!} }$$
Linear Combination of Convergent Series
$$\le \sum_{n \mathop = 2}^\infty \cmod {\frac {z^n} {n!} }$$
Triangle Inequality for Series
$$\le \sum_{n \mathop = 2}^\infty \frac {\cmod z^n} 2$$
as $n \ge 2$
$$= \frac {\cmod z^2 / 2} {1 - \cmod z}$$
Sum of Geometric Sequence
$$\le \frac 1 2 \cmod z$$
as $\cmod z \le \dfrac 1 2$
By the Triangle Inequality:
$\dfrac 1 2 \cmod z \le \cmod {\exp z - 1} \le \dfrac 3 2 \cmod z$

title: Sum of 2 Squares in 2 Distinct Ways/Examples/50
theorem_text:
$50$ is the smallest positive integer which can be expressed as the sum of two square numbers in two distinct ways:
$$50 = 5^2 + 5^2$$
$$= 7^2 + 1^2$$
proof_text:
The smallest two positive integers which can be expressed as the sum of two distinct square numbers are:
$$5 = 1^2 + 2^2$$
$$10 = 1^2 + 3^2$$
We have that:
$50 = 5 \times 10$
Thus:
$$= \paren {1^2 + 2^2} \paren {1^2 + 3^2}$$
$$= \paren {1 \times 1 + 2 \times 3}^2 + \paren {1 \times 3 - 2 \times 1}^2$$
Brahmagupta-Fibonacci Identity
$$= \paren {1 + 6}^2 + \paren {3 - 2}^2$$
$$= 7^2 + 1^2$$
$$= 49 + 1$$
$$= 50$$
and:
$$= \paren {1^2 + 2^2} \paren {1^2 + 3^2}$$
$$= \paren {1 \times 1 - 2 \times 3}^2 + \paren {1 \times 3 + 2 \times 1}^2$$
Brahmagupta-Fibonacci Identity: Corollary
$$= \paren {1 - 6}^2 + \paren {3 + 2}^2$$
$$= \paren {6 - 1}^2 + \paren {3 + 2}^2$$
$$= 5^2 + 5^2$$
$$= 25 + 25$$
$$= 50$$

title: Sum of 2 Squares in 2 Distinct Ways/Examples/65
theorem_text:
$65$ can be expressed as the sum of two square numbers in two distinct ways:
$$65 = 8^2 + 1^2$$
$$= 7^2 + 4^2$$
proof_text:
We have that:
$65 = 5 \times 13$
Both $5$ and $13$ can be expressed as the sum of two distinct square numbers:
$$5 = 1^2 + 2^2$$
$$13 = 2^2 + 3^2$$
Thus:
$$= \paren {1^2 + 2^2} \paren {2^2 + 3^2}$$
$$= \paren {1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3}^2 + \paren {1 \times 3 - 2 \times 2}^2$$
Brahmagupta-Fibonacci Identity
$$= \paren {2 + 6}^2 + \paren {3 - 4}^2$$
$$= \paren {2 + 6}^2 + \paren {4 - 3}^2$$
$$= 8^2 + 1^2$$
$$= 64 + 1$$
$$= 65$$
and:
$$= \paren {1^2 + 2^2} \paren {2^2 + 3^2}$$
$$= \paren {1 \times 2 - 2 \times 3}^2 + \paren {1 \times 3 + 2 \times 2}^2$$
Brahmagupta-Fibonacci Identity: Corollary
$$= \paren {2 - 6}^2 + \paren {3 + 4}^2$$
$$= \paren {6 - 2}^2 + \paren {3 + 4}^2$$
$$= 4^2 + 7^2$$
$$= 16 + 49$$
$$= 65$$

title: Lower Adjoint at Element is Minimum of Preimage of Singleton of Element implies Composition is Identity
theorem_text:
Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}, R = \struct {T, \precsim}$ be ordered sets.
Let $g: S \to T, d: T \to S$ be mappings such that
$\forall t \in T: \map d t = \min \set {g^{-1} \sqbrk {\set t} }$
Then $g \circ d = I_T$
where $I_T$ denotes the identity mapping of $T$.
proof_text:
Let $t \in T$.
By assumption:
$\map d t = \min \set {g^{-1} \sqbrk {\set t} }$
By definition of min operation:
$\map d t = \map \inf {g^{-1} \sqbrk {\set t} }$ and $\map d t \in g^{-1} \sqbrk {\set t}$
By definition of image of set:
$\map g {\map d t} \in \set t$
By definition of singleton:
$\map g {\map d t} = t$
Thus by definition of composition of mappings:
$\map {\paren {g \circ d} } t = t$

title: Order of Product of Entire Function with Polynomial
theorem_text:
Let $f:\C\to\C$ be an entire function of order $\omega$.
Let $P:\C\to\C$ be a nonzero polynomial.
Then $f\cdot P$ has order $\omega$.
proof_text:
By Order of Product of Entire Functions and Polynomial has Order Zero, $f\cdot P$ has order at most $\omega$.
By Limit at Infinity of Polynomial, there exist $r,\delta>0$ such that $|P(z)| \geq \delta$ for $|z|\geq r$.
Suppose $\displaystyle \log\left(\max_{|z|\leq R}|f(z)P(z)|\right) = O(R^\beta)$ for some $\beta < \omega$.
By the Maximum Modulus Principle $\max_{|z|\leq R}|f(z)| \leq \frac1\delta \max_{|z|\leq R}|f(z)P(z)|$ for $R\geq r$.
Thus $\displaystyle \log\left(\max_{|z|\leq R}|f(z)|\right) = O(R^\beta)$.
This is a contradiction.
Thus $f\cdot P$ has order $\omega$.

title: Order is Maximum of Exponent of Convergence and Degree
theorem_text:
Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function.
Let $\omega$ be its order.
Let $\tau$ be its exponent of convergence.
Let $h$ be the degree of the polynomial in its canonical factorization.
Then:
$\omega = \map \max {\tau, h}$
proof_text:
By Exponent of Convergence is Less Than Order:
$\tau \le \omega$
By Hadamard Factorization Theorem:
$h \le \omega$
Thus:
$\map \max {\tau, h} \le \omega$
By Order is Less Than Maximum of Exponent of Convergence and Degree:
$\omega \le \map \max {\tau, h}$

title: Jacobi's Necessary Condition/Dependent on N Functions
theorem_text:
Let $J$ be a functional, such that:
$J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \displaystyle \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$
where $\mathbf y = \paren {\sequence {y_i}_{1 \le i \le N} }$ is an N-dimensional real vector.
Let $\map {\mathbf y} x$ correspond to the minimum of $J$.
Let the $N\times N$ matrix $\mathbf P = F_{y_i' y_j'}$ be positive definite along $\map {\mathbf y} x$.
Then the open interval $\openint a b$ contains no points conjugate to $a$.
proof_text:
By Necessary Condition for Twice Differentiable N Function dependent Functional to have Minimum, $J$ is minimised by $y = \map {\mathbf {\hat y} } x$ if:
$\delta^2 J \sqbrk {\mathbf {\hat y}; \mathbf h} \ge 0$
for all admissable real functions $\mathbf h$.
By lemma 1 of Legendre's Condition:
$\ds \delta^2 J \sqbrk {\mathbf y; \mathbf h} = \int_a^b \paren {\mathbf h' \mathbf P \mathbf h' + \mathbf h \mathbf Q \mathbf h} \rd x$
where:
$\mathbf P = F_{y_i' y_j'}$
By Nonnegative Quadratic N function dependent Functional implies no Interior Conjugate Points, $\openint a b$ does not contain any conjugate points with respect to $J$.

title: Dirichlet Convolution is Commutative
theorem_text: $f * g = g * f$
proof_text:
From the definition of the Dirichlet convolution:
$\displaystyle \left({f * g}\right) \left({n}\right) = \sum_{a b \mathop = n} f \left({a}\right) g \left({b}\right)$
By definition, arithmetic functions are mappings from the natural numbers $\N$ to the complex numbers $\C$.
Thus $f \left({a}\right), g \left({b}\right) \in \C$ and commutativity follows from commutativity of multiplication of complex numbers.

title: Even Integer with Abundancy Index greater than 9
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ have an abundancy index greater than $9$.
Then $n$ has at least $35$ distinct prime factors.
proof_text:
Since Sigma Function is Multiplicative, it follows easily that abundancy index is multiplicative as well.
We have for any prime $p$ and positive integer $k$:
$$\frac {\map \sigma {p^k} } {p^k} = \frac {p^{k + 1} - 1} {p^k \paren {p - 1} }$$
Sigma Function of Power of Prime
$$= \frac {p - p^{-k} } {p - 1}$$
$$< \frac p {p - 1}$$
as $p^{-k} > 0$
$$= 1 + \frac 1 {p - 1}$$
In fact this is the limit of the abundancy index of a prime power.
The greater the prime, the smaller this value is.
Therefore finding the least number of prime factors a number needs to have its abundancy index exceed $9$ is to find the least $m$ such that:
$\displaystyle \prod_{i = 1}^m \frac {p_i} {p_i - 1} > 9$
where $p_i$ is the $i$th prime ordered by size.
The result can be verified by direct computation.

title: Tetrahedral Number as Sum of Squares
theorem_text:
$H_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n / 2} \paren {n - 2 k}^2$
where $H_n$ denotes the $n$th tetrahedral number.
proof_text:
Let $n$ be even such that $n = 2 m$.
We have:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n / 2} \paren {n - 2 k}^2 = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^m \paren {2 m - 2 k}^2$$
$$= \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^m \paren {2 k}^2$$
Permutation of Indices of Summation
$$= \frac {2 m \paren {m + 1} \paren {2 m + 1} } 3$$
Sum of Sequence of Even Squares
$$= \frac {2 m \paren {2 m + 1} \paren {2 m + 2} } 6$$
$$= H_{2 m}$$
Closed Form for Tetrahedral Numbers
Let $n$ be odd such that $n = 2 m + 1$.
We have:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n / 2} \paren {n - 2 k}^2 = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^m \paren {2 m + 1 - 2 k}^2$$
$$= \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^m \paren {2 k + 1}^2$$
Permutation of Indices of Summation
$$= \frac {\paren {m + 1} \paren {2 m + 1} \paren {2 m + 3} } 3$$
Sum of Sequence of Odd Squares: Formulation 1
$$= \frac {\paren {2 m + 1} \paren {2 m + 2} \paren {2 m + 3} } 6$$
$$= H_{2 m + 1}$$
Closed Form for Tetrahedral Numbers

title: Sum of Sequence of Odd Squares/Formulation 1
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \forall n \in \N: \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \paren {2 i + 1}^2 = \frac {\paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} \paren {2 n + 3} } 3$
proof_text:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \paren {2 i + 1}^2 = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \paren {2 i}^2 + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n 4 i + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n 1$$
$$= \frac {2 n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 3 + 4 \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n i + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n 1$$
Sum of Sequence of Even Squares
$$= \frac {2 n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 3 + 4 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n 1$$
adjustment of indices: $4 i = 0$ when $i = 0$
$$= \frac {2 n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 3 + 4 \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2 + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n 1$$
Closed Form for Triangular Numbers
$$= \frac {2 n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 3 + 2 n \paren {n + 1} + \paren {n + 1}$$
further simplification
$$= \frac {\paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n \paren {2 n + 1} + 6 n + 3} } 3$$
factorising
$$= \frac {\paren {n + 1} \paren {4 n^2 + 8 n + 3} } 3$$
multiplying out
$$= \frac {\paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} \paren {2 n + 3} } 3$$
factorising

title: Internal Angle of Equilateral Triangle
theorem_text: The internal angles of an equilateral triangle measure $60^\circ$ or $\dfrac \pi 3$ radians.
proof_text:
By definition, an equilateral triangle is a regular polygon with $3$ sides.
From Internal Angles of Regular Polygon, the size $A$ of each internal angle of a regular $n$-gon is given by:
$A = \dfrac {\paren {n - 2} 180^\circ} n$
Thus:
$A = \dfrac {180^\circ} n = 60^\circ$
From Value of Degree in Radians:
$1^\circ = \dfrac {\pi} {180^\circ} \mathrm {rad}$
and so:
$A = 60^\circ \times \dfrac {\pi} {180^\circ} = \dfrac \pi 3 \mathrm {rad}$

title: Smallest Positive Integer which is Sum of 2 Odd Primes in 6 Ways
theorem_text: The smallest positive integer which is the sum of $2$ odd primes in $6$ different ways is $60$.
proof_text:
$$60 = 7 + 53$$
$6$ ways
$$= 13 + 47$$
$$= 17 + 43$$
$$= 19 + 41$$
$$= 23 + 37$$
$$= 29 + 31$$
It is determined that there are no smaller numbers with this property by inspection:
$$58 = 53 + 5$$
$3$ ways
$$= 47 + 11$$
$$= 41 + 17$$
$$= 29 + 29$$
$$56 = 53 + 3$$
$3$ ways
$$= 43 + 13$$
$$= 37 + 19$$
$$54 = 47 + 7$$
$5$ ways
$$= 43 + 11$$
$$= 41 + 13$$
$$= 37 + 17$$
$$= 31 + 23$$
$$52 = 47 + 5$$
$3$ ways
$$= 41 + 11$$
$$= 29 + 23$$
$$50 = 47 + 3$$
$4$ ways
$$= 43 + 7$$
$$= 37 + 13$$
$$= 31 + 19$$
From the workings of Smallest Positive Integer which is Sum of 2 Odd Primes in n Ways, $48$ is the smallest positive integer which is the sum of $2$ odd primes in $5$ different ways.
Thus there is no need to explore smaller numbers.

title: Vector Space has Basis
theorem_text:
Let $K$ be a division ring.
Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$.
Then $V$ has a basis.
proof_text:
The result follows from Vector Space has Basis between Linearly Independent Set and Spanning Set.
It suffices to find a linearly independent subset $L \subseteq V$ that is contained in a spanning set $S \subseteq V$.
By Empty Set is Linearly Independent, $L$ can be taken to be the empty set.
Or if $V$ is nonzero, by Singleton is Linearly Independent, $L$ can be taken to be any singleton of $V$.
$S$ can be taken to be $V$, since $V$ trivially spans itself.
Therefore, $L$ and $S$ exist and $L \subseteq S$ so $V$ has a basis $B$ with $L \subseteq B \subseteq S$.

title: Reflexive Bilinear Form is Symmetric or Alternating
theorem_text:
Let $\mathbb K$ be a field.
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$.
Let $f$ be a bilinear form on $V$.
Let $f$ be reflexive.
Then $f$ is symmetric or alternating.
proof_text:
Let $x, y, z \in V$.
Because $f$ is bilinear:
$\map f {x, \map f {x, y} z - \map f {x, z} y} = \map f {x, y} \, \map f {x, z} - \map f {x, z} \, \map f {x, y} = 0$
Because $f$ is reflexive:
$\map f {\map f {x, y} z - \map f {x, z} y, x} = 0$
Because $f$ is bilinear:
$(1): \quad \map f {x, y} \, \map f {z, x} = \map f {x, z} \, \map f {y, x}$
Letting $z = x$, we obtain:
$\map f {x, x} \, \map f {x, y} = \map f {x, x} \, \map f {y, x}$
Thus:
$(2): \quad$ if $\map f {x, x} \ne 0$, then $\map f {x, y} = \map f {y, x}$ for all $y \in V$.
Suppose $f$ is not symmetric.
We show that $\map f {u, u} = 0$ for all $u \in V$.
Let $v, w \in V$ with $\map f {v, w} \ne \map f {w, v}$.
By $(2)$, $\map f {v, v} = \map f {w, w} = 0$.
Suppose $u \in V$ with $\map f {u, u} \ne 0$.
By $(2)$, $\map f {u, v} = \map f {v, u}$ and $\map f {u, w} = \map f {w, u}$.
By $(1)$, we have:
$\begin{cases} \map f {v, w} \, \map f {u, v} = \map f {v, u} \, \map f {w, v} \\ \map f {w, v} \, \map f {u, w} = \map f {w, u} \, \map f {v, w} \end{cases}$.
Because $\map f {v, w} \ne \map f {w, v}$:
$\begin{cases} \map f {u, v} = \map f {v, u} = 0 \\ \map f {u, w} = \map f {w, u} = 0 \end{cases}$.
Because $f$ is bilinear, $\map f {u + v, w} = \map f {v, w} \ne \map f {v, w} = \map f {u + v, w}$.
By $(2)$, $\map f {u + v, u + v} = 0$.
Because $f$ is bilinear and $\map f {u, v} = \map f {v, u} = \map f {v, v} = 0$, $\map f {u, u} = 0$.
This contradicts the assumption $\map f {u, u} \ne 0$.
Thus $f$ is alternating.

title: Pluperfect Digital Invariant has less than 61 Digits
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a pluperfect digital invariant.
Then $n$ has less than $61$ digits.
proof_text:
We have that:
$n \times 9^n < 10^\left({n - 1}\right)$
when $n > 60$.
So an $n$-digit integer, for $n > 60$, is always greater than the sum of the $n$th powers of its digits.

title: Extended Rolle's Theorem
theorem_text:
Let $f: D \to \R$ be differentiable on a closed interval $I \subseteq \R$.
Let $x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n \in I$.
Let $f \left({x_i}\right) = 0$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n$.
Then for all $i = 0, \ldots, n-1$:
$\exists \xi_i \in \left({x_i \,.\,.\, x_{i+1}}\right): f' \left({\xi_i}\right) = 0$
proof_text:
Since $f$ is differentiable on $I$, f is differentiable on $\left[{x_i \,.\,.\, x_{i+1}}\right]$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n-1$.
Thus a fortiori, $f$ is also continuous on the closed interval $\left[{x_i \,.\,.\, x_{i+1}}\right]$ and differentiable on the open interval $\left({x_i \,.\,.\, x_{i+1}}\right)$.
For $i = 0, \ldots, n$ we have $f \left({x_i}\right) = 0$.
Hence the conditions of Rolle's Theorem are fulfilled on each interval which yields the result.

title: Pell's Equation/Examples/61
theorem_text:
$x^2 - 61 y^2 = 1$
has the smallest positive integral solution:
$x = 1 \, 766 \, 319 \, 049$
$y = 226 \, 153 \, 980$
proof_text:
From Continued Fraction Expansion of $\sqrt {61}$:
$\sqrt {61} = \left[{7, \left\langle{1, 4, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3, 4, 1, 14}\right\rangle}\right]$
The cycle is of length is $11$.
By the solution of Pell's Equation, the only solutions of $x^2 - 61 y^2 = 1$ are:
${p_{11 r} }^2 - 61 {q_{11 r} }^2 = \left({-1}\right)^{11 r}$
for $r = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
When $r = 1$ this gives:
${p_{11}}^2 - 61 {q_{11}}^2 = -1$
which is not the solution required.
When $r = 2$ this gives:
${p_{22} }^2 - 61 {q_{22} }^2 = 1$
From Convergents of Continued Fraction Expansion of $\sqrt {61}$:
$p_{22} = 1 \, 766 \, 319 \, 049$
$q_{22} = 226 \, 153 \, 980$
although on that page the numbering goes from $p_0$ to $p_{21}$, and $q_0$ to $q_{21}$.

title: No Infinitely Descending Membership Chains/Corollary
theorem_text:
There cannot exist a sequence $\left\langle{x_n}\right\rangle$ whose domain is $\N_{\gt 0}$ such that:
$\forall n \in \N_{\gt 0}: x_{n+1} \in x_n$
proof_text:
Aiming for contradiction, suppose that there is a sequence like that.
From the definition of a sequence, let $f$ be the the mapping that is defined by $\left\langle{x_n}\right\rangle$.
Let $\omega$ denote the minimal infinite successor set.
Let $g: \omega \to \N_{\gt 0}$ be defined as:
$g \left({\alpha}\right) = \alpha + 1$
Then the composition $f \circ g$ is a mapping whose domain is $\omega$ such that:
$\forall n \in \omega: \left({f \circ g}\right) \left({n^+}\right) \in \left({f \circ g}\right) \left({n}\right)$
But this contradicts No Infinitely Descending Membership Chains.
Therefore by contradiction there cannot exist such a sequence.
Hence the result.

title: Kaprekar's Process for 2-Digit Numbers
theorem_text:
Kaprekar's process, when applied to a non-repdigit $2$-digit positive integer leads to the cycle:
$09 \to 81 \to 63 \to 27 \to 45 \to 09$
Note that it is important to retain the leading zero on the $9$, or the process trivially terminates in $0$.
proof_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a $2$-digit positive integer.
without loss of generality, let $n$ be expressed in decimal notation as:
$n = 10 x + y$
where:
$x > y$
$0 \le x \le 9, 0 \le y \le 9$
The reversal of $n$ is $10 y + x$.
We have:
$$10x + y - 10 y - x = 9 \left({x - y}\right)$$
where $1 \le x - y \le 9$
Thus after the first iteration of Kaprekar's process, $n$ is one of:
$09$
$18$
$27$
$36$
$45$
or their reversals.
Applying Kaprekar's process to $09$ gives:
$$09 = 90 - 09$$
$$= 81$$
$$\to 81 - 18$$
$$= 63$$
$$\to 63 - 36$$
$$= 27$$
$$\to 72 - 27$$
$$= 45$$
$$\to 45 - 54$$
$$= 09$$
All those multiples of $9$ can be seen to be in (or end up in) this loop.
Hence the result.

title: Cube as Sum of Sequence of Centered Hexagonal Numbers
theorem_text:
$C_n = \displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n H_i$
where:
$C_n$ denotes the $n$th cube number
$H_i$ denotes the $i$th centered hexagonal number.
proof_text:
From Closed Form for Centered Hexagonal Numbers:
$H_n = 3 n \paren {n - 1} + 1$
Hence:
$$\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n H_i = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {3 i \paren {i - 1} + 1}$$
$$= \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {3 i^2 - 3 i + 1}$$
$$= 3 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i^2  - 3 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n 1$$
$$= 3 \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6 - 3 \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n 1$$
Sum of Sequence of Squares
$$= 3 \frac {n \paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} } 6 - 3 \frac {n \paren {n + 1} } 2 + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n 1$$
Closed Form for Triangular Numbers
$$= \frac {n \paren {\paren {n + 1} \paren {2 n + 1} - 3 \paren {n + 1} + 2} } 2$$
simplification
$$= \frac {n \paren {2 n^2 + 3 n + 1 - 3 n - 3 + 2} } 2$$
multiplying out
$$= \frac {n \paren {2 n^2} } 2$$
simplification
$$= n^3$$
simplification

title: Magic Constant of Order 5 Magic Square
theorem_text: The magic constant of the order $5$ magic square is $65$.
proof_text:
Let $M_5$ denote an order $5$ magic square
By Sum of Terms of Magic Square, the total of all the entries in $M_5$ is given by:
$T_5 = \dfrac {5^2 \left({5^2 + 1}\right)} 2 = \dfrac {25 \times 26} 2 = 325$
As there are $5$ rows of $M_5$, the magic constant of $M_5$ is given by:
$S_5 = \dfrac {325} 5 = 65$

title: Triple of Triangular Numbers whose Pairwise Sums are Triangular
theorem_text:
The following triplet of triangular numbers has the property that the sum of each pair of them, and their total, are all triangular numbers:
$66, 105, 105$
proof_text:
Throughout we use Closed Form for Triangular Numbers, which gives that the $n$th triangular number can be expressed as:
$T_n = \dfrac {11 \times 12} 2$
We have:
$$66 = \frac {11 \times 12} 2$$
and so is triangular
$$105 = \frac {14 \times 15} 2$$
and so is triangular
Then:
$$66 + 105 = 171$$
$$= \frac {18 \times 19} 2$$
and so is triangular
$$105 + 105 = 210$$
$$= \frac {20 \times 21} 2$$
and so is triangular
$$66 + 105 + 105 = 210$$
$$= \frac {23 \times 24} 2$$
and so is triangular

title: Euler Phi Function of Non-Square Semiprime
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a semiprime with distinct prime factors $p$ and $q$.
Let $\map \phi n$ denote the Euler $\phi$ function.
Then:
$\map \phi n = \paren {p - 1} \paren {q - 1}$
proof_text:
As $p$ and $q$ are distinct prime numbers, it follows that $p$ and $q$ are coprime.
Thus by Euler Phi Function is Multiplicative:
$\map \phi n = \map \phi p \, \map \phi q$
From Euler Phi Function of Prime:
$\map \phi p = p - 1$
$\map \phi q = q - 1$
Hence the result.

title: Euler Phi Function of Non-Square Semiprime
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a semiprime with distinct prime factors $p$ and $q$.
Let $\map \phi n$ denote the Euler $\phi$ function.
Then:
$\map \phi n = \paren {p - 1} \paren {q - 1}$
proof_text:
A semiprime with distinct prime factors is a square-free integer.
$\map \phi n = \displaystyle \prod_{\substack {p \mathop \divides n \\ p \mathop > 2} } \paren {p - 1}$
where $p \divides n$ denotes the primes which divide $n$.
As there are $2$ prime factors: $p$ and $q$, this devolves to:
$\map \phi n = \paren {p - 1} \paren {q - 1}$
except when $p = 2$, in which case:
$\map \phi n = q - 1$
But when $p = 2$, we have that $p - 1 = 1$ and so:
$\paren {p - 1} \paren {q - 1} = q - 1$
Hence the result.

title: Euler Phi Function of Square-Free Integer
theorem_text:
Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 2$.
Let $n$ be square-free.
Let $\map \phi n$ be the Euler $\phi$ function of $n$.
That is, let $\map \phi n$ be the count of strictly positive integers less than or equal to $n$ which are prime to $n$.
Then:
$\map \phi n = \displaystyle \prod_{\substack {p \mathop \divides n \\ p \mathop > 2} } \paren {p - 1}$
where $p \divides n$ denotes the primes which divide $n$.
proof_text:
We have that the Euler Phi Function is Multiplicative.
Let the prime decomposition of $n$ be:
$\displaystyle n = \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le r} p_i =  p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r$
From the definition of prime number, each of the prime factors of $n$ is coprime to all other divisors of $n$.
From Euler Phi Function of Prime, we have:
$\map \phi {p_i} = \paren {p_i - 1}$
Thus:
$\map \phi n = \displaystyle \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le r} \paren {p_i - 1}$
or:
$\map \phi n = \displaystyle \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} \paren {p - 1}$
where $p$ ranges over all prime numbers
When $p = 2$ we have that:
$p - 1 = 1$
and so:
$\displaystyle \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} \paren {p - 1} = \prod_{\substack {p \mathop \divides n \\ p \mathop > 2} } \paren {p - 1}$
Hence the result.

title: Euler Phi Function of Square-Free Integer
theorem_text:
Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 2$.
Let $n$ be square-free.
Let $\map \phi n$ be the Euler $\phi$ function of $n$.
That is, let $\map \phi n$ be the count of strictly positive integers less than or equal to $n$ which are prime to $n$.
Then:
$\map \phi n = \displaystyle \prod_{\substack {p \mathop \divides n \\ p \mathop > 2} } \paren {p - 1}$
where $p \divides n$ denotes the primes which divide $n$.
proof_text:
From Euler Phi Function of Integer:
$\displaystyle \map \phi n = n \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} \paren {1 - \frac 1 p}$
As $n$ is square-free:
$\displaystyle n = \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} p$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \map \phi n = \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} p \paren {1 - \frac 1 p}$
and so:
$\displaystyle \map \phi n = \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} \paren {p - 1}$
When $p = 2$ we have that:
$p - 1 = 1$
and so:
$\displaystyle \prod_{p \mathop \divides n} \paren {p - 1} = \prod_{\substack {p \mathop \divides n \\ p \mathop > 2} } \paren {p - 1}$
Hence the result.

title: Euler Phi Function of 2 times Odd Prime
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a semiprime of the form $2 p$, where $p$ is an odd prime.
Let $\map \phi n$ denote the Euler $\phi$ function.
Then:
$\map \phi n = p - 1$
proof_text:
By definition $n$ is a semiprime.
As $p$ is an odd prime, $n$ is not square.
Thus from Euler Phi Function of Non-Square Semiprime:
$\map \phi n = \paren {2 - 1} \paren {p - 1}$
Hence the result.

title: Product of Number of Edges, Edges per Face and Faces of Tetrahedron
theorem_text: The product of the number of edges, edges per face and faces of a tetrahedron is $72$.
proof_text:
A tetrahedron has:
$6$ edges
and:
$4$ faces.
Each face is a triangle, and so has $3$ edges.
Hence:
$6 \times 4 \times 3 = 72$

title: Product of Number of Edges, Edges per Face and Faces of Cube
theorem_text: The product of the number of edges, edges per face and faces of a cube is $288$.
proof_text:
A cube has:
$12$ edges
and:
$6$ faces.
Each face is a square, and so has $4$ edges.
Hence:
$12 \times 6 \times 4 = 288$

title: Product of Number of Edges, Edges per Face and Faces of Regular Octahedron
theorem_text: The product of the number of edges, edges per face and faces of a regular octahedron is $288$.
proof_text:
A regular octahedron has:
$12$ edges
and:
$8$ faces.
Each face is a triangle, and so has $3$ edges.
Hence:
$12 \times 8 \times 3 = 288$

title: Ordinals are Well-Ordered/Corollary
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a set of ordinals.
Let $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ denote the epsilon restriction on $A$.
Then $A$ is strictly well-ordered by $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$.
proof_text:
Let $A$ be a set of ordinals.
Let $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ denote the epsilon restriction on $A$.
It is to be shown that $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ is antireflexive.
Suppose there is a $a \in A$ such that $a \in a$.
Then by ordinal is element of ordinal iff proper subset of ordinal, we have $a \subsetneq a$.
And so:
$\exists x \in a: x \notin a$
But this is a contradiction, so $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ must be antireflexive.
By Strict Subset Relation is Transitive, it follows that $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ is transitive.
By Ordinals are Well-Ordered, it follows that for any non-empty subset $B \subseteq A$ there is a smallest element $x \in B$ such that:
$\forall y \in B: x \in y \lor x = y$
It has been shown that $\Epsilon {\restriction_A}$ is a strict ordering such that every non-empty subset of $A$ has a smallest element.
Hence the result.

title: Product of Number of Edges, Edges per Face and Faces of Regular Dodecahedron
theorem_text: The product of the number of edges, edges per face and faces of a regular dodecahedron is $1800$.
proof_text:
A regular dodecahedron has:
$30$ edges
and:
$12$ faces.
Each face is a pentagon, and so has $5$ edges.
Hence:
$30 \times 12 \times 5 = 1800$

title: Product of Number of Edges, Edges per Face and Faces of Regular Icosahedron
theorem_text: The product of the number of edges, edges per face and faces of a regular icosahedron is $1800$.
proof_text:
A regular icosahedron has:
$30$ edges
and:
$20$ faces.
Each face is a triangle, and so has $3$ edges.
Hence:
$30 \times 20 \times 3 = 1800$

title: Positive Integers whose Square Root equals Sum of Digits
theorem_text:
The following positive integers have a square root that equals the sum of their digits:
$0, 1, 81$
and there are no more.
proof_text:
$$\sqrt 0 = 0$$
$$\sqrt 1 = 1$$
$$\sqrt {81} = 9$$
$$= 8 + 1$$
By considering the square roots, we are looking for positive integers with a square for which its sum of digits is equal to the original number.
It is easy to verify the result up to $36$.
We prove that for $n > 36$, the sum of digits of $n^2$ cannot equal $n$.
Let $n$ be a $d$-digit number.
Then $n < 10^d$.
Thus $n^2 < 10^{2 d}$.
Therefore $n^2$ has at most $2 d$ digits.
Hence the sum of digits of $n^2$ is at most $18 d$.
If $n$ is a $2$-digit number, we have $n > 36 = 18 d$.
Now suppose $d \ge 3$.
Then:
$$n \ge 10^{d - 1}$$
$$= 10 \times 10^{d - 2}$$
$$\ge 10 \paren {1 + 9 \paren {d - 2} }$$
Bernoulli's Inequality
$$= 90 d - 170$$
$$\ge 18 d + 216 - 170$$
as $d \ge 3$
$$> 18 d$$
Therefore for $n > 36$, the sum of digits of $n^2$ cannot equal $n$.

title: Closed Form for Heptagonal Numbers
theorem_text:
The closed-form expression for the $n$th heptagonal number is:
$H_n = \dfrac {n \paren {5 n - 3} } 2$
proof_text:
Heptagonal numbers are $k$-gonal numbers where $k = 7$.
From Closed Form for Polygonal Numbers we have that:
$\map P {k, n} = \dfrac n 2 \paren {\paren {k - 2} n - k + 4}$
Hence:
$$H_n = \frac n 2 \paren {\paren {7 - 2} n - 7 + 4}$$
Closed Form for Polygonal Numbers
$$= \dfrac {n \paren {5 n - 3} } 2$$
Hence the result.

title: Repdigit Number consisting of Instances of 9 is Kaprekar
theorem_text: A repdigit number that consists entirely of the digit $9$ is a Kaprekar number.
proof_text:
We note as examples:
$$9^2 = 81$$
$$8 + 1 = 9$$
$$99^2 = 9801$$
$$98 + 01 = 99$$
$$999^2 = 998001$$
$$998 + 001 = 999$$
Now we consider:
$$\paren {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n 9 \times 10^k}^2 = \paren {10^{n + 1} - 1}^2$$
Sum of Geometric Sequence
$$= 10^{n + 1} \paren {10^{n + 1} - 2} + 1$$
So $\paren {10^{n + 1} - 1}^2$ can be split as:
$\paren {10^{n + 1} - 2} + 1 = 10^{n + 1} - 1 = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n 9 \times 10^k$
Thus $\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n 9 \times 10^k$ is a Kaprekar number.

title: Difference between Two Squares equal to Repunit
proof_text:
Let $x^2 - y^2 = R_n$ for some $n$, where $R_n$ denotes the $n$-digit repunit.
From Integer as Difference between Two Squares:
$R_n$ has at least two distinct divisors of the same parity.
Then from Difference of Two Squares:
$x = \dfrac {a + b} 2$
$y = \dfrac {a - b} 2$
where:
$R_n = a b$
for all $a, b$ where:
$a b = R_n$
$a$ and $b$ are of the same parity.
Here we have that $R_n$ is odd.
So both $a$ and $b$ are always odd and therefore always of the same parity.
It remains to perform the calculations and evaluate the examples.

title: Smallest 3-Digit Permutable Prime
theorem_text: The smallest $3$-digit permutable prime is $113$.
proof_text:
$113$ is prime.
$131$ is prime.
$311$ is prime.
Consider the $3$-digit primes smaller than $113$:
$101, 103, 107, 109$
They all contain a zero.
Thus, for each of these, at least one permutation ends in a zero.
Hence it is divisible by $10$ and so is not prime.

title: 3-Digit Permutable Primes
theorem_text:
The $3$-digit permutable primes are:
$311, 199, 337$
and their anagrams, and no other.
proof_text:
It is confirmed that:
$113, 131, 311$ are all prime
$199, 919, 991$ are all prime
$337, 373, 733$ are all prime.
From Digits of Permutable Prime, all permutable primes contain digits in the set:
$\left\{ {1, 3, 7, 9}\right\}$
The sum of a $3$-digit repdigit number is divisible by $3$.
By Divisibility by 3 it follows that all $3$-digit repdigit numbers are divisible by $3$ and therefore composite.
Hence the possibly permutable primes are:
$113, 117, 119, 133, 137, 139, 177, 179, 199, 337, 339, 377, 379, 399, 779, 799$
and their anagrams.
We eliminate $113, 199, 337$ from this list, as it has been established that they are permutable primes.
Of those remaining, the following are composite:
$$117 = 3^2 \times 13$$
$$119 = 7 \times 17$$
$$133 = 7 \times 19$$
$$177 = 3 \times 59$$
$$339 = 3 \times 113$$
$$377 = 13 \times 29$$
$$779 = 19 \times 41$$
$$799 = 17 \times 47$$
It remains to demonstrate that at least one anagram of the remaining numbers:
$137, 139, 179, 379$
is composite.
We find that:
$$371 = 7 \times 53$$
$$319 = 11 \times 29$$
$$791 = 7 \times 113$$
$$793 = 13 \times 61$$
All contenders are eliminated except for the established permutable primes $113, 119, 337$ and their anagrams.

title: Digits of Permutable Prime
theorem_text:
Let $p$ be a permutable prime with more than $1$ digit.
Then $p$ contains only digits from the set:
$\left\{ {1, 3, 7, 9}\right\}$
proof_text:
First note that from 3-Digit Permutable Primes, both $337$ and $199$ are permutable primes.
Hence it follows that all the elements of $\left\{ {1, 3, 7, 9}\right\}$ appear in at least one permutable prime.
Let $p$ contain an even digit $d$.
Then at least one anagram $p'$ of $p$ has $d$ at the end.
From Divisibility by 2, it follows that $p'$ is even.
As $p$ has more than $1$ digit it follows that $p'$ is composite.
Let $p$ contain the digit $5$.
Then at least one anagram $p'$ of $p$ has $5$ at the end.
From Divisibility by 5, it follows that $p'$ is divisible by $5$.
Except for $5$ itself, all integers which are divisible by $5$ are composite.
As $p$ has more than $1$ digit it follows that $p'$ is composite.
The result follows by definition of permutable prime.

title: Prime Repdigit Number is Repunit
theorem_text:
Let $b \in \Z_{>0}$ be an integer greater than $1$.
Let $n \in \Z$ expressed in base $b$ be a repdigit number with more than $1$ digit.
Let $n$ be prime.
Then $n$ is a repunit (in base $b$).
proof_text:
Let $n$ be a repdigit number with $k$ digits.
Then by the Basis Representation Theorem:
$\displaystyle n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^k m b^j$
for some $m$ such that $1 \le m < b$.
Let $m \ge 2$.
Then:
$\displaystyle n = m \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^k b^j$
and so has $m$ as a divisor.
Hence $n$ is not prime.
The result follows by the Rule of Transposition.

title: 2-Digit Permutable Primes
theorem_text:
The $2$-digit permutable primes are:
$11, 13, 17, 37, 79$
and their anagrams, and no other.
proof_text:
It is confirmed that:
$13$ and $31$ are both prime
$17$ and $71$ are both prime
$37$ and $73$ are both prime.
$79$ and $97$ are both prime.
From Digits of Permutable Prime, all permutable primes contain digits in the set:
$\left\{ {1, 3, 7, 9}\right\}$
By Prime Repdigit Number is Repunit, all $2$-digit repdigit numbers are composite except for $11$ which is prime.
From Repunit Prime is Permutable Prime, it follows that $11$ is a permutable prime.
Apart from $11$ whose status is known, the possibly permutable primes are:
$13, 17, 19, 37, 39, 79$
and their anagrams.
We eliminate $13, 17, 37, 79$ from this list, as it has been established that they are permutable primes.
Of those remaining, the following is composite:
$$39 = 3 \times 13$$
It remains to demonstrate that the anagram of $19$, that is, $91$, composite.
We find that:
$$91 = 7 \times 13$$
All contenders are eliminated except for the established permutable primes $11, 13, 17, 37, 79$ and their anagrams.

title: Smallest Number to appear 6 Times in Pascal's Triangle
theorem_text: The smallest positive integer greater than $1$ to appear $6$ times in Pascal's Triangle is $120$.
proof_text:
We have:
$\dbinom {120} 1 = \dbinom {16} 2 = \dbinom {10} 3 = \dbinom {10} 7 = \dbinom {16} {14} = \dbinom {120} {119} = 120$
To verify that this is the smallest, we look at binomial coefficients that are no more than $120$.
Observe that for $n > 120$, $1 \le k \le n - 1$:
$\dbinom n k \ge \dbinom n 1 = n > 120$
For $n > 16$, $2 \le k \le n - 2$:
$\dbinom n k \ge \dbinom n 2 = \dfrac {n \paren {n - 1}} {2!} > \dfrac {16 \paren {15}} {2!} = 120$
For $n > 10$, $3 \le k \le n - 3$:
$\dbinom n k \ge \dbinom n 3 = \dfrac {n \paren {n - 1} \paren {n - 2}} {3!} > \dfrac {10 \paren 9 \paren 8} {3!} = 120$
Any number, except $2$, appears twice in the form $\dbinom n 1$ and $\dbinom n {n - 1}$.
Therefore we scout for numbers appearing four times, not as those forms, by listing $\dbinom n k$ for:
$n \le 10$ and $2 \le k \le n - 2$;
$n \le 16$ and $k = 2$ or $n - 2$
They are:
$6$
$10, 10$
$15, 20, 15$
$21, 35, 35, 21$
$28, 56, 70, 56, 28$
$36, 84, 126, 126, 84, 36$
$45, 120, *, *, *, 120, 45$
$55, 55$
$66, 66$
$78, 78$
$91, 91$
$105, 105$
$120, 120$
and we see that the only number appearing four times is $120$.

title: Smallest Number with 16 Divisors
theorem_text: The smallest positive integer with $16$ divisors is $120$.
proof_text:
From Tau Function of 120:
$\map \tau {120} = 16$
The result is a specific instance of Smallest Number with $2^n$ Divisors:
$120 = 2 \times 3 \times 4 \times 5$

theorem_text:
The number defined as:

$\times 37 \times 41 \times 53 \times 61 \times 67^2 \times 71^2 \times 73 \times 83 \times 89 \times 103 \times 127 \times 131$
$\times 149 \times 211 \times 307 \times 331 \times 463 \times 521 \times 683 \times 709 \times 1279 \times 2141 \times 2557 \times 5113$

is multiply perfect of order $8$.

From Sigma Function is Multiplicative, we may take each prime factor separately and form $\map \sigma n$ as the product of the $\sigma$ function of each.
