For a simple connected planar graph $G_n$, where $n \geq 3$ is a number of vertices:
$m \leq 3 n − 6$, where $m$ is a number of edges.
proof_text:
Let $f$ denote the number of faces of $G_n$.
Let the sequence $\left\langle{s_i}\right\rangle_{i \mathop = 1}^f$ be the regions of a planar embedding of $G_n$.
Consider the sequence $\left\langle{r_i}\right\rangle_{i \mathop = 1}^f$ where $r_i$ denotes the number of boundary edges for $s_i$.
Since $G$ is simple, then (by the definition of planar embedding):
* every region has at least $3$ boundary edges
* every edge is a boundary edge of at most two regions in the planar embedding.
Using this two facts, we can find the boundary for $\displaystyle \sum \limits_{i + 1}^f r_i$ as:
$3 f \le \displaystyle \sum \limits_{i + 1}^f r_i \le 2m$
Now calculating the Euler Polyhedron Formula with $f \le 2 m /3$, we will arrive to $m \le 3 n − 6$.

title: Existence of Connected Space which is Totally Pathwise Disconnected
theorem_text: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is both connected and totally pathwise disconnected.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be Gustin's sequence space.
From Gustin's Sequence Space is Connected, $T$ is a connected space.
From Gustin's Sequence Space is Totally Pathwise Disconnected, $T$ is a totally pathwise disconnected space.
Hence the result.

title: Zero Dimensional Space is not necessarily T0
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a zero dimensional topological space.
Then $T$ is not necessarily a $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) space.
proof_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a partition space.
From Partition Topology is Zero Dimensional, $T$ is a zero dimensional topological space.
From Partition Topology is not $T_0$, $T$ is not a $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) space.

title: Scattered Space is not necessarily T1
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a scattered topological space.
Then $T$ is not necessarily a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
proof_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a non-trivial particular point space.
From Particular Point Space is Scattered, $T$ is a scattered space.
From Non-Trivial Particular Point Topology is not $T_1$, $T$ is not a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.

title: Existence of Connected Non-T1 Scattered Space
theorem_text: There exists at least one example of a connected topological space which is not a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space, which is also a scattered space.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be a divisor space.
From Divisor Space is Connected, $T$ is a connected space.
From Divisor Space is not $T_1$, $T$ is not a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
From Divisor Space is Scattered, $T$ is a scattered space.
Hence the result.

title: Sorgenfrey Line is not Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {\mathbb R, \tau}$ be the Sorgenfrey line.
Then $T$ is not second-countable.
proof_text:
Suppose $\BB$ is a basis for $\tau$.
By definition of basis:
$\forall U \in \tau: \forall x \in U: \exists B \in \BB: x \in B \subseteq U$
For all $x \in \R$, pick $U = \hointr x {x + \epsilon} \in \tau$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.
Now:
$\forall x \in \R: \exists B_x \in \BB: x \in B_x \subseteq \hointr x {x + \epsilon}$
This $\BB_x$ has an infimum equal to $x$.
So for different $x$, the corresponding $\BB_x$ is different.
So the cardinality of $\BB$ is at least $\size \R$, which is uncountable.

title: Existence of Biconnected Set without Dispersion Point
theorem_text: There exists at least one example of a biconnected set which does not have a dispersion point.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be a Miller's biconnected set.
From Miller's Biconnected Set is Biconnected, $T$ is a biconnected set.
From Miller's Biconnected Set is has no Dispersion Point, $T$  does not have a dispersion point.
Hence the result.

title: Existence of Connected Punctiform Space
theorem_text: There exists at least one example of a connected topological space which is also punctiform.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be Cantor's leaky tent.
From Cantor's Leaky Tent is Connected, $T$ is a connected topological space.
From Cantor's Leaky Tent is Punctiform, $T$ is a punctiform space.
Hence the result.

title: Metric Space is Completely Normal
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
Then $M$ is a completely normal space.
proof_text:
By definition, a topological space is completely normal space if and only if it is:
:a $T_5$ space
:a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
We have that:
:a Metric Space is $T_5$
:a Metric Space is $T_2$ (Hausdorff)
:a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) Space is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) Space.
Hence the result.

title: Metric Space is Perfectly Normal
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
Then $M$ is a perfectly normal space.
proof_text:
By definition, a topological space is perfectly normal space if and only if it is:
:a perfectly $T_4$ space
:a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
We have that:
:a Metric Space is Perfectly $T_4$
:a Metric Space is $T_2$ (Hausdorff)
:a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) Space is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) Space.

title: Bounded Metric Space is not necessarily Totally Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a bounded metric space.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $M$ is totally bounded.
proof_text:
Let $M = \struct {\R, d}$ be the real number line with the Euclidean metric.
Let $M' = \struct {\R, \delta}$ be the unity-bounded metric space on $M$ where $\delta$ is defined as:
$\delta = \dfrac d {1 + d}$
From Unity-Bounded Metric Space is Bounded, $M'$ is a bounded metric space.
From Unity-Bounded Metric Space on Real Number Line is not Totally Bounded, $M'$ is not a totally bounded metric space.

title: Topological Completeness is not Hereditary
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space which is topologically complete.
Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.
Let $\struct {H, \tau_H}$ be the topological subspace of $T$ induced by $H$.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $\struct {H, \tau_H}$ is also topologically complete.
That is, topological completeness is not hereditary.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {\R, d}$ denote the real number line under the Euclidean metric.
Let $\struct {\Q, d}$ denote the rational number space under the Euclidean metric.
We have that $\Q \subset \R$ by definition.
Let $T = \struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the topological space induced on $\R$ by $d$.
By Real Number Line is Complete Metric Space, $\struct {\R, d}$ is a complete metric space.
Thus, by definition, $T$ is topologically complete.
Let $T' = \struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ be the topological space induced on $\Q$ by $d$.
By Rational Number Space is not Complete Metric Space, $\struct {\Q, d}$ is not a complete metric space.
Thus, by definition, $T'$ is not topologically complete.
Hence the result.

title: Sorgenfrey Line is First-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers.
Let $\BB = \set {\hointr a b: a, b \in \R}$.
Let $\tau$ be the topology generated by $\BB$, that is, the Sorgenfrey line.
Then $\tau$ is first-countable.
proof_text:
Let $\BB_x = \set {\hointr x {x + \dfrac 1 n} : n \in \N_{>0} }$.
We will show that:
$(1): \quad \BB_x$ is countable
$(2): \quad \BB_x$ is a local basis at $x$
$(1)$ follows from the fact that $\BB_x$ is a bijection from the set of natural numbers.
$(2)$ is demonstrated as follows:
By definition of local basis, it suffices to show that $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U: \exists B \in \BB_x: B \subseteq U$.
Pick any $U$ in $\tau$.
By definition of $\tau$, there exists $\hointr x {x + \epsilon} \subseteq U$ for some $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$.
By the Archimedean Principle there exists $n \in \N$ such that $n > \dfrac 1 \epsilon$ (that is, $\dfrac 1 n < \epsilon$).
So:
$x \in \hointr x {x + \dfrac 1 n} \subseteq \hointr x {x + \epsilon} \subseteq U$
Therefore $\BB_x$ is a local basis at $x$.
We have seen that the Sorgenfrey line has a countable local basis at every point.
By definition of first-countability, $\tau$ is first-countable.

title: Metrizable Space is not necessarily Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space which is metrizable.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $T$ is second-countable.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be an uncountable discrete space.
From Standard Discrete Metric induces Discrete Topology, $T$ is metrizable.
From Uncountable Discrete Space is not Second-Countable, $T$ is not second-countable.

title: Regular Paracompact Space is not necessarily Metrizable
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space which is regular and paracompact.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $T$ is metrizable.
proof_text:
Let $T$ be the Sorgenfrey line.
From Sorgenfrey Line satisfies all Separation Axioms, $T$ is a regular space.
From Sorgenfrey Line is Paracompact, $T$ is a paracompact space.
From Sorgenfrey Line is not Metrizable, $T$ is not a metrizable space.

title: Uniform Space whose Topology is Metrizable is not necessarily Metrizable
theorem_text:
Let $\UU$ be a uniformity on a set $S$.
Let $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$ be the uniform space generated from $\UU$.
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the uniformizable space yielded by $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$.
Let $T$ be a metrizable space.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $\UU$ is itself a metrizable uniformity.
proof_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be an uncountable discrete ordinal space.
From Uncountable Discrete Ordinal Space is Metrizable, $T$ is a metrizable space.
However, from Uncountable Discrete Ordinal Space has Unmetrizable Uniformity, there exists a uniformity $\UU$ which yields the uniformizable space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ which is not itself a metrizable uniformity.

title: Open Sets in Indiscrete Topology
theorem_text: $H$ is an open set of $T$ if and only if either $H = S$ or $H = \O$.
proof_text:
A set $U$ is open in a topology $\tau$ if $U \in \tau$.
In $\tau = \set {\O, S}$, the only open sets are $\O$ and $S$.

title: Closed Sets in Indiscrete Topology
theorem_text: $H$ is a closed set of $T$ if and only if either $H = S$ or $H = \O$.
proof_text:
A set $U$ is closed in a topology $\tau$ if and only if:
$\relcomp S U \in \tau$
where $\relcomp S U$ denotes the complement of $U$ in $S$.
That is, the closed sets are the complements of the open sets.
From Open Sets in Indiscrete Topology, in $\tau = \set {\O, S}$, the only open sets are $\O$ and $S$.
Hence the only closed sets in the indiscrete topology on $S$ are:
$\relcomp S \O = S$ from Relative Complement of Empty Set
and:
$\relcomp S S = \O$ from Relative Complement with Self is Empty Set
as stated.

title: F-Sigma Sets in Indiscrete Topology
theorem_text: $H$ is an $F_\sigma$ ($F$-sigma) set of $T$ if and only if either $H = S$ or $H = \O$.
proof_text:
An $F_\sigma$ set is a set which can be written as a countable union of closed sets of $S$.
Hence the only $F_\sigma$ sets of $T$ are made from unions of $T$ and $\O$.
So $T$ and $\O$ are the only $F_\sigma$ sets of $T$.

title: G-Delta Sets in Indiscrete Topology
theorem_text: $H$ is a $G_\delta$ ($G$-delta) set of $T$ if and only if either $H = S$ or $H = \O$.
proof_text:
A $G_\delta$ set is a set which can be written as a countable intersection of open sets of $S$.
Hence the only $G_\delta$ sets of $T$ are made from intersections of $T$ and $\O$.
So $T$ and $\O$ are the only $G_\delta$ sets of $T$.

title: Subset of Indiscrete Space is Compact
theorem_text: $H$ is compact in $T$.
proof_text:
The subspace $T_H = \struct {H, \set {\O, S \cap H} }$ is trivially also an indiscrete space.
The only open cover of $T_H$ is $\set H$ itself.
The only subcover of $H$ is, trivially, also $\set H$, which is finite.
So $H$ is (trivially) compact in $T$.

title: Subset of Indiscrete Space is Sequentially Compact
theorem_text: $H$ is sequentially compact in $T$.
proof_text:
From Sequence in Indiscrete Space converges to Every Point, every sequence in $T$ converges to every point of $S$.
So every infinite sequence has a subsequence which converges to every point in $S$.
Hence $H$ is (trivially) sequentially compact in $T$.

title: Limit Points of Sequence in Indiscrete Space on Uncountable Set
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be an uncountable set.
Let $T = \struct {S, \set {\O, S} }$ be the indiscrete topological space on $S$.
Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence in $T$.
Then every sequence in $T$ has an uncountable number of limit points.
proof_text:
From Sequence in Indiscrete Space converges to Every Point, $\sequence {s_n}$ converges to every point of $S$.
As $S$ is uncountable, the result follows.

title: Odd-Even Topology is Lindelöf
theorem_text: $T$ is Lindelöf.
proof_text:
From Odd-Even Topology is Second-Countable, $T$ is second-countable.
The result follows from Second-Countable Space is Lindelöf.

title: Odd-Even Topology is Separable
theorem_text: $T$ is separable.
proof_text:
From Odd-Even Topology is Second-Countable, $T$ is second-countable.
The result follows from Second-Countable Space is Separable.

title: Odd-Even Topology is First-Countable
theorem_text: $T$ is first-countable.
proof_text:
From Odd-Even Topology is Second-Countable, $T$ is second-countable.
The result follows from Second-Countable Space is First-Countable.

title: Zero is Accumulation Point of Sequence in Sierpiński Space
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {\set {0, 1}, \tau_0}$ be a Sierpiński space.
The sequence in $T$:
$\sigma = \sequence {0, 1, 0, 1, \ldots}$
has $0$ as an accumulation point.
proof_text:
By definition, $\alpha$ is an accumulation point of $\sigma$ if and only if:
$\forall U \in \tau_0: \alpha \in U \implies \set {n \in \N: x_n \in U}$ is infinite.
Both $\set 0$ and $\set {0, 1}$ contain $0$, which occurs an infinite number of times in $\sigma$.
Hence, by definition, $0$ is an accumulation point of $\sigma$.

title: 1 is Limit Point of Sequence in Sierpiński Space
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {\set {0, 1}, \tau_0}$ be a Sierpiński space.
The sequence in $T$:
$\sigma = \sequence {0, 1, 0, 1, \ldots}$
has $1$ as a limit point.
proof_text:
By definition, $\alpha$ is a limit point of $\sigma$ if and only if:
$\forall U \in \tau_0: \alpha \in U \implies \set {n \in \N: x_n \notin U}$ is finite.
The only open set of $T$ containing $1$ is $\set {0, 1}$.
It contains all but a finite number (that is: $0$) elements of $\sigma$.
Hence, by definition, $1$ is a limit point of $\sigma$.

title: Closed Extension Topology is not T3
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.
Let $T^*_p = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p}$ be the closed extension space of $T$.
Then $T^*_p$ is not a $T_3$ space.
proof_text:
By Underlying Set of Topological Space is Closed, $S$ is closed in $T$.
By Closed Sets of Closed Extension Topology, $S$ is closed in $T^*_p$.
definition of Closed Extension Space gives:
$p \notin S$
:Every open set in $T^*_p$ is either $\O$ or it contains $p$.
Thus no open set containing $S$ is disjoint from $\set p$.
This shows that $T^*_p$ is not a $T_3$ space.

title: Real Number Line is First-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology.
Then $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ is first-countable.
proof_text:
From Real Number Line is Second-Countable we have that $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ is a second-countable space.
The result follows from Second-Countable Space is First-Countable.

title: Alexandroff Extension is Compact
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a non-empty topological space.
Let $p$ be a new element not in $S$.
Let $S^* := S \cup \set p$.
Let $T^* = \struct {S^*, \tau^*}$ be the Alexandroff extension on $S$.
Then $T^*$ is a compact topological space.
proof_text:
Let $\UU$ be an open cover of $T^*$.
At least one $V \in \UU$ contains $p$.
Because $p \notin S$, $V$ is not an open set of $T$.
Therefore, by definition of the Alexandroff extension, $V$ must be the complement relative to $S^*$ of a closed, compact subset $\relcomp {S^*} V$ of $T$.
Because $\relcomp {S^*} V$ is compact, it can be covered by a finite number of sets in $\UU$.
So:
$T^*$ can be covered by $V$
and:
:that finite number of sets in $\UU$ are a cover for $\relcomp {S^*} V$.
That is, $\UU$ has a finite subcover.
Hence the result by definition of compact topological space.

title: Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is not Hausdorff
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology $\tau_d$.
Let $p$ be a new element not in $\Q$.
Let $\Q^* := \Q \cup \set p$.
Let $T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*}$ be the Alexandroff extension on $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$.
Then $T^*$ is not a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space.
proof_text:
From Condition for Alexandroff Extension to be $T_2$ Space, $T^*$ is a $T_2$ space if and only if $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ is a locally compact Hausdorff Space.
But from Rational Number Space is not Locally Compact Hausdorff Space, $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ is not a locally compact Hausdorff Space.
Hence the result.

title: Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is T1 Space
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology $\tau_d$.
Let $p$ be a new element not in $\Q$.
Let $\Q^* := \Q \cup \set p$.
Let $T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*}$ be the Alexandroff extension on $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$.
Then $T^*$ is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
proof_text:
From Condition for Alexandroff Extension to be $T_1$ Space, $T^*$ is a $T_1$ space if and only if $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ is also a $T_1$ space.
From Rational Numbers form Metric Space, $\struct {\Q, d}$ is a metric space.
From Metric Space fulfils all Separation Axioms, $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ is a $T_1$ space.
Hence the result.

title: Particular Point of Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Dispersion Point
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology $\tau_d$.
Let $p$ be a new element not in $\Q$.
Let $\Q^* := \Q \cup \set p$.
Let $T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*}$ be the Alexandroff extension on $\left({\Q, \tau_d}\right)$.
Then $p$ is a dispersion point of $T^*$.
proof_text:
By definition, $p$ is a dispersion point of $T^*$ if and only if:
$\Q^*$ is a connected set in $T^*$
$\Q^* \setminus \set p$ is totally disconnected in $T^*$.
From Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Connected, $\Q^*$ is a connected set in $T^*$.
It remains to be shown that $\Q^* \setminus \set p$ is totally disconnected in $T^*$.
By definition, $\Q^* \setminus \set p$ is the rational number space $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$.
The result follows from Rational Numbers are Totally Disconnected.

title: Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Biconnected
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology $\tau_d$.
Let $p$ be a new element not in $\Q$.
Let $\Q^* := \Q \cup \set p$.
Let $T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*}$ be the Alexandroff extension on $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$.
Then $T^*$ is a biconnected space.
proof_text:
From Particular Point of Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Dispersion Point, $p$ is a dispersion point of $T^*$.
The result follows from Set with Dispersion Point is Biconnected.

title: Hilbert Sequence Space is Complete Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then $\ell^2$ is a complete metric space.
proof_text:
We have that Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space.
It remains to be shown that it is complete.
Recall that from Real Number Line is Complete Metric Space, $\R$ is a complete metric space.
Let $x^1, x^2, x^3, \ldots$ be a Cauchy sequence $\ell^2$.
Then for each $i \in \N_{>0}$, we have that $\sequence { {x_i}^j}_{j \mathop \in \N_{>0} }$ is a Cauchy sequence in the complete metric space $\R$.
Thus $\sequence { {x_i}^j}_{j \mathop \in \N_{>0} }$ converges to a point in $\R$, say $x_i$.
Then if $x = \sequence {x_i}$, the points $x - x_j$ eventually belong to $H$.
So $x = \paren {x - x_j} + x^j$ must also belong to $H$.
Thus $\map {d_2} {x, x^j} = 0$.
Hence the result.

title: Hilbert Sequence Space is Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\ell^2$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then $\ell^2$ is a second-countable space.
proof_text:
From Hilbert Sequence Space is Separable, $\ell^2$ is a separable space.
We also have that Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space.
The result follows from Separable Metric Space is Second-Countable.

title: Hilbert Sequence Space is Lindelöf
theorem_text:
Let $\ell^2$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then $\ell^2$ is a Lindelöf space.
proof_text:
From Hilbert Sequence Space is Second-Countable, $\ell^2$ is a second-countable space.
The result follows from Second-Countable Space is Lindelöf.

title: Hilbert Sequence Space is not Locally Compact Hausdorff Space
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\sequence {x_i}$ such that the series $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then $\ell^2$ is not a locally compact Hausdorff space.
proof_text:
From Metric Space fulfils all Separation Axioms, $\ell^2$ is a Hausdorff space.
Let $x = \sequence {x_i} \in A$ be a point of $\ell^2$.
From Point in Hilbert Sequence Space has no Compact Neighborhood, $x$ has no compact neighborhood.
Hence the result by definition of locally compact Hausdorff space.

title: Compact Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space is Closed
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\sequence {x_i}$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Let $H$ be a compact subset of $\ell^2$
Then $H$ is closed in $\ell^2$.
proof_text:
From Metric Space fulfils all Separation Axioms, $\ell^2$ is a Hausdorff space.
The result follows from Compact Subspace of Hausdorff Space is Closed.

title: Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space with Non-Empty Interior is not Compact
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Let $H$ be a subset of $\ell^2$ whose interior  is non-empty.
Then $H$ is not compact in $\ell^2$.
proof_text:
Let $x \in H^\circ$, where $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$.
By definition, $H^\circ$ is an open set of $\ell^2$ containing $x$.
Again by definition, $H$ is a neighborhood of $x$.
But from Point in Hilbert Sequence Space has no Compact Neighborhood, $x$ has no compact neighborhood in $\ell^2$.
Thus $H$ cannot be compact in $\ell^2$.

title: Point in Hilbert Sequence Space has no Compact Neighborhood
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Then no point of $\ell^2$ has a compact neighborhood.
proof_text:
From Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space, $\ell^2$ is a metric space.
Let $x = \sequence {x_i} \in A$ be a point of $\ell^2$.
Consider the closed $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $\ell^2$:
$\map { {B_\epsilon}^-} x := \set {y \in A: \map {d_2} {x, y} \le \epsilon}$
for some $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$.
Consider the point:
$\sequence {y_n} = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n - 1}, x_n + \epsilon, x_{n + 1}, \ldots}$
We have that $\sequence {y_n} \in \map { {B_\epsilon}^-} x$.
But for $m \ne n$ we have that:
$\map {d_2} {y_m, y_n} = \epsilon \sqrt 2$
and so $\sequence {y_n}$ has no convergent subsequence.
Thus $\map { {B_\epsilon}^-} x$ is not compact.
So $x$ has no compact neighborhood.

title: Compact Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space is Nowhere Dense
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\sequence {x_i}$ such that the series $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent.
Let $\ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be the Hilbert sequence space on $\R$.
Let $H$ be a compact subset of $\ell^2$.
Then $H$ is nowhere dense in $\ell^2$.
proof_text:
By Compact Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space is Closed, $H$ is a closed set of $\ell^2$.
From Set is Closed iff Equals Topological Closure:
$H^- = H$
where $H^-$ denotes the closure of $H$.
From Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space with Non-Empty Interior is not Compact:
$H^\circ = \O$
where $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$.
Thus:
$\left({H^-}\right)^\circ = \O$
and the result follows by definition of nowhere dense.

title: Hilbert Cube is Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2}$ be the Hilbert cube.
Then $M$ is a metric space.
proof_text:
As defined, $M$ is a subspace of the Hilbert sequence space $\ell^2$.
We have that Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space.
The result follows from Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space.

title: Hilbert Cube is Completely Normal
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2}$ be the Hilbert cube.
Then $M$ is a completely normal space.
proof_text:
We have that Hilbert Cube is Metric Space.
The result follows from Metric Space is Completely Normal.

title: Hilbert Cube is Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2}$ be the Hilbert cube.
Then $M$ is a second-countable space.
proof_text:
From Hilbert Cube is Separable, $M$ is a separable space.
We also have that Hilbert Cube is Metric Space.
The result follows from Separable Metric Space is Second-Countable.

title: Convex Set of Ordered Set is not necessarily Interval
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set.
Let $C$ be a convex set of $S$.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $C$ is an interval of $S$.
proof_text:
Consider the open ray of $S$:
$R = \set {x \in S: a \prec x}$
for some $a \in S$.
From Ray is Convex, $R$ is a convex set of $S$.
But $R$ is not an interval of $S$.

title: Union of Non-Disjoint Convex Sets is Convex Set
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set.
Let $\CC$ be a set of convex sets of $S$ such that their intersection is non-empty:
$\displaystyle \bigcap \CC \ne \O$
Then the union $\displaystyle \bigcup \CC$ is also convex.
proof_text:
Let $x, y, z \in S$ be arbitrary elements of $S$ such that $x \prec y \prec z$.
Let $x, z \in \displaystyle \bigcup \CC$.
First let $x, z \in C$ where $C \in \CC$.
Then as $C$ is convex, $y \in C$.
Hence, by definition of union, $y \in \displaystyle \bigcup \CC$.
Now let $x \in C_1, z \in C_2$ where $C_1, C_2 \in \CC$.
We have that $\displaystyle \bigcap \CC \ne \O$.
Thus $C_1 \cap C_2 \ne \O$.
Then $\exists a \in C_1 \cap C_2: x < a < z$.
Hence one of the following cases holds:
$(1): \quad x < y < a < z$, whence $y \in C_1$, by convexity of $C_1$
$(2): \quad x < a < y < z$, whence $y \in C_2$, by convexity of $C_2$
$(3): \quad y = a$, whence $y \in C_1$ and $y \in C_2$, by definition of $a$.
Thus in all cases $y \in \displaystyle \bigcup \CC$.
Thus $\displaystyle \bigcup \CC$ is convex by definition.

title: Generators of Special Linear Group of Order 2 over Integers
theorem_text:
Let:
$ S = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & - 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$
and:
$T = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$
Then $S$ and $T$ are generators for the special linear group of order $2$ over $\Z$.
proof_text:
Let:
$ g = \begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}$
be an element of $\SL {2, \Z}$.
Observe that:
$T^n = \begin{pmatrix} 
1 & n \\ 
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$
so that:
$T^n g = \begin{pmatrix}
a + nc & b + nd \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}$
Also note that:
$S^2 = -I$
and:
$S g = \begin{pmatrix}
-c & -d \\
a & b
\end{pmatrix}$
We now describe an algorithm to reduce $g$ to the identity matrix only using multiplication by $S$ and $T$.
This will show that $g^{-1}$ can be written as a word in $S$ and $T$.
We can then take the inverse of this expression in $S$ and $T$ and it too will be a word in $S$ and $T$.
Recall $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$.
If $c = 0$ then, since $\map \det g = 1$, we must have $a d = 1$.
Thus $a = d = \pm 1$. In this case:
$g = \pm\begin{pmatrix}
1 & b' \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix} = \pm T^{b'}$
where $b' = \pm b$.
Since $S^2 = -I$ we either have $g = T^{b'}$ or $g = S^2 T^{b'}$.
If $c \ne 0$ we proceed as follows.
Without loss of generality we may suppose $\size a \ge \size c$, for if $\size a < \size c$ we could apply $S$ to swap $a$ and $c$.
By the Division Algorithm, we can write $a = c q + r$ where $q, r \in \Z$ and $0 \le r < \size c$.
Then $T^{-q} g$ has upper left entry $a - q c = r$ which is smaller than $\size c$.
Applying $S$ switches the rows (with a sign change), which then makes our lower left entry $-r$.
We have applied a combination of $S$ and $T$ to turn $g$ into a matrix where the absolute value of the lower left entry is strictly less than the one we started with.
If $r = 0$ then we're in our original case, and we know we can multiply by a multiple of $T$ and $S$ to get to the identity matrix.
Note that this process can have at most $r$ steps, since there are only $r$ natural numbers between $r$ and $0$.
Thus the process terminates in a finite number of steps.

title: Successor Sets of Linearly Ordered Set Induced by Convex Component Partition
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ be a linearly ordered space.
Let $A$ and $B$ be separated sets of $T$.
Let $A^*$ and $B^*$ be defined as:
$A^* := \displaystyle \bigcup \set {\closedint a b: a, b \in A, \closedint a b \cap B^- = \O}$
$B^* := \displaystyle \bigcup \set {\closedint a b: a, b \in B, \closedint a b \cap A^- = \O}$
where $A^-$ and $B^-$ denote the closure of $A$ and $B$ in $T$.
Let $A^*$, $B^*$ and $\relcomp S {A^* \cup B^*}$ be expressed as the union of convex components of $S$:
$\displaystyle A^* = \bigcup A_\alpha, \quad B^* = \bigcup B_\beta, \quad \relcomp S {A^* \cup B^*} = \bigcup C_\gamma$
where $\relcomp S X$ denotes the complement of $X$ with respect to $S$.
Let $M$ be the linearly ordered set:
$M = \set {A_\alpha, B_\beta, C_\gamma}$
as defined in Partition of Linearly Ordered Space by Convex Components is Linearly Ordered Set.
Then each of the sets $A_\alpha \in M$ has an immediate successor in $M$ if $A_\alpha$ intersects the closure of $S_\alpha$, the set of strict upper bounds for $A_\alpha$.
Similarly for $B_\beta$.
That immediate successor ${C_\alpha}^+$ to $A_\alpha$ is an element in $\set {C_\gamma}$.
proof_text:
Let $A_\alpha \cap {S_\alpha}^- \ne \O$.
Then $A_\alpha \cap {S_\alpha}^-$ contains exactly $1$ point, say $p$.
This belongs to the complement in $S$ of the closed set $\paren {B^*}^-$.
Hence there exists a neighborhood $\openint x y$ of $p$ which is disjoint from $\paren {B^*}^-$.
Then:
$\openint x y \cap S_\alpha \ne \O$
and so:
$\openint p y \ne \O$
But $\openint p y$ is disjoint from both $A^*$ and $B^*$.
Thus there must exist some $C_\gamma$ which contains $\openint p y$.

title: Linearly Ordered Space is T1
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ be a linearly ordered space.
Then $T$ is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
proof_text:
Let $p \in S$.
By definition of linearly ordered space, the rays:
$R_1 := \set {x \in S: x \prec p}$
$R_2 := \set {x \in S: p \prec x}$
are open in $T$.
Thus their union:
$R_1 \cup R_2 = \set {x \in S: x \prec p \lor p \prec x}$
is also open in $T$.
Consider the complement in $S$ of $R_1 \cup R_2$:
$\relcomp S {R_1 \cup R_2} = \set {y \in S: y \notin R_1 \cup R_2}$
By definition of closed set, $\relcomp S {R_1 \cup R_2}$ is closed in $T$
But $\relcomp S {R_1 \cup R_2} = \set p$.
Thus $p$ is a closed point of $T$.
Hence the result, by definition of $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.

title: Linearly Ordered Space is Completely Normal
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ be a linearly ordered space.
Then $T$ is a completely normal space.
proof_text:
By Linearly Ordered Space is $T_1$, $T$ is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
By Linearly Ordered Space is $T_5$, $T$ is a $T_5$ space.
Hence the result, by definition of completely normal space.

title: Every Point except Endpoint in Connected Linearly Ordered Space is Cut Point
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ be a linearly ordered space.
Let $A \subseteq S$ be a connected space.
Let $p \in A$ be a point of $A$ which is not an endpoint of $A$.
Then $p$ is a cut point of $A$.
proof_text:
We have that $A \setminus \set p$ is separated by $\set {x \in A: x \prec p}$ and $\set {x \in A: p \prec x}$.
If $p$ is an endpoint of $A$, then either:
$\set {x \in A: x \prec p} = \O$
or:
$\set {x \in A: p \prec x} = \O$

title: Omega is Closed in Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space but not G-Delta Set
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Omega$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Omega$.
Then $\set \Omega$ is a closed set of $\closedint 0 \Omega$ but not a $G_\delta$ set.
proof_text:
The complement relative to $\closedint 0 \Omega$ of $\set \Omega$ is $\hointr 0 \Omega$, which is open in $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Hence, by definition, $\set \Omega$ is a closed set of $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Let $G_i$ be a countable set of open sets of $\closedint 0 \Omega$ which contain $\Omega$.
Then we can find a set of basis elements of $\closedint 0 \Omega$ of the form $\hointl {\alpha_i} \Omega \subseteq G_i$ for each $i$.
Each $\hointr 0 {\alpha_i}$ is countable.
We also have Countable Union of Countable Sets is Countable.
Thus the infimum of the $\alpha_i$ is an ordinal $\gamma$ which is less than $\Omega$.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \bigcap G_i \supseteq \hointl \gamma \Omega \ne \set \Omega$
That is, $\set \Omega$ cannot be expressed as a countable intersection of open sets of $\closedint 0 \Omega$.

title: Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not First-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Omega$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Omega$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Omega$ is not a first-countable space.
proof_text:
From Omega is Closed in Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space but not G-Delta Set, $\set \Omega$ cannot be expressed as a countable intersection of open sets of $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Thus, by definition, $\Omega$ does not have a countable local basis.
Hence the result by definition of first-countable space.

title: Uncountable Open Ordinal Space is not Separable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\hointr 0 \Omega$ denote the open ordinal space on $\Omega$.
Then $\hointr 0 \Omega$ is not a separable space.
proof_text:
Because $\Omega$ is the first uncountable ordinal, any ordinal which strictly precedes $\Omega$ is countable.
Let $H \subseteq \hointr 0 \Omega$ be a countable subset of $\hointr 0 \Omega$.
Let $\sigma$ be the supremum of $H$.
As $H$ by definition strictly precedes $\Omega$, $H$ itself is countable.
Thus $\sigma$ strictly precedes $\Omega$.
The closed interval $\closedint 0 \sigma$ is such that $H \subseteq \closedint 0 \sigma$.
By definition of the closure $H^-$ of $H$ as the smallest closed set of $\hointr 0 \Omega$ containing $H$, it follows that $H^- \subseteq \closedint 0 \sigma$.
Therefore, there exists an open interval $\openint \sigma \Omega$ in the complement of $H^-$ in $\hointr 0 \Omega$.
Thus the closure of $H$ does not equal $\hointr 0 \Omega$.
Thus $H$ is not everywhere dense in $\hointr 0 \Omega$.
Hence, by definition, $\hointr 0 \Omega$ is not separable.

title: Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not Separable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Omega$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Omega$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Omega$ is not a separable space.
proof_text:
Let $H \subseteq \closedint 0 \Omega$ be a countable subset of $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
From Uncountable Open Ordinal Space is not Separable, there exists an open interval $\openint \sigma \Omega$ in the complement of $H^-$ in $\hointr 0 \Omega$, and so also in $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Thus the closure of $H$ in $\closedint 0 \Omega$ does not equal $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Thus $H$ is not everywhere dense in $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Hence, by definition, $\closedint 0 \Omega$ is not separable.

title: Ordinal Space is Completely Normal
theorem_text:
Let $\Gamma$ denote a limit ordinal.
Let $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ denote the open ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Let $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ and $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ are both completely normal.
proof_text:
By definition, $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ and $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ are both linearly ordered spaces.
The result follows from Linearly Ordered Space is Completely Normal.

title: Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not Perfectly Normal
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Omega$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Omega$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Omega$ is not a perfectly normal space.
proof_text:
From Omega is Closed in Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space but not $G_\delta$ Set, $\set \Omega$ is not a $G_\delta$ set.
From Ordinal Space is Completely Normal, $\closedint 0 \Omega$ is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
Thus by definition $\set \Omega$ is closed in $\closedint 0 \Omega$.
Thus we have that $\set \Omega$ is a closed set of $\closedint 0 \Omega$ which is not a $G_\delta$ set.
The result follows by definition of perfectly normal space.

title: Finite Orbit under Group of Automorphisms of Field implies Separable over Fixed Field
theorem_text:
Let $E$ be a field.
Let $G \le \Aut E$ be a subgroup of its automorphism group.
Let $F = \map {\operatorname {Fix}_E} G$ be its fixed field.
Let $\alpha \in E$ have a finite orbit under $G$.
Then $\alpha$ is separable over $F$.
proof_text:
Let $\Lambda$ be the orbit of $\alpha$ under $G$.
By:
:Minimal Polynomial of Element with Finite Orbit under Group of Automorphisms over Fixed Field in terms of Orbit
the product:
$\map p x = \displaystyle \prod_{\beta \in \Lambda} \paren {x - \beta}$
is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$.
By Product of Distinct Monic Linear Polynomials is Separable, $p$ is separable.
Thus $\alpha$ is separable over $F$.

title: Countable Closed Ordinal Space is Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes $\Omega$.
Let $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a second-countable space.
proof_text:
From Basis for Open Ordinal Topology, the set $\mathcal B$ of subsets of $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ of the form:
$\openint \alpha {\beta + 1} = \hointl \alpha \beta = \set {x \in \hointr 0 \Gamma: \alpha < x < \beta + 1}$
for $\alpha, \beta \in \hointr 0 \Gamma$, forms a basis for $\closedint 0 \Gamma$.
As $\Gamma$ strictly precedes $\Omega$, there are a countable number of points of $\closedint 0 \Gamma$.
Each point in $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ has a countable basis.
From Countable Union of Countable Sets is Countable, it follows that $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ has a countable basis.

title: Countable Open Ordinal Space is Second-Countable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes $\Omega$.
Let $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ denote the open ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ is a second-countable space.
proof_text:
From Basis for Open Ordinal Topology, the set $\BB$ of subsets of $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ of the form:
$\openint \alpha {\beta + 1} = \hointl \alpha \beta = \set {x \in \hointr 0 \Gamma: \alpha < x < \beta + 1}$
for $\alpha, \beta \in \hointr 0 \Gamma$, forms a basis for $\hointr 0 \Gamma$.
As $\Gamma$ strictly precedes $\Omega$, there are a countable number of points of $\hointr 0 \Gamma$.
Each point in $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ has a countable basis.
From Countable Union of Countable Sets is Countable, it follows that $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ has a countable basis.

title: Countable Closed Ordinal Space is Metrizable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes $\Omega$.
Let $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a metrizable space.
proof_text:
From Countable Closed Ordinal Space is Second-Countable, $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ has a basis which is $\sigma$-locally finite.
From Ordinal Space is Completely Normal, $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a completely normal space.
From Sequence of Implications of Separation Axioms it follows that $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a regular space.
The result follows from Metrizable iff Regular and has Sigma-Locally Finite Basis.

title: Countable Open Ordinal Space is Metrizable
theorem_text:
Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal.
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes $\Omega$.
Let $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ denote the open ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ is a metrizable space.
proof_text:
From Countable Open Ordinal Space is Second-Countable, $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ has a basis which is $\sigma$-locally finite.
From Ordinal Space is Completely Normal, $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ is a completely normal space.
From Sequence of Implications of Separation Axioms it follows that $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ is a regular space.
The result follows from Metrizable iff Regular and has Sigma-Locally Finite Basis.

title: Closed Ordinal Space is Complete Order Space
theorem_text:
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a complete order space.
proof_text:
Let $H$ be a subset of an ordinal space.
Then $H$ has an infimum: its first element.
Let $H$ be a subset of $\closedint 0 \Gamma$.
Then $H$ has a supremum.
Therefore $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a complete order space.

title: Closed Ordinal Space is Compact
theorem_text:
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal.
Let $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Then $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a compact space.
proof_text:
By definition, $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ is a linearly ordered space.
The result follows from Linearly Ordered Space is Compact iff Complete.

title: Open Ordinal Space is not Compact in Closed Ordinal Space
theorem_text:
Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal.
Let $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ denote the open ordinal space on $\Gamma$.
Consider the compact subspace $\hointr 0 \Gamma$.
Then $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ is not compact in $\closedint 0 \Gamma$.
proof_text:
Consider the set:
$\set {\hointr 0 \Gamma: \alpha < \Gamma}$
This is an open cover of $\hointr 0 \Gamma$.
But because $\Gamma$ is a limit ordinal, it has no finite subcover.
Hence the result by definition of compact.

title: Inverse Integral Operator is Linear if Unique
theorem_text:
Let $T$ be an integral operator.
Let $f$ be an integrable real function on a domain appropriate to $T$.
Let $F = \map T f$ and $G = \map T g$.
Let $T$ have a unique inverse $T^{-1}$.
Then $T^{-1}$ is a linear operator:
$\forall p, q \in \R: \map {T^{-1} } {p F + q G} = p \map {T^{-1} } F + q \map {T^{-1} } G$
proof_text:
Let:
$x_1 = \map {T^{-1} } F$
$x_2 = \map {T^{-1} } G$
Thus:
$F = \map T {x_1}$
$G = \map T {x_2}$
Then for all $p, q \in \R$:
$$\map T {p x_1 + q x_2} = p \map T {x_1} + q \map T {x_2}$$
Integral Operator is Linear
$$= p F + q G$$
and so $x = p F + q G$ is a solution to the equation:
$\map T x = p F + q G$
But this equation has only one solution:
$x = \map {T^{-1} } {p F + q G}$
Thus $p F + q G$ must coincide with the above:
$p \map {T^{-1} } F + q \map {T^{-1} } G = \map {T^{-1} } {p F + q G}$
which proves that $T^{-1}$ is a linear operator.

title: Convergent Trigonometric Series is Periodic
theorem_text:
Let $\map S x$ be a trigonometric series:
$\map S x = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x}$
Let $S$ be convergent.
Then $S$ is periodic:
$\forall r \in \Z: \map S {x + 2 r \pi} = \map S x$
proof_text:
Let $\map S x$ converge to some $L \in \R$.
Let $r \in \Z$ be arbitrary.
Then:
$$\map S {x + 2 r \pi} = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n \paren {x + 2 r \pi} + b_n \sin n \paren {x + 2 r \pi} }$$
Definition of $\map S {x + 2 r \pi}$
$$= \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \map \cos {n x + 2 r n \pi} + b_n \map \sin {n x + 2 r n \pi} }$$
$$= \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x}$$
Sine and Cosine are Periodic on Reals
$$= \map S x$$
Definition of $\map S x$

title: Sum of Infinite Series of Product of Power and Sine
theorem_text:
Let $r \in \R$ such that $\size r < 1$.
Let $x \in \R$ such that $x \ne 2 m \pi$ for any $m \in \Z$.
Then:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty r^k \sin k x = r \sin x + r^2 \sin 2 x + r^3 \sin 3 x + \cdots$$
$$= \dfrac {r \sin x} {1 - 2 r \cos x + r^2}$$
proof_text:
From Euler's Formula:
$e^{i \theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta$
Hence:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty r^k \sin k x = \map \Im {\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty r^k e^{i k x} }$$
$$= \map \Im {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {r e^{i x} }^k}$$
as $\map \Im {e^{i \times 0 \times x} } = \map \Im 1 = 0$
$$= \map \Im {\frac 1 {1 - r e^{i x} } }$$
Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence: valid because $\size r < 1$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {1 - r e^{-i x} } {\paren {1 - r e^{-i x} } \paren {1 - r e^{i x} } } }$$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {1 - r e^{-i x} } {1 - r \paren {e^{i x} + e^{- i x} } + r^2} }$$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {1 - r \paren {\cos x - i \sin x} } {1 - 2 r \cos x + r^2} }$$
Corollary to Euler's Formula
$$= \dfrac {r \sin x} {1 - 2 r \cos x + r^2}$$
after simplification
It is noted that when $x$ is a multiple of $2 \pi$ then:
$1 - 2 r \cos x + r^2 = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$
leaving the right-hand side undefined.

title: Sine of Angle plus Full Angle/Corollary
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer.
Then:
$\map \sin {x + 2 n \pi} = \sin x$
proof_text:
From Sine of Angle plus Full Angle:
$\map \sin {x + 2 \pi} = \sin x$
The result follows from the General Periodicity Property:
If:
$\forall x \in X: \map f x = \map f {x + L}$
then:
$\forall n \in \Z: \forall x \in X: \map f x = \map f {x + n L}$

title: Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle/Corollary
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer.
Then:
$\cos \left({x + 2 n \pi}\right) = \cos x$
proof_text:
From Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle:
$\cos \left({x + 2 \pi}\right) = \cos x$
The result follows from the General Periodicity Property:
If:
$\forall x \in X: f \left({x}\right) = f \left({x + L}\right)$
then:
$\forall n \in \Z: \forall x \in X: f \left({x}\right) = f \left({x + n L}\right)$

title: Sum of Reciprocals of Squares Alternating in Sign
theorem_text:
$$\dfrac {\pi^2} {12} = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \dfrac {\paren {-1}^{n + 1} } {n^2}$$
$$= \frac 1 {1^2} - \frac 1 {2^2} + \frac 1 {3^2} - \frac 1 {4^2} + \cdots$$
proof_text:
$$\sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {\left({-1}\right)^{n + 1} } {n^2} = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\left({2 n - 1}\right)^2} - \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\left({2 n}\right)^2}$$
separating odd positive terms from even negative terms
$$= \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\left({2 n - 1}\right)^2} - \frac 1 4 \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^2}$$
$$= \frac {\pi^2} 8 - \frac 1 4 \times \frac {\pi^2} 6$$
Sum of Reciprocals of Squares of Odd Integers, Basel Problem
$$= \frac {\pi^2 \left({3 - 1}\right)} {24}$$
$$= \frac {\pi^2} {12}$$

title: Odd Function of Zero is Zero
theorem_text:
Let $f: \R \to \R$ be an odd function.
Let $f$ be defined at the point $x = 0$.
Then:
$\map f 0 = 0$
proof_text:
By definition of odd function:
$\map f {-x} = -\map f x$
and so:
$$\map f {-0} = \map f 0$$
$$= -\map f 0$$
The only real number $a$ for which $a = -a$ is $0$.
Hence the result.

title: Fourier Cosine Coefficients for Even Function over Symmetric Range
theorem_text:
Let $\map f x$ be an even real function defined on the interval $\openint {-\lambda} \lambda$.
Let the Fourier series of $\map f x$ be expressed as:
$\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda}$
Then for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$:
$a_n = \dfrac 2 \lambda \displaystyle \int_0^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$
proof_text:
As suggested, let the Fourier series of $\map f x$ be expressed as:
$\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda}$
By definition of Fourier series:
$a_n = \dfrac 1 \lambda \displaystyle \int_{-\lambda}^{-\lambda + 2 \lambda} \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$
From Cosine Function is Even:
$\cos a = \map \cos {-a}$
for all $a$.
By Even Function Times Even Function is Even, $\map f x \cos \dfrac {n \pi x} \lambda$ is even.
Thus:
$$a_n = \frac 1 \lambda \int_{-\lambda}^{-\lambda + 2 \lambda} \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$$
$$= \frac 1 \lambda \int_{-\lambda}^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$$
$$= \frac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$$
Definite Integral of Odd Function: Corollary

title: Correspondence Theorem for Ring Epimorphisms/Bijection
theorem_text:
The direct image mapping $\pi^\to$ and the inverse image mapping $\pi^\gets$ induce reverse bijections between $I$ and $J$, specifically:
#For every ideal $\mathfrak a \in I$, its image $\pi^{\to}(\mathfrak a) = \pi(\mathfrak a) \in J$.
#For every ideal $\mathfrak b \in J$, its preimage $\pi^{\gets}(\mathfrak b) = \pi^{-1}(\mathfrak b) \in I$.
#The restrictions $\pi^\to : I \to J$ and $\pi^\gets : J \to I$ are reverse bijections.
proof_text:
The first statements follow from:
* Preimage of Ideal under Ring Homomorphism is Ideal
* Image of Ideal under Ring Epimorphism is Ideal
The last statement follows from:
* Image of Preimage of Ideal under Ring Epimorphism
* Preimage of Image of Ideal under Ring Homomorphism

title: Kernel of Composition of Ring Homomorphisms
theorem_text:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$ be ring homomorphisms.
Let $g \circ f$ be their composition.
Then the kernel of $g \circ f$ is the preimage under $f$ of the kernel of $g$:
$\map \ker {g \circ f} = f^{-1} \sqbrk {\ker g}$
proof_text:
By definition, the kernel of a ring homomorphism is its kernel when considered as a group homomorphism between the additive groups.
The result follows from Kernel of Composition of Group Homomorphisms.

title: Ring Epimorphism Preserves Unity
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a ring with unity $1$.
Let $B$ be a ring.
Let $f: A \to B$ be a ring epimorphism.
Then $\map f 1$ is a unity of $B$.
proof_text:
By definition, $f$ is a semigroup homomorphism between multiplicative semigroups.
A unity of a ring is by definition an identity element of its multiplicative semigroup.
Thus the result follows from Epimorphism Preserves Identity.

title: Ring with Unity has Prime Ideal
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a non-trivial commutative ring with unity.
Then $A$ has a prime ideal.
proof_text:
By Krull's Theorem, $A$ has a maximal ideal.
By Maximal Ideal of Commutative and Unitary Ring is Prime Ideal, $A$ has a prime ideal.

title: Proper Ideal of Ring is Contained in Maximal Ideal
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.
Let $\mathfrak a \subseteq A$ be a proper ideal.
Then there exists a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ with $\mathfrak a \subseteq \mathfrak m$.
proof_text:
Let $A / \mathfrak a$ be the quotient ring.
By Proper Ideal iff Quotient Ring is Nontrivial, $A / \mathfrak a$ is non-trivial.
By Krull's Theorem, $A / \mathfrak a$ has a maximal ideal.
By Correspondence Theorem for Quotient Rings, $A$ has a maximal ideal containing $\mathfrak a$.

title: Series Expansion for Pi over Root 2
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \frac \pi {\sqrt 2} = \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^{r - 1} \frac {r - \frac 1 2} {r^2 - r + \frac 3 {16} }$
proof_text:
We have:
$$\frac {r - \frac 1 2} {r^2 - r + \frac 3 {16} } = \frac {16 r - 8} {16 r^2 - 16 r + 3}$$
$$= 2 \paren {\frac {8 r - 4} {\paren {4 r - 1} \paren {4 r - 3} } }$$
factorising, extracting a factor of $2$
$$= 2 \paren {\frac {\paren {4 r - 3} + \paren {4 r - 1} } {\paren {4 r - 1} \paren {4 r - 3} } }$$
$$= 2 \paren {\frac 1 {4 r - 1} + \frac 1 {4 r - 3} }$$
So, we have:
$$\sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^r \frac {r - \frac 1 2} {r^2 - r + \frac 3 {16} } = -2 \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^r \paren {\frac 1 {4 r - 1} + \frac 1 {4 r - 3} }$$
$$= -2 \sum_{r = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^r \paren {\int_0^1 x^{4 r - 2} \rd x + \int_0^1 x^{4 r - 4} \rd x}$$
Primitive of Power, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
$$= -2 \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^r \int_0^1 \paren {x^{4 r - 2} + x^{4 r - 4} } \rd x$$
Linear Combination of Definite Integrals
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^r \paren {x^{4 r - 2} + x^{4 r - 4} } } \rd x$$
Fubini's Theorem
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\frac 1 {x^2} \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-x^4}^r - \sum_{r \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-x^4}^r} \rd x$$
shifting the index in the second sum, and extracting a factor of $x^{-4}$ from the first
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\frac 1 {x^2} \paren {\sum_{r \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-x^4}^r - 1} - \sum_{r \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-x^4}^r} \rd x$$
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\paren {\frac 1 {x^2} - 1} \sum_{r \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-x^4}^r - \frac 1 {x^2} } \rd x$$
grouping terms
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\paren {\frac {1 - x^2} {x^2} } \paren {\frac 1 {1 + x^4} } - \frac 1 {x^2} } \rd x$$
Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence
$$= -2 \int_0^1 \paren {\frac {1 - x^2 - \paren {1 + x^4} } {x^2 \paren {1 + x^4} } } \rd x$$
writing as a single fraction
$$= 2 \int_0^1 \paren {\frac {x^2 \paren {1 + x^2} } {x^2 \paren {1 + x^4} } } \rd x$$
extracting a factor of $x^2$
$$= 2 \int_0^1 \frac {1 + x^2} {1 + x^4} \rd x$$
cancelling the factor of $x^2$
$$= \sqrt 2 \intlimits {\map \arctan {\frac 1 {\sqrt 2} \paren {x - \frac 1 x} } } 0 1$$
Primitive of $\dfrac {1 + x^2} {1 + x^4}$
$$= \sqrt 2 \paren {\arctan 0 - \lim_{x \mathop \to 0^+} \map \arctan {\frac 1 {\sqrt 2} \paren {x - \frac 1 x} } }$$
$$= -\sqrt 2 \lim_{u \mathop \to -\infty} \arctan u$$
setting $\displaystyle \frac 1 {\sqrt 2} \paren {x - \frac 1 x} = u$, Arctangent of Zero is Zero
$$= -\sqrt 2 \paren {-\frac \pi 2}$$
Limit to Infinity of Arctangent Function
$$= \frac \pi {\sqrt 2}$$

title: Holomorphic Function is Analytic
theorem_text:
Let $a \in \C$ be a complex number.
Let $r > 0$ be a real number.
Let $f$ be a function holomorphic on some open ball $D = \map B {a, r}$.
Then $f$ is complex analytic on $D$.
proof_text:
Let $z \in D$.
Then:
$$\map f z = \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \frac {\map f t} {t - z} \rd t$$
Cauchy's Integral Formula
$$= \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \frac {\map f t} {\paren {t - a} \paren {1 - \frac {z - a} {t - a} } } \rd t$$
Note that for all $t \in \partial D$, we have:
$\cmod {z - a} < \cmod {t - a} = r$.
Therefore:
$\cmod {\dfrac {z - a} {t - a} } < 1$
so Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence may be applied.
This gives:
$$\map f z = \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \frac {\map f t} {t - a} \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {\frac {z - a} {t - a} }^n \rd t$$
$$= \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f t \frac {\paren {z - a}^n} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} } \rd t$$
From Continuous Function on Compact Space is Bounded, there exists a real $M \ge 0$, such that:
$\forall t \in \partial D: \cmod {\map f t} \le M$
As $\cmod {\dfrac {z - a} {t - a} } < 1$, there exists a real $0 \le N < 1$ such that:
$\cmod {\dfrac {z - a} {t - a} } \le N$
Then:
$\displaystyle \cmod {\dfrac {\paren {z - a}^n} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} } \map f t} = \cmod {\frac 1 {t - a} } \cmod {\dfrac {\paren {z - a}^n} {\paren {t - a}^n} } \cmod {\map f t} \le \frac 1 r M N^n$
As $N < 1$, we have that $\displaystyle \frac 1 r \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty M N^n$ converges by Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence.
Therefore by the Weierstrass M-Test, we have that:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f t \frac {\paren {z - a}^n} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} }$
converges uniformly on $D$.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f t \frac {\paren {z - a}^n} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} } \rd t = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {z - a}^n \paren {\frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \frac {\map f t} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} } \rd t}$
Let:
$\displaystyle c_n = \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \int_{\partial D} \frac {\map f t} {\paren {t - a}^{n + 1} } \rd t$
Then:
$\displaystyle \map f z = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty c_n \paren {z - a}^n$
so $f$ is complex analytic on $D$.

title: Leading Coefficient of Product of Polynomials over Integral Domain
theorem_text:
Let $R$ be an integral domain.
Let $f, g \in R \sqbrk x$ be polynomials.
Let $c$ and $d$ be their leading coefficients.
Then $f g$ has leading coefficient $c d$.
proof_text:
Let $p = \deg f$ and $q = \deg g$ be their degrees.
By Degree of Product of Polynomials over Integral Domain, $\map \deg {f g} = p + q$.
For a natural number $n \ge 0$, let:
$a_n$ be the coefficient of the monomial $x^n$ in $f$.
$b_n$ be the coefficient of the monomial $x^n$ in $g$.
By Coefficients of Product of Two Polynomials, the coefficient of $x^{p + q}$ in $f g$ is the sum:
$\ds \sum_{k \mathop = p}^p a_k b_{p + q - k}$
By Indexed Summation over Interval of Length One:
$\ds \sum_{k \mathop = p}^p a_k b_{p + q - k} = a_p b_q = c d$

title: Product of Coprime Ideals equals Intersection
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.
Let $\mathfrak a, \mathfrak b \subseteq A$ be coprime ideals.
Then their product equals their intersection:
$\mathfrak a \mathfrak b = \mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$
proof_text:
By Intersection of Ideals of Ring contains Product, $\mathfrak a \mathfrak b \subseteq \mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$.
It remains to show that $\mathfrak a \mathfrak b \supseteq \mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$.
Let $c \in \mathfrak a \cap \mathfrak b$.
Because $\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak b$ are coprime, there exist $x \in \mathfrak a$, $y \in \mathfrak b$ with $x+y = 1$.
Then $c = cx + cy$.
Because:
$c \in \mathfrak b$ and $x \in \mathfrak a$
$c \in \mathfrak a$ and $y \in \mathfrak b$
we have $c \in \mathfrak a \mathfrak b$.

title: Modulus of Gamma Function of Imaginary Number
theorem_text:
Let $t \in \R$ be a real number.
Then:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} } = \sqrt {\dfrac {\pi \csch \pi t} t}$
where:
$\Gamma$ is the Gamma function
$\csch$ is the hyperbolic cosecant function.
proof_text:
By Euler's Reflection Formula:
$\map \Gamma {i t} \, \map \Gamma {1 - i t} = \pi \, \map \csc {\pi i t}$
From Gamma Difference Equation:
$-i t \, \map \Gamma {i t} \, \map \Gamma {-i t} = \pi \, \map \csc {\pi i t}$
Then:
$$\cmod {-i t} \cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} } \cmod {\map \Gamma {-i t} } = \cmod t \cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} } \cmod {\overline {\map \Gamma {i t} } }$$
Complex Conjugate of Gamma Function
$$= \cmod t \cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} }^2$$
$\cmod z = \cmod {\overline z}$
and:
$$\cmod {\pi \, \map \csc {\pi i t} } = \cmod {-i \pi \, \map \csch {\pi t} }$$
Hyperbolic Sine in terms of Sine
$$= \pi \, \map \csch {\pi \cmod t}$$
Hyperbolic Sine Function is Odd
So:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} }^2 = \dfrac {\pi \, \map \csch {\pi \cmod t} } {\cmod t}$
As $\cmod z \ge 0$ for all complex numbers $z$, we can take the non-negative square root and write:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} } = \sqrt {\dfrac {\pi \, \map \csch {\pi \cmod t} } {\cmod t} }$
However, by Hyperbolic Sine Function is Odd:
$\dfrac {\pi \, \map \csch {-\pi t} } {-t} = \dfrac {-\pi \, \map \csch {\pi t} } {-t} = \dfrac {\pi \, \map \csch {\pi t} } t$
Hence we can remove the modulus and simply write:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {i t} } = \sqrt {\dfrac {\pi \csch \pi t} t}$

title: Subalgebra of Algebraic Field Extension is Field
theorem_text:
Let $E / F$ be an algebraic field extension.
Let $A \subseteq E$ be a unital subalgebra over $F$.
Then $A$ is a field.
proof_text:
By Integral Ring Extension is Integral over Intermediate Ring, $E$ is integral over $A$.
Let $a \in A$ be nonzero.
Because $E$ is a field, $a$ is a unit of $E$.
By Ring Element is Unit iff Unit in Integral Extension, $a$ is a unit of $A$.
Thus $A$ is a field.

title: Piecewise Continuous Function with Improper Integrals may not be Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $f$ be a real function defined on a closed interval $\closedint a b$, $a < b$.
Let $f$ be a piecewise continuous function with improper integrals.
Then $f$ may not be piecewise continuous and bounded on $\closedint a b$.
proof_text:
Consider the function:
$\map f x = \begin{cases}
0 & : x = a \\
\dfrac 1 {\sqrt{x - a} } & : x \in \hointl a b
\end{cases}$
Since $\dfrac 1 {\sqrt{x - a} }$ is continuous on $\openint a b$, $f$ is continuous on $\openint a b$.
Therefore, $f$ satisfies $(1)$ in the requirements of a piecewise continuous function with improper integrals for the subdivision $\set {a, b}$ of $\closedint a b$.
Also:
$$\int_{a+}^{b-} \map f x \rd x = \int_{a+}^{b-} \dfrac 1 {\sqrt{x - a} } \rd x$$
$$= \bigintlimits {2 \sqrt {x - a} } {a+} {b-}$$
$$= \lim_{x \mathop \to b-} 2 \sqrt{x - a} - \lim_{x \mathop \to a+} 2 \sqrt{x - a}$$
$$= 2 \sqrt {b - a} - 2 \sqrt {a - a}$$
as $2 \sqrt{x - a}$ is left-continuous at $b$ and right-continuous at $a$
$$= 2 \sqrt{b - a}$$
Hence $\displaystyle \int_{a+}^{b-} \map f x \rd x$ exists.
Thus $f$ is a piecewise continuous function with improper integrals.
However, we have that $\map f x$ approaches $\infty$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from above.
Thus $f$ is not bounded.
Therefore $f$ is not piecewise continuous and bounded.
Hence the result.

title: Modulus of Gamma Function of One Half plus Imaginary Number
theorem_text:
Let $t \in \R$ be a real number.
Then:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {\dfrac 1 2 + i t} } = \sqrt {\pi \map \sech {\pi t} }$
where:
$\Gamma$ is the Gamma function
$\sech$ is the hyperbolic secant function.
proof_text:
$$\cmod {\map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + i t} }^2 = \map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + i t} \overline {\map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + i t} }$$
Modulus in Terms of Conjugate
$$= \map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + i t} \map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 - i t}$$
Complex Conjugate of Gamma Function
$$= \map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + i t} \map \Gamma {1 - \paren {\frac 1 2 + i t} }$$
applying some algebra
$$= \pi \map \csc {\pi \paren {\frac 1 2 + i t} }$$
Euler's Reflection Formula
$$= \pi \map \sec {\pi i t}$$
Sine of Complement equals Cosine
$$= \pi \map \sech {\pi t}$$
Hyperbolic Cosine in terms of Cosine
As $\cmod z \ge 0$ for all complex numbers $z$, we can take the non-negative square root of both sides and write:
$\cmod {\map \Gamma {\dfrac 1 2 + i t} } = \sqrt {\pi \map \sech {\pi t} }$

title: Integral to Infinity of Sine p x over x
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \frac {\sin p x} x \rd x = \begin{cases} \dfrac \pi 2 & : p > 0 \\
0 & : p = 0 \\
-\dfrac \pi 2 & : p < 0 \end{cases}$
proof_text:
Let $p > 0$.
We have:
$$\int_0^\infty \frac {\sin p x} x \rd x = \frac 1 p \int_0^\infty \frac {\sin t} { \frac 1 p t} \rd t$$
substituting $t = p x$
$$= \int_0^\infty \frac {\sin t} t \rd t$$
$$= \frac \pi 2$$
Dirichlet Integral
Then:
$$\int_0^\infty \frac {\sin \left({- p x}\right)} x \rd x = -\int_0^\infty \frac {\sin p x} x \rd x$$
Sine Function is Odd
$$= -\frac \pi 2$$
per above computation
For $p = 0$, we have:
$$\int_0^\infty \frac {\sin 0 x} x \rd x = \int_0^\infty \frac 0 x \rd x$$
Sine of Zero is Zero
$$= 0$$
Hence the result.

title: Radical of Ideal Preserves Inclusion
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.
Let $\mathfrak a \subseteq \mathfrak b \subseteq A$ be an ideals.
Then we have an inclusion of their radicals:
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a}\right) \subseteq \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right)$
proof_text:
Let $x \in \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a}\right)$.
We show that $x \in \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right)$.
By definition of radical, there exists $n \in \N$ such that the power $x^n \in \mathfrak a$.
Because $\mathfrak a \subseteq \mathfrak b$, also $x^n \in \mathfrak b$.
Thus $x \in \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right)$.

title: Ideals with Coprime Radicals are Coprime
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.
Let $\mathfrak a, \mathfrak b \subseteq A$ be ideals.
Let their radicals be coprime:
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a}\right) + \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right) = \left({1}\right)$
Then $\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak b$ are coprime.
proof_text:
We have:
$$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a + \mathfrak b}\right) = \operatorname{Rad} \left({\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a}\right) + \operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right)}\right)$$
Radical of Sum of Ideals
$$= \operatorname{Rad} \left({\left({1}\right)}\right)$$
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak a}\right)$ and $\operatorname{Rad} \left({\mathfrak b}\right)$ are coprime
$$= \left({1}\right)$$
Radical of Unit Ideal
By Unit Ideal iff Radical is Unit Ideal:
$\mathfrak a + \mathfrak b = \left({1}\right)$
That is, $\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak b$ are coprime.

title: Radical of Unit Ideal
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.
Let $\left({1}\right)$ be its unit ideal.
Then its radical equals $(1)$:
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\left({1}\right)}\right) = \left({1}\right)$.
proof_text:
By definition of ideal:
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\left({1}\right)}\right) \subseteq A$
By Ideal of Ring is Contained in Radical:
$\left({1}\right) = A \subseteq \operatorname{Rad} \left({\left({1}\right)}\right)$.
By definition of set equality:
$\operatorname{Rad} \left({\left({1}\right)}\right) = \left({1}\right)$

title: Nilpotent Ring Element plus Unity is Unit
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be a ring with unity.
Let $1 \in A$ be its unity.
Let $a \in A$ be nilpotent.
Then $1 + a$ is a unit of $A$.
proof_text:
Because $a$ is nilpotent, there exists a natural number $n > 0$ with $a^n = 0$.
By Sum of Geometric Sequence in Ring:
$\paren {1 + a} \cdot \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {-a}^k = 1 + \paren {-a}^n$
$\paren {\displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {-a}^k} \cdot \paren {1 + a} = 1 + \paren {-a}^n$
where $\sum$ denotes summation.
By Negative of Nilpotent Ring Element:
$\paren {-a}^n = 0$
Thus $1 + a$ is a unit.

title: Ideal is Contained in Contraction of Extension
theorem_text:
Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative ring with unity.
Let $f : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism.
Let $\mathfrak a \subseteq A$ be an ideal.
Then $\mathfrak a$ is contained in the contraction of its extension by $f$:
$\mathfrak a \subseteq \mathfrak a^{ec}$
proof_text:
By definition of extension and generated ideal:
$f(\mathfrak a) \subseteq \mathfrak a^e$
By Subset of Domain is Subset of Preimage of Image:
$\mathfrak a \subseteq f^{-1}(f(\mathfrak a))$
By Preimage Preserves Inclusion of Subsets:
$\mathfrak a \subseteq f^{-1}(f(\mathfrak a)) \subseteq f^{-1}(\mathfrak a^e)$

title: Linear Combination of Integrals/Indefinite
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int \paren {\lambda \map f x + \mu \map g x} \rd x = \lambda \int \map f x \rd x + \mu \int \map g x \rd x$
proof_text:
Let $F$ and $G$ be primitives of $f$ and $g$ respectively on $\closedint a b$.
By Linear Combination of Derivatives, $H = \lambda F + \mu G$ is a primitive of $\lambda f + \mu g$ on $\closedint a b$.
Hence:
$$\int \paren {\lambda \map f t + \mu \map g t} \rd t = \lambda \map F t + \mu \map G t$$
$$= \lambda \int \map f t \rd t + \mu \int \map g t \rd t$$

title: Definite Integral to Infinity of Reciprocal of x Squared plus a Squared
theorem_text:
$\ds \int_0^\infty \dfrac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2} = \frac \pi {2 a}$
for $a \ne 0$.
proof_text:
Let $C_R$ be the semicircular contour of radius $R$ situated on the upper half plane, centred at the origin, traversed anti-clockwise.
Let $\Gamma_R = C_R \cup \left[{-R \,.\,.\, R}\right]$.
Then, by Contour Integral of Concatenation of Contours:
$\displaystyle \oint_{\Gamma_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} = \int_{C_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} + \int_{-R}^R \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2}$
we have:
$$\left\vert \int_{C_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} \right\vert \le \pi R \cdot \max_{0 \le \theta \le \pi} \left\vert \frac 1 {R^2 e^{2 i \theta} + a^2} \right\vert$$
Estimation Lemma
$$= \frac {\pi R} {R^2 + a^2}$$
$$\le \frac {\pi R} {R^2}$$
$$= \frac \pi R$$
$$\to 0$$
as $R \to \infty$
from which:
$\displaystyle \lim_{R \to \infty} \oint_{\Gamma_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} = \lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{-R}^R \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2}$
The integrand is meromorphic.
So by the Residue Theorem:
$\displaystyle \lim_{R \to \infty} \oint_{\Gamma_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} = 2 \pi i \sum \operatorname{Res} \left({\frac 1 {z^2 + a^2}, z_0}\right)$
where the sum runs over the poles of $\dfrac 1 {z^2 + a^2}$.
The integrand can be written as:
$\dfrac 1 {\left({z - ai}\right) \left({z + ai}\right)}$
From this it can be observed that the integrand has only two simple poles: $z_0 = a i$ and $z_0 = -a i$.
Only the former of these lies in the contour, so:
$$\lim_{R \to \infty} \oint_{\Gamma_R} \frac {\d z} {z^2 + a^2} = 2 \pi i \operatorname{Res} \left({\frac 1 {z^2 + a^2}, ai}\right)$$
$$= 2 \pi i \cdot \frac 1 { \frac \d {\d z}\left({z^2 + a^2}\right)_{z \mathop = a i} }$$
Residue at Simple Pole
$$= 2 \pi i \cdot \frac 1 {2 a i}$$
Derivative of Power
$$= \frac \pi a$$
So:
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2} = \frac \pi a$
From Definite Integral of Even Function:
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2} = 2 \int_0^\infty \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2}$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \frac {\d x} {x^2 + a^2} = \frac \pi {2 a}$

title: Definite Integral from 0 to a of Root of a Squared minus x Squared
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int_0^a \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} \rd x = \frac {\pi a^2} 4$
for $a > 0$.
proof_text:
$$\int_0^a \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} \rd x = \intlimits {\frac {x \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} } 2 + \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin \frac x a} 0 a$$
Primitive of $\sqrt {a^2 - x^2}$
$$= \paren {\frac {a \sqrt {a^2 - a^2} } 2 + \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin \frac a a} - \paren {\frac {0 \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} } 2 + \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin \frac 0 a}$$
$$= \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin 1 - \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin 0$$
removing vanishing terms
$$= \frac {a^2} 2 \arcsin 1$$
Sine of Zero is Zero
$$= \frac \pi 2 \frac {a^2} 2$$
Sine of Right Angle
Hence the result.

title: Definite Integral from 0 to a of Root of a Squared minus x Squared
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \int_0^a \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} \rd x = \frac {\pi a^2} 4$
for $a > 0$.
proof_text:
$$\int_0^a \sqrt {a^2 - x^2} \rd x = \frac {a^{1 + \frac 2 2} } 2 \frac {\map \Gamma {\frac 1 2} \map \Gamma {1 + \frac 1 2} } {\map \Gamma {\frac 1 2 + \frac 1 2 + 1} }$$
Definite Integral from 0 to a of $x^m \paren {a^n - x^n}^p$
$$= \frac {a^2} 2 \frac {\map \Gamma {\frac 3 2} \map \Gamma {\frac 1 2} } {\map \Gamma 2}$$
$$= \frac {a^2} {2 \times 1!} \paren {\frac 1 2} \paren {\map \Gamma {\frac 1 2} }^2$$
Gamma Difference Equation, Gamma Function Extends Factorial
$$= \frac {\pi a^2} 4$$
Gamma Function of One Half

title: Universal Property of Abelianization of Group
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a group.
Let $G^{\operatorname {ab} }$ be its abelianization.
Let $\pi : G \to G^{\operatorname {ab} }$ be the quotient group epimorphism.
Let $H$ be an abelian group.
Let $f: G \to H$ be a group homomorphism.
Then there exists a unique group homomorphism $g : G^{\operatorname {ab}} \to H$ such that $g \circ \pi = f$:
$\xymatrix {
G \ar[d]_\pi \ar[r]^{\forall f} & H\\
G^{\operatorname {ab} } \ar[ru]_{\exists ! g} }$
proof_text:
By Universal Property of Quotient Group, it suffices to show that the kernel $\ker f$ contains the commutator subgroup $\sqbrk {G, G}$.
By definition of generated subgroup, this is equivalent to showing that $\ker f$ contains all commutators of $G$.
Let $g, h \in G$.
Then by Group Homomorphism Preserves Inverses:
$\map f {g^{-1} h^{-1} g h} = \map f g^{-1} \, \map f h^{-1} \, \map f g \, \map f g = 1 \in H$
Thus the commutator $\sqbrk {g, h} = g^{-1} h^{-1} g h$ is in $\ker f$.

title: Definite Integral from 0 to Half Pi of Square of Sine x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 x \rd x = \frac \pi 4$
proof_text:
We have:
$$\int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 x \rd x = \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 \paren {\frac \pi 2 - x} \rd x$$
Integral between Limits is Independent of Direction
$$= \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x$$
Sine of Complement equals Cosine
So:
$$2 \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 x \rd x = \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \paren {\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x} \rd x$$
$$= \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \rd x$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \frac \pi 2$$
Primitive of Constant
giving:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 x \rd x = \frac \pi 4$

title: Definite Integral from 0 to Half Pi of Square of Cosine x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x = \frac \pi 4$
proof_text:
We have:
$$\int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x = \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \map {\cos^2} {\frac \pi 2 - x} \rd x$$
Integral between Limits is Independent of Direction
$$= \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \sin^2 x \rd x$$
Cosine of Complement equals Sine
So:
$$2 \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x = \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \paren {\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x} \rd x$$
$$= \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \rd x$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \frac \pi 2$$
Primitive of Constant
giving:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x = \frac \pi 4$

title: Definite Integral from 0 to Half Pi of Even Power of Cosine x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n} x \rd x = \dfrac {\paren {2 n}!} {\paren {2^n n!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$, let $\map P n$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n} x \rd x = \dfrac {\paren {2 n}!} {\paren {2^n n!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 1$ is the case:
$$\int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^2 x \rd x = \frac \pi 4$$
Definite Integral from 0 to Half Pi of Square of Cosine x
$$= \dfrac 1 2 \times \dfrac \pi 2$$
$$= \dfrac 2 {\paren {2 \times 1}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$$
$$= \dfrac {\paren {2 \times 1}!} {\paren {2^1 \times 1!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$$
Thus $\map P 1$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 k} x \rd x = \dfrac {\paren {2 k}!} {\paren {2^k k!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 \paren {k + 1} } x \rd x = \dfrac {\paren {2 \paren {k + 1} }!} {\paren {2^{k + 1} \paren {k + 1}!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
Let $I_k = \displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 k} x \rd x$.
$$I_{k + 1} = \frac {2 \paren {k + 1} - 1} {2 \paren {k + 1} } I_k$$
Reduction Formula for Definite Integral of Power of Cosine
$$= \frac {2 \paren {k + 1} - 1} {2 \paren {k + 1} } \dfrac {\paren {2 k}!} {\paren {2^k k!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \frac {2 \paren {k + 1} \paren {2 \paren {k + 1} - 1} } {2^2 \paren {k + 1}^2} \dfrac {\paren {2 k}!} {\paren {2^k k!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$$
$$= \dfrac {\paren {2 \paren {k + 1} }!} {\paren {2^{k + 1} \paren {k + 1}!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \forall n \in \Z_{> 0}: \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n} x \rd x = \dfrac {\paren {2 n}!} {\paren {2^n n!}^2} \dfrac \pi 2$

title: Definite Integral from 0 to Half Pi of Odd Power of Cosine x
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n + 1} x \rd x = \dfrac {\left({2^n n!}\right)^2} {\left({2 n + 1}\right)!}$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, let $P \left({n}\right)$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n + 1} x \rd x = \dfrac {\left({2^n n!}\right)^2} {\left({2 n + 1}\right)!}$
Basis for the Induction
$P \left({0}\right)$ is the case:
$$\int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos x \rd x = \left[{\sin x}\right]_0^{\frac \pi 2}$$
Primitive of $\cos x$
$$= \sin \frac \pi 2 - \sin 0$$
$$= 1$$
Sine of Right Angle, Sine of Zero is Zero
$$= \frac {\left({2^0 \times 1!}\right)^2} {\left({2 \times 0 + 1}\right)!}$$
Thus $P \left({0}\right)$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that, if $P \left({k}\right)$ is true, where $k \ge 0$, then it logically follows that $P \left({k + 1}\right)$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 k + 1} x \rd x = \dfrac {\left({2^k k!}\right)^2} {\left({2 k + 1}\right)!}$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1} x \rd x = \dfrac {\left({2^{k + 1} \left({k + 1}\right)!}\right)^2} {\left({2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1}\right)!}$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
Let $I_k = \displaystyle \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 k + 1} x \rd x$.
$$I_{k + 1} = \frac {2 \left({k + 1}\right)} {2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1} I_k$$
Reduction Formula for Definite Integral of Power of Cosine
$$= \frac {2 \left({k + 1}\right)} {2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1} \dfrac {\left({2^k k!}\right)^2} {\left({2 k + 1}\right)!}$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \frac {\left({2 \left({k + 1}\right)}\right)^2} {\left({2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1}\right) \left({2 \left({k + 1}\right)}\right)} \dfrac {\left({2^k k!}\right)^2} {\left({2 k + 1}\right)!}$$
multiplying top and bottom by $2 \left({k + 1}\right)$
$$= \dfrac {\left({2^{k + 1} \left({k + 1}\right)!}\right)^2} {\left({2 \left({k + 1}\right) + 1}\right)!}$$
So $P \left({k}\right) \implies P \left({k + 1}\right)$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: \int_0^{\frac \pi 2} \cos^{2 n + 1} x \rd x = \dfrac {\left({2^n n!}\right)^2} {\left({2 n + 1}\right)!}$

title: Arctangent of Zero is Zero
theorem_text: $\arctan 0 = 0$
proof_text:
By definition, $\arctan$ is the inverse of the tangent function's restriction to $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$.
By Tangent of Zero:
$\tan 0 = 0$
As $0 \in \openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$, we have $\arctan 0 = 0$ by the definition of an inverse function.

title: Order of Finite p-Group is Power of p
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a finite group.
Let $p$ be a prime number.
Let all elements of $G$ have order a power of $p$.
Then $G$ is a $p$-group.
proof_text:
Let every element of $G$ be a $p$-element.
Let $q$ be a prime number which is a divisor of the order $\order G$ of $G$.
By Cauchy's Lemma (Group Theory), there exists an element of $G$ whose order is a divisor of $q$.
But as the order of all elements of $G$ divide $p^n$ it follows that $q = p$.
Thus $G$ is a group whose order is $p^n$ for some $n \in \Z_{>0}$.

title: Sum of Reciprocals of Fourth Powers Alternating in Sign
theorem_text:
$$\sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \dfrac {\paren {-1}^{n + 1} } {n^4} = \frac 1 {1^4} - \frac 1 {2^4} + \frac 1 {3^4} - \frac 1 {4^4} + \cdots$$
$$= \dfrac {7 \pi^4} {720}$$
proof_text:
$$\sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {\paren {-1}^{n + 1} } {n^4} = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\paren {2 n - 1}^4} - \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\paren {2 n}^4}$$
separating odd positive terms from even negative terms
$$= \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {\paren {2 n - 1}^4} - \frac 1 {16} \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^4}$$
$$= \frac {\pi^4} {96} - \frac 1 {16} \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^4}$$
Sum of Reciprocals of Fourth Powers of Odd Integers
$$= \frac {\pi^4} {96} - \frac 1 {16} \times \frac {\pi^4} {90}$$
Riemann Zeta Function of 4
$$= \frac {\pi^4 \paren {15 - 1} } {1440}$$
$$= \frac {7 \pi^4} {720}$$

title: Sum of Reciprocals of Sixth Powers Alternating in Sign
proof_text:
