$S_r = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = a}^b {x_k}^r$ for $r \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.
Setting $m = 1$, and setting $x_i := x_{j_1}$:
$$\sum_{a \mathop \le i \mathop \le b} x_{j_1} = \sum_{\substack {k_1, k_2 \mathop \ge 0 \\ k_1 \mathop + 2 k_2 \mathop = 2} } \dfrac { {S_1}^{k_1} } {1^{k_1} k_1 !}$$
$$= \dfrac { {S_1}^1} {1^1 \times 1!}$$
as $k_1 = 1$ is the only $k_1$ to fulfil the criteria
$$= S_1$$
simplifying

title: Limit of Rational Sequence is not necessarily Rational
theorem_text:
Let $S = \left\langle{a_n}\right\rangle$ be a rational sequence.
Let $S$ be convergent to a limit $L$.
Then it is not necessarily the case that $L$ is itself a rational number.
proof_text:
Proof by Counterexample:
By definition, Euler's number $e$ can be defined as:
$e = \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 1 {n!}$
Each of the terms of the sequence of partial sums is rational.
However, from Euler's Number is Irrational, $e$ itself is not.

title: Product of Negative Real Numbers is Positive
theorem_text:
Let $a, b \in \R_{\le 0}$ be negative real numbers.
Then:
$a \times b \in \R_{\ge 0}$
That is, their product $a \times b$ is a positive real number.
proof_text:
From Real Numbers form Ring, the set $\R$ of real numbers forms a ring.
The result then follows from Product of Ring Negatives.

title: Real Number Multiplied by Complex Number
theorem_text:
Let $a \in \R$ be a real number.
Let $c + d i \in \C$ be a complex number.
Then:
$a \times \left({c + d i}\right) = \left({c + d i}\right) \times a = a c + i a d$
proof_text:
$a$ can be expressed as a wholly real complex number $a + 0 i$.
Then we have:
$$a \times \left({c + d i}\right) = \left({a + 0 i}\right) \times \left({c + d i}\right)$$
$$= \left({a c - 0 d}\right) + \left({a d + 0 c}\right) i$$
$$= a c + i a d$$
The result for $\left({c + d i}\right) \times a$ follows from Complex Multiplication is Commutative.

title: Power of Complex Modulus equals Complex Modulus of Power
theorem_text:
Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number.
Let $\left\vert{z}\right\vert$ be the modulus of $z$.
Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.
Then:
$\left\vert{z^n}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^n$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, let $P \left({n}\right)$ be the proposition:
$\left\vert{z^n}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^n$
$P \left({0}\right)$ is the case:
$$\left\vert{z^0}\right\vert = \left\vert{1}\right\vert$$
$$= 1$$
$$= \left\vert{z}\right\vert^0$$
Thus $P \left({0}\right)$ is seen to hold.
Basis for the Induction
$P \left({1}\right)$ is the case:
$$\left\vert{z^1}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert$$
$$= \left\vert{z}\right\vert^1$$
Thus $P \left({1}\right)$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Basis for the Induction
$P \left({2}\right)$ is the case:
$\left\vert{z^2}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^2$
which is demonstrated in Square of Complex Modulus equals Complex Modulus of Square.
Thus $P \left({2}\right)$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that, if $P \left({k}\right)$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $P \left({k + 1}\right)$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\left\vert{z^k}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^k$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\left\vert{z^{k + 1} }\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^{k + 1}$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
$$\left\vert{z^{k + 1} }\right\vert = \left\vert{z^k \cdot z}\right\vert$$
$$= \left\vert{z^k}\right\vert \cdot \left\vert{z}\right\vert$$
Complex Modulus of Product of Complex Numbers
$$= \left\vert{z}\right\vert^k \cdot \left\vert{z}\right\vert$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \left\vert{z}\right\vert^{k + 1}$$
So $P \left({k}\right) \implies P \left({k + 1}\right)$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\forall n \in \ Z_{\ge 0}: \left\vert{z^n}\right\vert = \left\vert{z}\right\vert^n$

title: Power of Complex Conjugate is Complex Conjugate of Power
theorem_text:
Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number.
Let $\overline z$ denote the complex conjugate of $z$.
Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.
Then:
$\overline {z^n} = \left({\overline z}\right)^n$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, let $P \left({n}\right)$ be the proposition:
$\overline {z^n} = \left({\overline z}\right)^n$
$P \left({0}\right)$ is the case:
$$\overline {z^0} = \overline 1$$
$$= 1$$
$$= \left({\overline z}\right)^0$$
Thus $P \left({0}\right)$ is seen to hold.
Basis for the Induction
$P \left({1}\right)$ is the case:
$$\overline {z^1} = \overline z$$
$$= \left({\overline z}\right)^1$$
Thus $P \left({1}\right)$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Basis for the Induction
$P \left({2}\right)$ is the case:
$\overline {z^2} = \left({\overline z}\right)^2$
which is demonstrated in Square of Complex Conjugate is Complex Conjugate of Square.
Thus $P \left({2}\right)$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that, if $P \left({k}\right)$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $P \left({k + 1}\right)$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\overline {z^k} = \left({\overline z}\right)^k$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\overline {z^{k + 1} } = \left({\overline z}\right)^{k + 1}$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
$$\overline {z^{k + 1} } = \overline {z^k \cdot z}$$
$$= \overline {z^k} \cdot \overline z$$
Product of Complex Conjugates
$$= \left({\overline z}\right)^k \cdot \overline z$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= \left({\overline z}\right)^{k + 1}$$
So $P \left({k}\right) \implies P \left({k + 1}\right)$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\forall n \in \ Z_{\ge 0}: \overline {z^n} = \left({\overline z}\right)^n$

title: Conjugate of Polynomial is Polynomial of Conjugate
theorem_text:
Let $f \left({z}\right) = a_n z^n + a_{n - 1} z^{n - 1} + \cdots + a_1 z + a_0$ be a polynomial over complex numbers where $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ are real numbers.
Let $\alpha \in \C$ be a complex number.
Then:
$\overline {f \left({\alpha}\right)} = f \left({\overline \alpha}\right)$
where $\overline \alpha$ denotes the complex conjugate of $\alpha$.
proof_text:
By Power of Complex Conjugate is Complex Conjugate of Power:
$\overline {\alpha^k} = \left({\overline \alpha}\right)^k$
for all $k$ between $0$ and $n$.
Then from Product of Complex Conjugates:
$\overline {a_k \alpha^k} = \overline {a_k} \cdot \overline {\alpha^k}$
But $a_k$ is real.
So by Complex Number equals Conjugate iff Wholly Real:
$\overline {a_k} = a_k$.
From Sum of Complex Conjugates, it follows that:
$\overline {f \left({\alpha}\right)} = a_n \left({\overline \alpha}\right)^n + a_{n - 1} \left({\overline \alpha}\right)^{n - 1} + \cdots + a_1 \overline \alpha + a_0$
Hence the result.

title: Complex Roots of Polynomial with Real Coefficients occur in Conjugate Pairs
theorem_text:
Let $\map f z = a_n z^n + a_{n - 1} z^{n - 1} + \cdots + a_1 z + a_0$ be a polynomial over complex numbers where $a_0, \ldots, a_n$ are real numbers.
Let $\alpha \in \C$ be a root of $f$.
Then $\overline \alpha$ is also a root of $f$, where $\overline \alpha$ denotes the complex conjugate of $\alpha$.
That is, all complex roots of $f$ appear as conjugate pairs.
proof_text:
Let $\alpha = p + q i$.
Let $p + q i$ be expressed in exponential form as $\alpha = r e^{i \theta}$.
As $\alpha = r e^{i \theta}$ satisfies $\map f \alpha = 0$, it follows that:
$a_n r^n e^{n i \theta} + a_{n - 1} r^{n - 1} e^{\paren {n - 1} i \theta} + \dotsb + a_1 r e^{i \theta} + a_0 = 0$
Taking the conjugate of both sides:
$a_n r^n e^{-n i \theta} + a_{n - 1} r^{n - 1} e^{-\paren {n - 1} i \theta} + \dotsb + a_1 r e^{-i \theta} + a_0 = 0$
it follows that $\overline \alpha = p - q i$ is also a root of $f$.
If any of the $a_k$ are complex, then the conjugate of $f$ is not the same polynomial as $f$.
Therefore the result holds only for real coefficients.

title: Argument of Complex Conjugate equals Argument of Reciprocal
theorem_text:
Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number.
Then:
$\arg {\overline z} = \arg \dfrac 1 z = -\arg z$
where:
$\arg$ denotes the argument of a complex number
$\overline z$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z$.
proof_text:
Let $z$ be expressed in polar form:
$z := r \left({\cos \theta + i \sin \theta}\right)$
Then:
$$\overline z = r \left({\cos \theta - i \sin \theta}\right)$$
Polar Form of Complex Conjugate
$$= r \left({\cos \left({-\theta}\right) + i \sin \left({-\theta}\right)}\right)$$
Cosine Function is Even, Sine Function is Odd
and:
$$\dfrac 1 z = \dfrac 1 r \left({\cos \theta - i \sin \theta}\right)$$
Polar Form of Reciprocal of Complex Number
$$= \dfrac 1 r \left({\cos \left({-\theta}\right) + i \sin \left({-\theta}\right)}\right)$$
Cosine Function is Even, Sine Function is Odd
The result follows by definition of the argument of a complex number

title: Condition for Collinearity of Points in Complex Plane/Formulation 1
theorem_text:
Let $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ be points in the complex plane.
Then $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ are collinear if and only if:
$\dfrac {z_1 - z_3} {z_3 - z_2} = \lambda$
where $\lambda \in \R$ is a real number.
If this is the case, then $z_3$ divides the line segment in the ratio $\lambda$.
If $\lambda > 0$ then $z_3$ is between $z_1$ and $z_2$, and if $\lambda < 0$ then $z_3$ is outside the line segment joining $z_1$ to $z_2$.
proof_text:
By Geometrical Interpretation of Complex Subtraction:
$z_1 - z_3$ can be represented as the line segment from $z_3$ to $z_1$
$z_3 - z_2$ can be represented as the line segment from $z_2$ to $z_3$.
Thus we have that $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ are collinear if and only if $z_1 - z_3$ is parallel to $z_3 - z_2$, when expressed as line segments.
Let $\dfrac {z_1 - z_3} {z_3 - z_2} = \lambda$ for $\lambda \in \C$.
That is:
$z_1 - z_3 = \lambda \paren {z_3 - z_2}$
By Complex Multiplication as Geometrical Transformation:
$\map \arg {z_1 - z_3} = \map \arg {z_3 - z_2} \iff \map \arg {z_3 - z_2} \arg \lambda \in \R_{>0}$
and:
$\map \arg {z_1 - z_3} = -\map \arg {z_3 - z_2} \iff \map \arg {z_3 - z_2} \arg \lambda \in \R_{<0}$
where $\arg$ denotes the argument of a complex number.
Also by Complex Multiplication as Geometrical Transformation, $z_1 - z_3$ is $\lambda$ the length of $z_3 - z_2$.
The result follows.

title: Equivalence of Definitions of Real Exponential Function/Inverse of Natural Logarithm implies Limit of Sequence
theorem_text: The following definition of the concept of the real exponential function:
proof_text:
Let $\exp x$ be the real function defined as the inverse of the natural logarithm:
$y = \exp x \iff x = \ln y$
Let $\left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle$ be the sequence in $\R$ defined as:
$x_n = \paren {1 + \dfrac x n}^n$
First it needs to be noted that $\sequence {x_n}$ does indeed converge to a limit.
From Equivalence of Definitions of Real Exponential Function: Limit of Sequence implies Sum of Series, we have:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {1 + \dfrac x n}^n = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {x^n} {n!}$
From Series of Power over Factorial Converges, the right-hand side is indeed shown to converge to a limit.
It will next be shown that:
$\displaystyle \map \ln {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sequence {x_n} } = x$
We have:
$$\map \ln {\paren {1 + \frac x n}^n} = n \, \map \ln {1 + x n^{-1} }$$
Logarithms of Powers
$$= x \frac {\map \ln {1 + x n^{-1} } } {x n^{-1} }$$
multiplying by $1 = \dfrac {x n^{-1} } {x n^{-1} }$
From Limit of Sequence is Limit of Real Function, we can consider the differentiable analogue of the sequence.
From Derivative of Logarithm at One we have:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map \ln {1 + x} } x = 1$
But $x n^{-1} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ from Sequence of Powers of Reciprocals is Null Sequence.
Thus:
$\displaystyle x \frac {\map \ln {1 + x n^{-1} } } {x n^{-1} } \to x$
as $n \to \infty$.
From Exponential Function is Continuous:
$\paren {1 + \dfrac x n}^n = \exp \paren {n \, \map \ln {1 + \dfrac x n} } \to \exp x = e^x$
as $n \to \infty$.

title: Exponential of Sum/Complex Numbers/General Result
theorem_text:
Let $m \in \N_{>0}$ be a natural number.
Let $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_m \in \C$ be complex numbers.
Let $\exp z$ be the exponential of $z$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^m z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^m \paren {\exp z_j}$
proof_text:
The proof proceeds by induction.
For all $m \in \N_{>0}$, let $\map P m$ be the proposition:
$\displaystyle \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^m z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^m \paren {\exp z_j}$
$\map P 1$ is the case:
$$\map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^1 z_j} = \exp z_j$$
$$= \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^1 \paren {\exp z_j}$$
Thus $\map P 1$ is seen to hold.
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 2$ is the case:
$\map \exp {z_1 + z_2} = \paren {\exp z_1} \paren {\exp z_2}$
This is proved in Exponential of Sum: Complex Numbers.
Thus $\map P 2$ is seen to hold.
This is the basis for the induction.
Induction Hypothesis
Now it needs to be shown that if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is the induction hypothesis:
$\displaystyle \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \paren {\exp z_j}$
from which it is to be shown that:
$\displaystyle \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} \paren {\exp z_j}$
Induction Step
This is the induction step:
$$\map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} z_j} = \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k z_j + z_{k + 1} }$$
$$= \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k z_j} \exp z_{k + 1}$$
Basis for the Induction
$$= \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \paren {\exp z_j} \exp z_{k + 1}$$
Induction Hypothesis
$$= prod_{j \mathop = 1}^{k + 1} \paren {\exp z_j}$$
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
Therefore:
$\forall m \in \N_{>0}: \displaystyle \map \exp {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^m z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^m \paren {\exp z_j}$

title: Exponential of Sum/Complex Numbers/General Result/Corollary
theorem_text:
Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer.
Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number.
Let $\exp z$ be the exponential of $z$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \exp \paren {m z} = \paren {\exp z}^m$
proof_text:
From Exponential of Sum: Complex Numbers: General Result:
$\displaystyle \exp \paren {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^m z_j} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^m \paren {\exp z_j}$
for complex numberst $z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_m \in \C$.
The result follows by setting $z = z_1 = z_2 = \cdots = z_m$.

title: Equation of Ellipse in Complex Plane
theorem_text:
Let $\C$ be the complex plane.
Let $E$ be an ellipse in $\C$ whose major axis is $d \in \R_{>0}$ and whose foci are at $\alpha, \beta \in \C$.
Then $C$ may be written as:
$\cmod {z - \alpha} + \cmod {z - \beta} = d$
where $\cmod {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes complex modulus.
proof_text:
By definition of complex modulus:
$\cmod {z - \alpha}$ is the distance from $z$ to $\alpha$
$\cmod {z - \beta}$ is the distance from $z$ to $\beta$.
Thus $\cmod {z - \alpha} + \cmod {z - \beta}$ is the sum of the distance from $z$ to $\alpha$ and from $z$ to $\beta$.
This is precisely the equidistance property of the ellipse.
From Equidistance of Ellipse equals Major Axis, the constant distance $d$ is equal to the major axis of $E$.

title: Cosine of Angle plus Integer Multiple of Pi
theorem_text: $\map \cos {\theta + n \pi} = \paren {-1}^n \cos \theta$
proof_text:
$$\map \cos {\theta + n \pi} = \cos \theta \cos n \pi - \sin \theta \sin n \pi$$
Cosine of Sum
$$= \cos \theta \cos n \pi$$
Sine of Integer Multiple of Pi
$$= \paren {-1}^n \cos \theta$$
Cosine of Integer Multiple of Pi

title: Sine of Angle plus Integer Multiple of Pi
theorem_text: $\map \sin {\theta + n \pi} = \paren {-1}^n \sin \theta$
proof_text:
$$\map \sin {\theta + n \pi} = \sin \theta \cos n \pi + \cos \theta \sin n \pi$$
Sine of Sum
$$= \sin \theta \cos n \pi$$
Sine of Integer Multiple of Pi
$$= \paren {-1}^n \sin \theta$$
Cosine of Integer Multiple of Pi

title: Sum of 1 + sin pi by 5 plus i cos pi by 5 to Fifth Power plus i times its Conjugate
theorem_text: $\paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 + i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 = 0$
proof_text:
$$\paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 + i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
$$= \frac {\paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 + i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5} {\paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5} \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
$$= \paren {\sin \dfrac \pi 5 + i \cos  \dfrac \pi 5}^5 \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
Complex Division Examples: $\dfrac {1 + \sin \theta + i \cos \theta} {1 + \sin \theta - i \cos \theta}$
$$= i^5 \paren {-i \sin \dfrac \pi 5 + \cos  \dfrac \pi 5}^5 \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
multiplying left hand term by $i^5 \times -i = 1$
$$= i \paren {\cos \pi - i \sin \pi} \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
De Moivre's Formula
$$= i \paren {-1} \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
Sine of Straight Angle and Cosine of Straight Angle
$$= -i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5 + i \paren {1 + \sin \dfrac \pi 5 - i \cos \dfrac \pi 5}^5$$
$$= 0$$

title: Positive Real Complex Root of Unity
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Let $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ be the set of complex $n$th roots of unity.
The only $x \in U_n$ such that $x \in \R_{>0}$ is:
$x = 1$
That is, $1$ is the only complex $n$th root of unity which is a positive real number.
proof_text:
We have that $1$ is a positive real number.
The result follows from Existence and Uniqueness of Positive Root of Positive Real Number.

title: Real Complex Roots of Unity for Even Index
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer such that $n$ is even.
Let $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ be the set of complex $n$th roots of unity.
The only $x \in U_n$ such that $x \in \R$ are:
$x = 1$ or $x \in -1$
That is, $1$ and $-1$ are the only complex $n$th roots of unity which are real number.
proof_text:
From Positive Real Complex Root of Unity, we have that $1$ is the only element of $U_n$ which is a positive real number.
We note that $\paren {-1}^n = 1$ as $n$ is even.
Thus $-1$ is also an element of $U_n$.
Now let $z \in U_n$ such that $\cmod z \ne 1$.
Let $z > 0$.
From Positive Power Function on Non-negative Reals is Strictly Increasing it follows that:
$z < 1 \implies z^n < 1$
and:
$z > 1 \implies z^n > 1$
Let $z < 0$.
From Positive Power Function on Negative Reals is Strictly Decreasing it follows that:
$z < -1 \implies z^n > 1$
and:
$z > -1 \implies z^n < 1$
That is, in all cases where $\cmod z \ne 1$ we have that $z^n \ne 1$.

title: First Complex Root of Unity is Primitive
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Let $U_n$ denote the complex $n$th roots of unity:
$U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$
Let $\alpha_1 = \exp \paren {\dfrac {2 \pi i} n}$ denote the first complex root of unity.
Then $\alpha_1$ is a primitive complex root of unity.
proof_text:
From Condition for Complex Root of Unity to be Primitive:
$\gcd \set {n, k} = 1$
where:
$\alpha_k = \exp \paren {\dfrac {2 k \pi i} n}$
Here we have:
$k = 1$
and:
$\gcd \set {n, 1} = 1$
Hence the result.

title: Powers of Primitive Complex Root of Unity form Complete Set
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Let $U_n$ denote the complex $n$th roots of unity:
$U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$
Let $\alpha_k = \exp \paren {\dfrac {2 k \pi i} n}$ denote the $k$th complex root of unity.
Let $\alpha_k$ be a primitive complex root of unity.
Let $V_k = \set { {\alpha_k}^r: r \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n - 1} }$.
Then:
$V_k = U_n$
That is, $V_k = \set { {\alpha_k}^r: r \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n - 1} }$ forms the complete set of complex $n$th roots of unity.
proof_text:
From Roots of Unity under Multiplication form Cyclic Group, $\struct {U_n, \times}$ is a group.
The result follows from Power of Generator of Cyclic Group is Generator iff Power is Coprime with Order.

title: Combination Theorem for Cauchy Sequences/Sum Rule
theorem_text: $\sequence {x_n + y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$ be given.
Then $\dfrac \epsilon 2 > 0$.
Since $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence, we can find $N_1$ such that:
$\forall n, m > N_1: \norm{x_n - x_m} < \dfrac \epsilon 2$
Similarly, $\sequence {y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence, we can find $N_2$ such that:
$\forall n, m > N_2: \norm{y_n - y_m} < \dfrac \epsilon 2$
Now let $N = \max \set {N_1, N_2}$.
Then if $n, m > N$, both the above inequalities will be true.
Thus $\forall n, m > N$:
$$\norm {\paren {x_n + y_n} - \paren {x_m + y_m} } = \norm {\paren {x_n - x_m} + \paren {y_n - y_m} }$$
$$\le \norm {x_n - x_m} + \norm {y_n - y_m}$$
Axiom $\text N 3$ of norm: Triangle Inequality
$$< \frac \epsilon 2 + \frac \epsilon 2 = \epsilon$$
Hence:
$\sequence {x_n + y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequences in $R$.

title: Power of Complex Number minus 1
theorem_text:
Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number.
Then:
$z^n - 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \alpha^k}$
where $\alpha$ is a primitive complex $n$th root of unity.
proof_text:
Follows directly from the corollary to the Polynomial Factor Theorem:
If $\zeta_1, \zeta_2, \ldots, \zeta_n \in \C$ such that all are different, and $P \paren {\zeta_1} = P \paren {\zeta_2} = \ldots = P \paren {\zeta_n} = 0$, then:
$\displaystyle P \paren z = k \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n \paren {z - \zeta_j}$
where $k \in \C$.
In this context, each of $\alpha^k$ is a primitive complex $n$th root of unity:
$\paren {\alpha^k}^n = 1$
and the result follows.

title: Factorisation of x^(2n+1)-1 in Real Domain
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Then:
$z^{2 n + 1} - 1 = \paren {z - 1} \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \paren {z^2 - 2 \cos \dfrac {2 \pi k} {2 n + 1} + 1}$
proof_text:
From Power of Complex Number minus 1:
$z^{2 n + 1} - 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{2 n} \paren {z - \alpha^k}$
where:
$$\alpha = e^{2 i \pi / \paren {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \cos \dfrac {2 \pi} {2 n + 1} + i \sin \dfrac {2 \pi} {2 n + 1}$$
From Complex Roots of Unity occur in Conjugate Pairs:
$U_{2 n + 1} = \set {1, \tuple {\alpha, \alpha^{2 n} }, \tuple {\alpha^2, \alpha^{2 n - 1} }, \ldots, \tuple {\alpha^k, \alpha^{2 n - k + 1} }, \ldots, \tuple {\alpha^n, \alpha^{n + 1} } }$
where $U_{2 n + 1}$ denotes the complex $2 n + 1$th roots of unity:
$U_{2 n + 1} = \set {z \in \C: z^{2 n + 1} = 1}$
The case $n = 0$ is taken care of by setting $\alpha^0 = 1$, from whence we have the factor $z - 1$.
Taking the product of each of the remaining factors of $z^{2 n + 1} - 1$ in pairs:
$$\paren {z - \alpha^k} \paren {z - \alpha^{2 n - k + 1} } = \paren {z - \alpha^k} \paren {z - \overline {\alpha^k} }$$
Complex Roots of Unity occur in Conjugate Pairs
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + \alpha^k \overline {\alpha^k}$$
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + \cmod {\alpha^k}^2$$
Modulus in Terms of Conjugate
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + 1$$
Modulus of Complex Root of Unity equals 1
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\cos \dfrac {2 k \pi} {2 n + 1} + i \sin \dfrac {2 k \pi} {2 n + 1} + \cos \dfrac {2 k \pi} {2 n + 1} - i \sin \dfrac {2 k \pi} {2 n + 1} } + 1$$
Definition of $\alpha$
$$= z^2 - 2 \cos \dfrac {2 k \pi} {2 n + 1} z + 1$$
simplification
Hence the result.

title: Factorisation of x^(2n)-1 in Real Domain
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Then:
$z^{2 n} - 1 = \paren {z - 1} \paren {z + 1} \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \paren {z^2 - 2 \cos \dfrac {k \pi} n + 1}$
proof_text:
From Power of Complex Number minus 1:
$z^{2 n} - 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{2 n - 1} \paren {z - \alpha^k}$
where:
$$\alpha = e^{2 i \pi / \paren {2 n} }$$
$$= \cos \dfrac {2 \pi} {2 n} + i \sin \dfrac {2 \pi} {2 n}$$
$$= \cos \dfrac \pi n + i \sin \dfrac \pi n$$
From Complex Roots of Unity occur in Conjugate Pairs:
$U_{2 n} = \set {1, \tuple {\alpha, \alpha^{2 n - 1} }, \tuple {\alpha^2, \alpha^{2 n - 2} }, \ldots, \tuple {\alpha^k, \alpha^{2 n - k} }, \ldots, \tuple {\alpha^{n - 1}, \alpha^{n + 1} }, -1}$
where $U_{2 n}$ denotes the complex $2 n$th roots of unity:
$U_{2 n} = \set {z \in \C: z^{2 n} = 1}$
The case $k = 0$ is taken care of by setting $\alpha^0 = 1$, from whence we have the factor $z - 1$.
The case $k = n$ is taken care of by setting $\alpha^k = -1$, from whence we have the factor $z + 1$.
Taking the product of each of the remaining factors of $z^{2 n} - 1$:
$$\paren {z - \alpha^k} \paren {z - \alpha^{2 n - k} } = \paren {z - \alpha^k} \paren {z - \overline {\alpha^k} }$$
Complex Roots of Unity occur in Conjugate Pairs
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + \alpha^k \overline {\alpha^k}$$
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + \cmod {\alpha^k}^2$$
Modulus in Terms of Conjugate
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\alpha^k + \overline {\alpha^k} } + 1$$
Modulus of Complex Root of Unity equals 1
$$= z^2 - z \paren {\cos \dfrac {k \pi} n + i \sin \dfrac {k \pi} n + \cos \dfrac {k \pi} n - i \sin \dfrac {k \pi} n} + 1$$
Definition of $\alpha$
$$= z^2 - 2 \cos \dfrac {k \pi} n z + 1$$
simplification
Hence the result.

title: Factorisation of z^n-a
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Let $a \in \C$ be a complex number.
Then:
$z^n - a = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \alpha^k b}$
where:
$\alpha$ is a primitive complex $n$th root of unity
$b$ is any complex number such that $b^n = a$.
proof_text:
From $z^n - a = 0$ we have that:
$a = z^n$
Let $b = a^{1 / n}$, hence $b^n = a$, with $a, b \in \C$.
From Roots of Complex Number:
$$z^{1 / n} = \set {a^{1 / n} e^{i \paren {\theta + 2 k \pi} / n}: k \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1}, \theta = \arg a}$$
$$= \set {a^{1 / n} e^{2 i k \pi / n}: k \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1} }$$
$\theta = 0$
$$= \set {b e^{2 i k \pi / n}: k \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1} }$$
$b = a^{1 / n}$
and so each of $b e^{2 i k \pi / n}$ is a root of $z^n - a$.
From First Complex Root of Unity is Primitive:
For each $n \in \Z_{>0}$ there exists at least one primitive complex $n$th root of unity, $\alpha$, hence each of $b \alpha^k$ is a unique root of $z^n - a$.
From the corollary to the Polynomial Factor Theorem:
If $\zeta_1, \zeta_2, \ldots, \zeta_n \in \C$ such that all are different, and $\map P {\zeta_1} = \map P {\zeta_2} = \cdots = \map P {\zeta_n} = 0$, then:
$\displaystyle \map P z = k \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n \paren {z - \zeta_j}$
where $k \in \C$.
$z^n - a$ is a monic polynomial, hence $k = 1$ in the above product.
Choose $\zeta_j = b \alpha^{j - 1}$ and we have the desired result.

title: Sum of Two Cubes in Complex Domain
theorem_text:
$a^3 + b^3 = \paren {a + b} \paren {a \omega + b \omega^2} \paren {a \omega^2 + b \omega}$
where:
$\omega = -\dfrac 1 2 + \dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2$
proof_text:
From Sum of Cubes of Three Indeterminates Minus 3 Times their Product:
$x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3 x y z = \paren {x + y + z} \paren {x + \omega y + \omega^2 z} \paren {x + \omega^2 y + \omega z}$
Setting $x \gets 0, y \gets a, z \gets b$:
$0^3 + a^3 + b^3 - 3 \times 0 \times a b = \paren {0 + a + b} \paren {0 + \omega a + \omega^2 b} \paren {0 + \omega^2 a + \omega b}$
The result follows.

title: Factorisation of z^n+1
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Then:
$z^n + 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} n}$
proof_text:
From Factorisation of $z^n - a$, setting $a = -1$:
$z^n + 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \alpha^k b}$
$\alpha$ is a primitive complex $n$th root of unity
$b$ is any complex number such that $b^n = a$.
From Euler's Identity:
$-1 = e^{i \pi}$
From Exponential of Product:
$\paren {\exp \dfrac {i \pi} n}^n = e^{i \pi}$
and so:
$b = \exp \dfrac {i \pi} n$
We also have by definition of the first complex $n$th root of unity, and from First Complex Root of Unity is Primitive:
$\alpha = \exp \dfrac {2 i \pi} n$
Hence:
$$z^n + 1 = \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \paren {\exp \dfrac {2 i \pi} n}^k \exp \dfrac {i \pi} n}$$
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {2 k i \pi} n \exp \dfrac {i \pi} n}$$
Exponential of Product
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} n}$$
Exponential of Sum

title: Combination Theorem for Cauchy Sequences/Quotient Rule
theorem_text:
Suppose $\sequence {y_n}$ does not converge to $0$.
Then:
$\exists K \in \N: \forall n > K : y_n \ne 0$
and the sequences:
$\sequence { {x_{K + n} } \paren {y_{K + n} }^{-1} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sequence {\paren {y_{K + n} }^{-1} {x_{K + n} } }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ are well-defined and Cauchy sequences.
proof_text:
By the Inverse Rule for Normed Division Ring:
$\exists K \in \N : \forall n > K : y_n \ne 0$.
and the sequence:
$\sequence {\paren {x_{K + n} }^{-1} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is well-defined and a Cauchy sequence.
By Subsequence of Cauchy Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Cauchy Sequence, $\sequence {x_{K + n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
By Product Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
:the sequences $\sequence { {x_{K + n} } \paren {y_{K + n} }^{-1} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sequence {\paren {y_{K + n} }^{-1} {x_{K + n} } }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ are Cauchy sequences.

title: Factorisation of z^(2n)+1 in Real Domain
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Then:
$z^{2 n} + 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \paren {z^2 - 2 z \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} + 1}$
proof_text:
From Factorisation of $z^n + 1$:
$(1): \quad z^{2 n} + 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{2 n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} }$
From Complex Roots of Polynomial with Real Coefficients occur in Conjugate Pairs, the roots of $(1)$ occur in conjugate pairs.
Hence we can express $(1)$ as:
$$z^{2 n} + 1 = \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} } \prod_{k \mathop = n}^{2 n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} }$$
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} } \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} }$$
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} + \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} } + \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} }$$
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} + \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n} } + 1}$$
simplifying
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} + i \sin \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} + \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} - i \sin \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} } + 1}$$
Euler's Formula
$$= \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - 2 z \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n} + 1}$$
Hence the result.

title: Factorisation of z^(2n+1)+1 in Real Domain
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Then:
$z^{2 n + 1} + 1 = \paren {z + 1} \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - 2 z \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} + 1}$
proof_text:
From Factorisation of $z^n + 1$:
$(1): \quad z^{2 n + 1} + 1 = \displaystyle \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{2 n} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$
From Complex Roots of Polynomial with Real Coefficients occur in Conjugate Pairs, the roots of $(1)$ occur in conjugate pairs.
Hence we can express $(1)$ as:
$$z^{2 n + 1} + 1 = \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^n \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } \prod_{k \mathop = n + 1}^{2 n} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 n + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } \prod_{k \mathop = n + 1}^{2 n} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {z - e^{i \pi} } \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } \prod_{k \mathop = n + 1}^{2 n} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {z + 1} \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } \paren {z - \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {z + 1} \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} + \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } + \exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {z + 1} \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\exp \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} + \exp \dfrac {-\paren {2 k + 1} i \pi} {2 n + 1} } + 1}$$
simplifying
$$= \paren {z + 1} \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - z \paren {\cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} + i \sin \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} + \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} - i \sin \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} } + 1}$$
Euler's Formula
$$= \paren {z + 1} \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {z^2 - 2 z \cos \dfrac {\paren {2 k + 1} \pi} {2 n + 1} + 1}$$
simplifying

title: 4 Sine Pi over 10 by Cosine Pi over 5
theorem_text: $4 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac \pi 5 = 1$
proof_text:
First, we must rewrite the left-hand side so that it reaches a form that is able to be substituted for what we determine is true through identities.
$$4 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac \pi 5 = 1$$
Given
$$4 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac {2 \pi} {10} = 1$$
multiplying the angle inside the cosine by $\dfrac 2 2$
$$4 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} = 1$$
Double-angle formula (cosine)
$$4 \sin \paren { \dfrac 1 2 \dfrac \pi {5} } \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} = 1$$
Factoring a $\dfrac 1 2$ out of $\dfrac \pi {10}$
$$4 \sqrt { \dfrac { 1 - \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} } 2 } \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} = 1$$
$\sin \dfrac \theta 2 = \sqrt { \dfrac { 1 - \cos \theta } 2 }$
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \cos^2 \dfrac \pi {10} } \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} = 1$$
Trivial simplification
Now that we have reduced the expression to just one trigonometric function of a single angle, we can use the fact that a multiple of the angle is $\dfrac \pi 2$, whose cosine is $0$, in order to solve for $\cos \dfrac \pi {10}$.
$$\cos \dfrac \pi 2 = 0$$
(New equation) Starting with $5 \theta$ and its value
$$\cos \paren { \dfrac \pi 5 + \dfrac {3\pi} {10} } = 0$$
Rewriting $5 \theta$ as $2 \theta + 3 \theta$
$$\cos \dfrac \pi 5 \cos \dfrac {3\pi} {10} - \sin \dfrac \pi 5 \sin \dfrac {3\pi} {10} = 0$$
Double-angle formula (cosine)
$$\paren { 2 \cos^2 \dfrac \pi {10} - 1 } \paren { 4 \cos^3 \dfrac {3\pi} {10} - 3 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} } - \paren { 2 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac \pi {10} } \paren { 3 \sin \dfrac \pi {10} - 4 \sin^3 \dfrac \pi {10} } = 0$$
Multiple-angle formulas (cosine, sine)
$$\paren { 8 \cos^5 \dfrac \pi {10} - 10 \cos^3 \dfrac \pi {10} + 3 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} } - \paren { 6 \sin^2 \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac \pi {10} - 8 \sin^4 \dfrac \pi {10} \cos \dfrac \pi {10} } = 0$$
Multiplication
$$\paren { 8 \cos^5 \dfrac \pi {10} - 10 \cos^3 \dfrac \pi {10} + 3 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} } - \paren { 6 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} - 6 \cos^3 \dfrac \pi {10} - 8 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} + 16 \cos^3 \dfrac \pi {10} - 8 \cos^5 \dfrac \pi {10} } = 0$$
Pythagorean Identity
$$16 \cos^5 \dfrac \pi {10} - 20 \cos^3 \dfrac \pi {10} + 5 \cos \dfrac \pi {10} = 0$$
Trivial simplification
Having realized that the above process is the same as the derivation of the expansion formula for $\cos {5 \theta}$, we can generalize this expression and then plug in $\dfrac \pi {10}$.
$$16u^5 - 20u^3 + 5u = 0$$
$u = \cos \theta$
$$u(16u^4 - 20u^2 + 5) = 0$$
Factoring a $u$ out of the polynomial
$$16u^4 - 20u^2 + 5 = 0$$
Dividing both sides by $u$
We were able to divide off the $u$ from both sides of that last line because we know that $\cos \dfrac \pi {10}$ cannot possibly equal $0$. From here, we use the quadratic formula to solve for $u^2$.
$$u^2 = \dfrac { - \paren { -20 } ± \sqrt { \paren { -20 }^2 - 4 \paren { 16 } \paren 5} } { 2 \paren { 16 } }$$
$$u^2 = \dfrac { 20 ± \sqrt { 80 } } {32}$$
$$u^2 = \dfrac { 5 ± \sqrt 5 } 8$$
Taking the square root of both sides, we can solve for $u$.
$$u^2 = \dfrac { 5 ± \sqrt 5 } 8$$
$$u = ± \dfrac 1 {\sqrt 8} \sqrt {5 ± \sqrt 5}$$
We know that $\dfrac \pi {10}$ is in the first quadrant, so we can change the exterior $±$ sign to a $+$ sign:
$$u = \dfrac 1 {\sqrt 8} \sqrt {5 ± \sqrt 5}$$
We know that $\dfrac \pi {10}$ is a lot closer to $0$ than to $\dfrac \pi 2$:
$\dfrac \pi {10} - 0 < \dfrac \pi 2 - \dfrac \pi {10}$
Therefore, the larger of the possible interior quantities of the radical should be correct.
$$u = \dfrac 1 {\sqrt 8} \sqrt {5 + \sqrt 5}$$
$$u = \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } }$$
Now that we have evaluated $\cos \dfrac \pi {10}$, we can substitute it for the most simplified expression from above with only $\cos \dfrac \pi {10}$:
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \cos^2 \dfrac \pi {10} } \paren { 2 \paren { \cos \dfrac \pi {10} }^2 - 1} = 1$$
Derived from original theorem
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } }^2 } \paren { 2 \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } }^2 - 1} = 1$$
$u = \cos \dfrac \pi {10} = \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } }$
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } }^2 } \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } - 1} = 1$$
$2 \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { a } } }^2 = \dfrac 4 {16} a = \dfrac 1 4 a$
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { \dfrac 1 4 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } - 1} = 1$$
$\paren { \dfrac 1 4 \sqrt { 2 \paren { a } } }^2 = \dfrac 2 {16} a = \dfrac 1 8 a$
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { \dfrac { 5 + \sqrt 5 } 4 - 1} = 1$$
Multiplication
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { \dfrac { 5 + \sqrt 5 } 4 - \dfrac 4 4} = 1$$
Common denominators
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { \dfrac { 5 + \sqrt 5 - 4 } 4} = 1$$
Combining fractions
$$4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { \dfrac { 1 + \sqrt 5 } 4} = 1$$
Trivial simplification
$$\dfrac 4 4 \sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Associative property
$$\sqrt { 1 - \dfrac 1 8 \paren { 5 + \sqrt 5 } } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Trivial simplification
$$\sqrt { \dfrac 8 8 - \dfrac { 5 + \sqrt 5 } 8 } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Common denominators
$$\sqrt { \dfrac { 8 - 5 - \sqrt 5 } 8 } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Combining fractions
$$\sqrt { \dfrac { 3 - \sqrt 5 } 8 } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Trivial simplification
$$\sqrt { \dfrac { 6 - 2 \sqrt 5 } {16} } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Multiplying the radicand by $\dfrac 2 2$
$$\sqrt { \dfrac { 1 - 2 \sqrt 5 + 5 } {16} } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Rewriting $k ± 2 \sqrt u$ as $\paren { k - u } ± 2 \sqrt u + u$ because $k - u + u = k$
$$\sqrt { \dfrac { \paren { 1 - \sqrt 5 }^2 } {16} } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Rewriting the quantity as a square
$$± \dfrac 1 4 \paren { 1 - \sqrt 5 } \paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 } = 1$$
Square root of the radicand
$$± \dfrac 1 4 \paren { 1 - 5 } = 1$$
Multiplying $\paren { 1 - \sqrt 5 }$ and $\paren { 1 + \sqrt 5 }$
$$± \dfrac 1 4 × -4 = 1$$
Trivial simplification
$$∓ 1 = 1$$
Multiplication
$$1 = 1$$
Sign rectification

title: Convergence of Modulus of Convergent Complex Sequence
theorem_text:
Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$.
Let $\sequence {z_n}$ converge to a value $c \in \C$.
Let $\cmod z$ denote the modulus of a complex number $z$.
Then:
$\sequence {\cmod {z_n} }$ converges to a value $\cmod c$.
proof_text:
By definition of convergent complex sequence:
$\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: n > N \implies \cmod {z_n - c} < \epsilon$
From the Reverse Triangle Inequality:
$\size {\cmod x - \cmod y} \le \cmod {x - y}$
and the result follows.

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Real/Difference Rule
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n - y_n} = l - m$
proof_text:
From Sum Rule for Real Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n + y_n} = l + m$
From Multiple Rule for Real Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {-y_n} = -m$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n + \paren {-y_n} } = l + \paren {-m}$
The result follows.

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Complex/Difference Rule
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {z_n - w_n} = c - d$
proof_text:
From Sum Rule for Complex Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {z_n + w_n} = c + d$
From Multiple Rule for Complex Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {-w_n} = -d$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {z_n + \paren {-w_n} } = c + \paren {-d}$
The result follows.

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Complex/Multiple Rule
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda z_n} = \lambda c$
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$.
We need to find $N$ such that:
$\forall n > N: \cmod {\lambda z_n - \lambda c} < \epsilon$
If $\lambda = 0$ the result is trivial.
So, assume $\lambda \ne 0$.
Then $\cmod \lambda > 0$ from the definition of the modulus of $\lambda$.
Hence $\dfrac \epsilon {\cmod \lambda} > 0$.
We have that $z_n \to c$ as $n \to \infty$.
Thus it follows that:
$\exists N: \forall n > N: \cmod {z_n - c} < \dfrac \epsilon {\cmod \lambda}$
That is:
$\forall n > N: \cmod \lambda \cmod {z_n - c} < \epsilon$
But we have:
$$\cmod \lambda \cmod {z_n - c} = \cmod {\lambda \paren {z_n - c} }$$
Complex Modulus of Product of Complex Numbers
$$= \cmod {\lambda x_n - \lambda l}$$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda x_n} = \lambda c$

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Complex/Combined Sum Rule
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda z_n + \mu w_n} = \lambda c + \mu d$
proof_text:
From the Multiple Rule for Complex Sequences, we have:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda z_n} = \lambda c$
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\mu w_n} = \mu d$
The result now follows directly from the Sum Rule for Complex Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda z_n + \mu w_n} = \lambda c + \mu d$

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Complex/Quotient Rule
theorem_text:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {z_n} {w_n} = \frac c d$
provided that $d \ne 0$.
proof_text:
As $z_n \to c$ as $n \to \infty$, it follows from Modulus of Limit that $\size {w_n} \to \size d$ as $n \to \infty$.
As $d \ne 0$, it follows from the definition of the modulus of $d$ that $\size d > 0$.
From Sequence Converges to Within Half Limit, we have $\exists N: \forall n > N: \size {w_n} > \dfrac {\size d} 2$.
Now, for $n > N$, consider:
$$\size {\frac {z_n} {w_n} - \frac c d} = \size {\frac {d z_n - w_n c} {d w_n} }$$
$$< \frac 2 {\size m^2} \size {d z_n - w_n c}$$
By the above, $d z_n - w_n c \to d c - d c = 0$ as $n \to \infty$.
The result follows by the Squeeze Theorem for Sequences of Complex Numbers (which applies as well to real as to complex sequences).

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Normed Division Ring/Combined Sum Rule
theorem_text: $\sequence {\lambda x_n + \mu y_n }$ is convergent and $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda x_n + \mu y_n} = \lambda l + \mu m$
proof_text:
From the Multiple Rule for Sequences in Normed Division Ring, we have:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda x_n} = \lambda l$
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\mu y_n} = \mu m$
The result now follows directly from the Sum Rule for Sequences in Normed Division Ring:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {\lambda x_n + \mu y_n} = \lambda l + \mu m$

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Normed Division Ring/Difference Rule
theorem_text: $\sequence {x_n - y_n}$ is convergent and $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n - y_n} = l - m$
proof_text:
From Sum Rule for Sequences in Normed Division Ring:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n + y_n} = l + m$
From Multiple Rule for Sequences in Normed Division Ring:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {-y_n} = -m$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {x_n + \paren {-y_n} } = l + \paren {-m}$
The result follows.

title: Absolutely Convergent Series is Convergent/Complex Numbers
theorem_text:
Let $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty z_n$ be an absolutely convergent series in $\C$.
Then $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty z_n$ is convergent.
proof_text:
Let $z_n = u_n + i v_n$.
We have that:
$$\cmod {z_n} = \sqrt { {u_n}^2 + {v_n}^2}$$
$$> \sqrt { {u_n}^2}$$
$$> \size {u_n}$$
and similarly:
$\cmod {z_n} > \size {v_n}$
From the Comparison Test, the series $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty u_n$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty v_n$ are absolutely convergent.
From Absolutely Convergent Series is Convergent: Real Numbers, $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty u_n$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty v_n$ are convergent.
By Convergence of Series of Complex Numbers by Real and Imaginary Part, it follows that $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty z_n$ is convergent.

title: Convergent Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ to the following limit:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$
Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.
proof_text:
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$ to the limit $l$, then:
$ orall \epsilon \in \R_{\gt 0}: \exists N \in \N :  orall n \ge N: 
orm {x_n - l} < \epsilon$
Let $n_1$ satisfy:
$ orall n \ge n_1: 
orm {x_n - l} < 1$
Then $ orall n \ge n_1$:
$$
orm {x_n} = 
orm {x_n - l + l}$$
$$\le 
orm {x_n - l} + 
orm l$$
Norm axiom (N3) (Triangle Inequality)
$$\le 1 + 
orm l$$
as $n \ge n_1$
Let $K = \max \set {
orm {x_1}, 
orm {x_2}, \dots, 
orm {x_{n_1 - 1} }, 1 + 
orm l}$.
Then:
$ orall n < n_1: 
orm {x_n} \le K$
$ orall n \ge n_1: 
orm {x_n} \le 1 + 
orm l \le K$
Thus, by definition, $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.

title: Convergent Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ to the following limit:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$
Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.
proof_text:
Let $d$ be the metric induced on $R$ be the norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent to the limit $l$ in $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$.
By the definition of a convergent sequence in a normed division ring, $\sequence {x_n} $ is convergent to the limit $l$ in $\struct {R, d}$.
By Convergent Sequence in Metric Space is Bounded, $\sequence {x_n} $ is a bounded sequence in $\struct {R, d}$.
By Sequence is Bounded in Norm iff Bounded in Metric, $\sequence {x_n} $ is a bounded sequence in $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$.

title: Convergent Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ to the following limit:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$
Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.
proof_text:
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent to the limit $l$ in $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$.
By modulus of limit in normed division ring, $\sequence {\norm {x_n} }$ is a convergent sequence in $\R$.
By Convergent Real Sequence is Bounded, $\sequence {\norm {x_n} }$ is bounded.
That is:
$\exists M \in \R_{> 0}: \forall n, \norm {x_n} = \size {\norm {x_n} } \le M$
Thus, by definition, $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.

title: Convergent Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ to the following limit:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$
Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded.
proof_text:
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent to the limit $l$ in $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}}$.
By Convergent Sequence is Cauchy Sequence in Normed Division Ring, $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}}$.
By Cauchy Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Bounded, $\sequence {x_n}$ is a bounded sequence in $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}}$.

title: Existence of Radius of Convergence of Complex Power Series/Absolute Convergence
theorem_text:
Let $B_R \paren \xi$ denote the open $R$-ball of $\xi$.
Let $z \in B_R \paren \xi$.
Then $S \paren z$ converges absolutely.
If $R = +\infty$, we define $B_R \paren \xi = \C$.
proof_text:
Let $z \in B_R \paren \xi$.
By definition of the open $R$-ball of $\xi$:
$\cmod {z - \xi} < R$
where $\cmod z$ denotes the complex modulus of $z$.
By definition of radius of convergence, it follows that $S \paren z$ converges.
Suppose $R$ is finite.
Let $\epsilon = R - \cmod {z - \xi} > 0$.
Now, let $w \in B_R \paren \xi$ be a complex number such that $R - \cmod {w - \xi} = \dfrac \epsilon 2$.
Such a $w$ exists because, if at a loss, we can always let $w = \xi + R - \dfrac \epsilon 2$.
If $R = +\infty$, then let $w \in C$ be any complex number such that $\cmod {z - \xi} < \cmod {w - \xi}$.
Then:
$$\limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n}^{1/n} < \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {a_n \paren {w - \xi}^n}^{1/n}$$
as $\cmod {z - \xi} < \cmod {w - \xi}$, we have $\cmod {z - \xi}^n < \cmod {w - \xi}^n$
$$\le 1$$
$n$th Root Test: $S \paren w$ is not divergent
From the $n$th Root Test, it follows that $S \paren z$ converges absolutely.

title: Existence of Radius of Convergence of Complex Power Series/Divergence
theorem_text:
Let ${B_R}^- \paren \xi$ denote the closed $R$-ball of $\xi$.
Let $z \notin {B_R}^- \paren \xi$.
Then $S \paren z$ is divergent.
proof_text:
Let $z \notin {B_R}^- \paren \xi$.
Then by definition of the closed $R$-ball of $\xi$:
$\cmod {z - \xi} > R$
where $\cmod z$ denotes the complex modulus of $z$.
By definition of radius of convergence, there exists $w \in \C$ such that:
$\cmod {w - \xi} < \cmod {z - \xi}$
and $S \paren w$ is divergent.
Then:
$$\limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n }^{1/n} > \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {a_n \paren {w - \xi}^n }^{1/n}$$
$$\ge 1$$
$n$th Root Test: $S \paren w$ is divergent
From the $n$th Root Test, it follows that $S \paren z$ is divergent.

title: Radius of Convergence of Power Series in Complex Plane
theorem_text:
Consider the complex power series:
$S = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty z^n$
The radius of convergence $S$ is $1$.
proof_text:
$$\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac {\cmod {z^n} } {\cmod {z^{n - 1} } } = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {z^n} {z^{n - 1} } }$$
$$= \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod z$$
$$= \cmod z$$
By the Ratio Test, it follows that:
$S$ is convergent for $\cmod z < 1$
$S$ is divergent for $\cmod z > 1$.
Hence the result by definition of radius of convergence.

title: Radius of Convergence of Power Series Expansion for Cosine Function
theorem_text:
The cosine function has the complex power series expansion:
$$C \paren z = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {z^{2 n} } {\paren {2 n}!}$$
$$= 1 - \frac {z^2} {2!} + \frac {z^4} {4!} - \frac {z^6} {6!} + \cdots$$
which is the power series expansion of the cosine function.
This is valid for all $z \in \C$.
proof_text:
Applying Radius of Convergence from Limit of Sequence: Complex Case, we find that:
$$\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {a_{n + 1} } {a_n} } = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {\frac {\paren {-1}^{n + 1} } {\paren {2 \paren {n + 1} }!} } {\frac {\paren {-1}^n} {\paren {2 n}!} } }$$
$$= \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {\paren {2 n}!} {\paren {2 \paren {n + 1} }!} }$$
as $\cmod {\paren {-1}^n} = 1$ for all $n$
$$= \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac 1 {\paren {2 n + 1} \paren {2 n + 2} } }$$
$$= 0$$
Sequence of Powers of Reciprocals is Null Sequence
Hence the result.

title: Radius of Convergence of Power Series Expansion for Sine Function
theorem_text:
The sine function has the complex power series expansion:
$$S \paren z = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {z^{2 n + 1} } {\paren {2 n + 1}!}$$
$$= z - \frac {z^3} {3!} + \frac {z^5} {5!} - \frac {z^7} {7!} + \cdots$$
which is the power series expansion of the sine function.
This is valid for all $z \in \C$.
proof_text:
Applying Radius of Convergence from Limit of Sequence: Complex Case, we find that:
$$\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {a_{n + 1} } {a_n} } = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {\frac {\paren {-1}^{n + 1} } {\paren {2 \paren {n + 1} + 1}!} } {\frac {\paren {-1}^n} {\paren {2 n + 1}!} } }$$
$$= \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac {\paren {2 n + 1}!} {\paren {2 \paren {n + 1} + 1}!} }$$
as $\cmod {\paren {-1}^n} = 1$ for all $n$
$$= \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \cmod {\dfrac 1 {\paren {2 n + 2} \paren {2 n + 3} } }$$
$$= 0$$
Sequence of Powers of Reciprocals is Null Sequence
Hence the result.

title: Reverse Triangle Inequality/Normed Division Ring
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring.
Then:
$ orall x, y \in R: 
orm {x - y} \ge  igsize {
orm x - 
orm y}$
proof_text:
Let $0$ be the zero of $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$.
Let $d$ denote the metric induced by $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$, that is:
$\map d {x, y} = 
orm {x - y}$
From Metric Induced by Norm on Normed Division Ring is Metric we have that $d$ is indeed a metric.
Then, from the Reverse Triangle Inequality as applied to metric spaces:
$ orall x, y, z \in R:  igsize {
orm {x - z} - 
orm {y - z} } \le 
orm {x - y}$
Then:
$ orall x, y \in R:  igsize {
orm x - 
orm y} =  igsize {
orm{x - 0} - 
orm{y - 0} } \le 
orm {x - y}$

title: Limit of Subsequence equals Limit of Sequence/Normed Division Ring
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring with zero: $0$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be convergent in the norm $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ to the following limit:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$
Let $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ be a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$.
Then:
$\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ is convergent and $\displaystyle \lim_{r \mathop \to \infty} x_{n_r} = l$
proof_text:
Let $d$ denote the metric induced by $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$, that is,
$d \tuple {x, y} = \norm {x - y}$
By definition of convergence in a normed division ring:
$\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $l$ in $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ if and only if $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $l$ in the metric space $\struct {R, d}$.
We can then apply the result of Limit of Subsequence equals Limit of Sequence for metric spaces to get the result for normed division rings.

title: Combination Theorem for Sequences/Normed Division Ring/Quotient Rule
theorem_text:
Suppose $m \ne 0$.
Then:
$\exists k \in \N : \forall n \in \N: y_{k + n} \ne 0$
and the sequences:
$\sequence {x_{k + n} \ {y_{k + n} }^{-1} }$ and $\sequence { {y_{k + n} }^{-1} \ x_{k + n} }$ are well-defined and convergent with:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_{k + n} \ {y_{k + n} }^{-1} = l m^{-1}$
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} {y_{k + n} }^{-1} \ x_{k + n} = m^{-1} l$
proof_text:
By the Inverse Rule for Normed Division Ring:
$\exists k \in \N : \forall n \in \N : y_{k + n} \ne 0$
and the sequence:
$\sequence { {y_{k + n} }^{-1} }$
is well-defined and convergent with:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} {y_{k + n} }^{-1} = m^{-1}$
By Limit of Subsequence equals Limit of Sequence, $\sequence {x_{k + n} }$ is convergent with:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_{k + n} = l$
By Product Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_{k + n} \ {y_{k + n} }^{-1} = l m^{-1}$
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} {y_{k + n} }^{-1} \ x_{k + n} = m^{-1} l$

title: Real Sine Function is Bounded
theorem_text: $\size {\sin x} \le 1$
proof_text:
From the algebraic definition of the real sine function:
$\displaystyle \sin x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n + 1} } {\paren {2 n + 1}!}$
it follows that $\sin x$ is a real function.
Thus $\sin^2 x \ge 0$.
From Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine, we have that $\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1$.
Thus it follows that:
$\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x \le 1$
From Ordering of Squares in Reals and the definition of absolute value, we have that:
$x^2 \le 1 \iff \size x \le 1$
The result follows.

title: Real Part of Complex Exponential Function
theorem_text:
Let $z = x + i y \in \C$ be a complex number, where $x, y \in \R$.
Let $\exp z$ denote the complex exponential function.
Then:
$\map \Re {\exp z} = e^x \cos y$
where:
$\Re z$ denotes the real part of a complex number $z$
$e^x$ denotes the real exponential function of $x$
$\cos y$ denotes the real cosine function of $y$.
proof_text:
From the definition of the complex exponential function:
$\exp z := e^x \paren {\cos y + i \sin y}$
The result follows by definition of the real part of a complex number.

title: Imaginary Part of Complex Exponential Function
theorem_text:
Let $z = x + i y \in \C$ be a complex number, where $x, y \in \R$.
Let $\exp z$ denote the complex exponential function.
Then:
$\Im \paren {\exp z} = e^x \sin y$
where:
$\Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of a complex number $z$
$e^x$ denotes the real exponential function of $x$
$\sin y$ denotes the real sine function of $y$.
proof_text:
From the definition of the complex exponential function:
$\exp z := e^x \paren {\cos y + i \sin y}$
The result follows by definition of the imaginary part of a complex number.

title: Real Part of Sine of Complex Number
theorem_text:
Let $z = x + i y \in \C$ be a complex number, where $x, y \in \R$.
Let $\sin z$ denote the complex sine function.
Then:
$\map \Re {\sin z} = \sin x \cosh y$
where:
$\Re z$ denotes the real part of a complex number $z$
$\sin$ denotes the sine function (real and complex)
$\cosh$ denotes the hyperbolic cosine function.
proof_text:
From Sine of Complex Number:
$\map \sin {x + i y} = \sin x \cosh y + i \cos x \sinh y$
The result follows by definition of the real part of a complex number.

title: Imaginary Part of Sine of Complex Number
theorem_text:
Let $z = x + i y \in \C$ be a complex number, where $x, y \in \R$.
Let $\sin z$ denote the complex sine function.
Then:
$\Im \paren {\sin z} = \cos x \sinh y$
where:
$\Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of a complex number $z$
$\sin$ denotes the complex sine function
$\cos$ denotes the real cosine function
$\sinh$ denotes the hyperbolic sine function.
proof_text:
From Sine of Complex Number:
$\sin \paren {x + i y} = \sin x \cosh y + i \cos x \sinh y$
The result follows by definition of the imaginary part of a complex number.

title: Hyperbolic Cosine of Complex Number
theorem_text:
Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers.
Let $i$ be the imaginary unit.
Then:
$\cosh \paren {a + b i} = \cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b$
where:
$\cos$ denotes the real cosine function
$\sin$ denotes the real sine function
$\sinh$ denotes the hyperbolic sine function
$\cosh$ denotes the hyperbolic cosine function
proof_text:
$$\map \cosh {a + b i} = \cosh a \map \cosh {b i} + \sinh a \map \sinh {b i}$$
Hyperbolic Cosine of Sum
$$= \cosh a \cos b + \sinh a \map \sinh {b i}$$
Cosine in terms of Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b$$
Sine in terms of Hyperbolic Sine

title: Hyperbolic Tangent of Complex Number/Formulation 2
theorem_text: $\tanh \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\tanh a + i \tan b} {1 + i \tanh a \tan b}$
proof_text:
$$\tanh \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\sinh a \cos b + i \cosh a \sin b} {\cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b}$$
Hyperbolic Tangent of Complex Number: Formulation 1
$$= \dfrac {\tanh a \cos b + i \sin b} {\cos b + i \tanh a \sin b}$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $\dfrac 1 {\cosh a}$
$$= \frac {\tanh a + i \tan b} {1 + i \tanh a \tan b}$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $\dfrac 1 {\cos b}$

title: Hyperbolic Cotangent of Complex Number/Formulation 2
theorem_text: $\map \coth {a + b i} = \dfrac {1 + i \coth a \cot b} {\coth a - i \cot b}$
proof_text:
$$\map \coth {a + b i} = \dfrac {\cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b} {\sinh a \cos b + i \cosh a \sin b}$$
Hyperbolic Cotangent of Complex Number: Formulation 1
$$= \dfrac {\coth a \cos b + i \sin b} {\cos b + i \coth a \sin b}$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $\dfrac 1 {\sinh a}$
$$= \dfrac {\coth a \cot b + i} {\cot b + i \coth a}$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $\dfrac 1 {\sin b}$
$$= \dfrac {1 + i \coth a \cot b} {\coth a - i \cot b}$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $-i$

title: Hyperbolic Cotangent of Complex Number/Formulation 3
theorem_text: $\map \coth {a + b i} = \dfrac {\coth a - \coth a \cot^2 b} {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b} + \dfrac {\coth b + \coth^2 a \cot b} {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b} i$
proof_text:
$$\map \coth {a + b i} = \dfrac {1 + i \coth a \cot b} {\coth a - i \cot b}$$
Hyperbolic Cotangent of Complex Number: Formulation 2
$$= \dfrac {\paren {1 + i \coth a \cot b} \paren {\coth a + i \cot b} } {\paren {\coth a - i \cot b} \paren {\coth a + i \cot b} }$$
multiplying denominator and numerator by $\coth a + i \cot b$
$$= \dfrac {\paren {1 + i \coth a \cot b} \paren {\coth a + i \cot b} } {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b}$$
Difference of Two Squares
$$= \dfrac {\coth a + i \coth b + i \coth^2 a \cot b - \coth a \cot^2 b} {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\coth a - \coth a \cot^2 b} {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b} + \dfrac {\coth b + \coth^2 a \cot b} {\coth^2 a + \cot^2 b} i$$

title: Hyperbolic Tangent of Complex Number/Formulation 4
theorem_text: $\tanh \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {\cosh 2 a + \cos 2 b}$
proof_text:
$$\tanh \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\sinh a \cos b + i \cosh a \sin b} {\cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b}$$
Hyperbolic Tangent of Complex Number: Formulation 1
$$= \dfrac {\paren {\sinh a \cos b + i \cosh a \sin b} \paren {\cosh a \cos b - i \sinh a \sin b} } {\paren {\cosh a \cos b + i \sinh a \sin b} \paren {\cosh a \cos b - i \sinh a \sin b} }$$
$$= \dfrac {\sinh a \cosh a \cos^2 b + i \cosh^2 a \cos b \sin b - i \sinh^2 a \cos b \sin b + \sinh a \cosh a \sin^2 b} {\cosh^2 a \cos^2 b + \sinh^2 a \sin^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sinh a \cosh a \paren {\cos^2 b + \sin^2 b} + i \paren {\cosh^2 a - \sinh^2 a} \cos b \sin b} {\cosh^2 a \cos^2 b + \sinh^2 a \sin^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sinh a \cosh a + i \paren {\cosh^2 a - \sinh^2 a} \cos b \sin b} {\cosh^2 a \cos^2 b + \sinh^2 a \sin^2 b}$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sinh a \cosh a + i \cos b \sin b} {\cosh^2 a \cos^2 b + \sinh^2 a \sin^2 b}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine
$$= \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {2 \paren {\cosh^2 a \cos^2 b + \sinh^2 a \sin^2 b} }$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Sine, Double Angle Formula for Sine
$$= \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {\cosh^2 a \paren {1 + \cos 2 b} +  \sinh^2 a \paren {1 - \cos 2 b} }$$
Double Angle Formula for Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {\cosh^2 a + \cosh^2 a \cos 2 b + \sinh^2 a - \sinh^2 a \cos 2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {\cosh 2 a + \paren {\cosh^2 a - \sinh^2 a} \cos 2 b}$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sinh 2 a + i \sin 2 b} {\cosh 2 a + \cos 2 b}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine

title: Tangent of Complex Number/Formulation 4
theorem_text: $\tan \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b} {\cos 2 a + \cosh 2 b}$
proof_text:
$$\tan \paren {a + b i} = \dfrac {\sin a \cosh b + i \cos a \sinh b} {\cos a \cosh b - i \sin a \sinh b}$$
Tangent of Complex Number: Formulation 1
$$= \dfrac {\paren {\sin a \cosh b + i \cos a \sinh b} \paren {\cos a \cosh b + i \sin a \sinh b} } {\paren {\cos a \cosh b - i \sin a \sinh b} \paren {\cos a \cosh b + i \sin a \sinh b} }$$
$$= \dfrac {\sin a \cos a \cosh^2 b + i \cos^2 a \cosh b \sinh b + i \sin^2 a \cosh b \sinh b - \sin a \cos b \sinh^2 b} {\cos^2 a \cosh^2 b + \sin^2 a \sinh^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sin a \cos a \paren {\cosh^2 b - \sinh^2 b} + i \paren {\cos^2 a + \sin^2 a} \cosh b \sinh b} {\cos^2 a \cosh^2 b + \sin^2 a \sinh^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sin a \cos a + i \paren {\cos^2 a + \sin^2 a} \cosh b \sinh b} {\cos^2 a \cosh^2 b + \sin^2 a \sinh^2 b}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine
$$= \dfrac {\sin a \cos a + i \cosh b \sinh b} {\cos^2 a \cosh^2 b + \sin^2 a \sinh^2 b}$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b} {2 \paren {\cos^2 a \cosh^2 b + \sin^2 a \sinh^2 b} }$$
Double Angle Formula for Sine, Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Sine
$$= \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b } {\paren {1 + \cos 2 a} \cosh^2 b + \paren {1 - \cos 2 a} \sinh^2 b}$$
Double Angle Formula for Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b } {\cosh^2 b + \cos 2 a \cosh^2 b + \sinh^2 b - \cos 2 a \sinh^2 b}$$
$$= \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b } {\cos 2 a \paren {\cosh^2 b - \sinh^2 b} + \cosh 2 b}$$
Double Angle Formula for Hyperbolic Cosine
$$= \dfrac {\sin 2 a + i \sinh 2 b } {\cos 2 a + \cosh 2 b}$$
Difference of Squares of Hyperbolic Cosine and Sine

title: Characterisation of Cauchy Sequence in Non-Archimedean Norm/Necessary Condition
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring with non-Archimedean norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $R$.
Then:
$\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} = 0$
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$ be given.
By the definition of a Cauchy sequence:
$\exists N: \forall n, m > N: \norm {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$
So
$\exists N: \forall n > N: \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} < \epsilon$
Hence the result follows:
$\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} = 0$.

title: Characterisation of Cauchy Sequence in Non-Archimedean Norm/Sufficient Condition
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring with non-Archimedean norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$.
Let $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} = 0$.
Then:
$\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$ be given.
By assumption $\exists N \in \N$ such that:
$(1) \quad  \forall n > N: \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} < 0$
Suppose $n, m > N$, and $m = n + r > n$.
Then:
$$\norm {x_m - x_n} = \norm {x_{n + r} - x_{n + r - 1} + x_{n + r - 1} - x_{n + r - 2} + \dotsb + x_{n + 1} - x_n}$$
$$= \max \set {\norm {x_{n + r} - x_{n + r - 1} }, \norm {x_{n + r - 1} - x_{n + r - 2} }, \dotsc, \norm {x_{n + 1} - x_n} }$$
as $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ is non-Archimedean
$$= \norm {x_{n + s} - x_{n + s - 1} }$$
for some $s$: $0 < s \le r$
$$< \epsilon$$
by $(1)$
It follows that:
$\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.

title: Power Series of Sine of Odd Theta
theorem_text:
Let $r \in \R$ such that $\size r < 1$.
Let $\theta \in \R$ such that $\theta \ne m \pi$ for any $m \in \Z$.
Then:
$$\sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} \map \sin {2 k + 1} \theta r^k = \sin \theta + r \sin 3 \theta + r^2 \sin 5 \theta + \cdots$$
$$= \dfrac {\paren {1 + r} \sin \theta} {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2}$$
proof_text:
From Euler's Formula:
$\map \exp {i \theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta$
Hence:
$$\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \map \sin {2 k + 1} \theta r^k = \map \Im {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty r^k \map \exp {\paren {2 k + 1} i \theta} }$$
$$= \map \Im {\map \exp {i \theta} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {r \map \exp {2 i \theta} }^k}$$
as $\map \Im {\exp \paren {i \times 0 \times x} } = \map \Im 1 = 0$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\map \exp {i \theta} } {1 - r \map \exp {2 i \theta} } }$$
Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence: valid because $\size r < 1$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\map \exp {i \theta} \paren {1 - r \map \exp {-2 i \theta} } } {\paren {1 - r \map \exp {-2 i \theta} } \paren {1 - r \map \exp {2 i \theta} } } }$$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\map \exp {i \theta} \paren {1 - r \map \exp {-2 i \theta} } } {1 - r \paren {\map \exp {2 i \theta} + \map \exp {- 2 i \theta} } + r^2} }$$
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\map \exp {i \theta} \paren {1 - r \map \exp {-2 i \theta} } } {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2} }$$
Cosine Exponential Formulation
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\paren {\cos \theta + i \sin \theta} \paren {1 - r \paren {\cos 2 \theta - i \sin 2 \theta} } } {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2} }$$
Euler's Formula, Corollaryto Euler's Formula
$$= \map \Im {\frac {\cos \theta + i \sin \theta - r \cos \theta \cos 2 \theta + i r \cos \theta \sin 2 \theta - i r \sin \theta \cos 2 \theta - r \sin \theta \sin 2 \theta} {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2} }$$
expanding
$$= \frac {\sin \theta + r \cos \theta \sin 2 \theta - r \sin \theta \cos 2 \theta} {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2}$$
taking imaginary part
$$= \frac {\sin \theta + r \paren {\sin 2 \theta \cos \theta - \cos 2 \theta \sin \theta} } {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2}$$
$$= \frac {\sin \theta + r \map \sin {2 \theta - \theta} } {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2}$$
Sine of Difference
$$= \dfrac {1 + r \sin \theta} {1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2}$$
after simplification
It is noted that when $\theta$ is a multiple of $\pi$ then:
$1 - 2 r \cos 2 \theta + r^2 = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$
leaving the right-hand side undefined.

title: Modulus of Limit/Normed Division Ring
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm { \, \cdot \, } }$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a convergent sequence in $R$ to the limit $l$.
That is, let $\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$.
Then
$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \norm {x_n} = \norm l$
proof_text:
By the Reverse Triangle Inequality, we have:
$\cmod {
orm {x_n} - 
orm l} \le 
orm {x_n - l}$
Hence by the Squeeze Theorem and Convergent Sequence Minus Limit, $
orm {x_n} 	o 
orm l$ as $n 	o \infty$.

title: Three Points in Ultrametric Space have Two Equal Distances/Corollary
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {X, d}$ be an ultrametric space.
Let $x, y, z \in X$.
Then:
:at least two of the distances $\map d {x, y}$, $\map d {x, z}$ and $\map d {y, z}$ are equal.
proof_text:
Either:
$\map d {x, z} = \map d {y, z}$
or:
$\map d {x, z} \ne \map d {y, z}$
By Three Points in Ultrametric Space have Two Equal Distances:
$\map d {x, z} = \map d {y, z}$ or $\map d {x, y} = \max \set {\map d {x, z}, \map d {y, z} }$
In either case two of the distances are equal.

title: Bell Number as Summation over Lower Index of Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind
theorem_text:
Let $B_n$ be the Bell number for $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.
Then:
$B_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n {n \brace k}$
where $\displaystyle {n \brace k}$ denotes a Stirling number of the second kind.
proof_text:
By definition of Bell numbers:
$B_n$ is the number of partitions of a (finite) set whose cardinality is $n$.
First consider the case where $n > 0$.
From Number of Set Partitions by Number of Components, the number of partitions of $S$ into $k$ components is $\displaystyle {n \brace k}$.
Thus the total number of all partitions of $S$ is the sum of $\displaystyle {n \brace k}$ where $k$ runs from $1$ to $n$.
Hence:
$B_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n {n \brace k}$
But $\displaystyle {n \brace 0} = 0$ for all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$, and so:
$B_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n {n \brace k}$
Now consider the edge case where $n = 0$, that is, $S = \O = \set{}$.
There is by conventional definition one partition of $\O$, that is: $\set \O$
In this case, we have:
$\displaystyle {0 \brace 0} = 1$
and so:
$B_0 = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^0 {n \brace k} = {0 \brace 0} = 1$

title: Bell Number as Summation over Lower Index of Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Corollary
theorem_text: $B_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n {n \brace k}$
proof_text:
From Bell Number as Summation over Lower Index of Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind, we have that:
$B_n = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n {n \brace k}$
But when $n > 0$:
$\displaystyle {n \brace 0} = 0$
Hence the result.

title: Floor Function/Examples/Floor of 14
proof_text:
We have that $14$ is an integer.
Thus this is a specific example of Real Number is Integer iff equals Floor:
$\floor x = x \iff x \in \Z$

title: Subsequence of Cauchy Sequence in Normed Division Ring is Cauchy Sequence
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring with zero: $0$.
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $R$.
Let $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ be a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$.
Then:
$\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ is a Cauchy sequence in $R$.
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$.
Since $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence then:
$\exists N: \forall n,m > N: \norm {x_n - x_m } < \epsilon$
Now let $R = N$.
Then from Strictly Increasing Sequence of Natural Numbers:
$\forall r, s > R: n_r \ge r$ and $n_s \ge s$
Thus $n_r, n_s > N$ and so:
$\norm {x_{n_r} - x_{n_s} } < \epsilon$
The result follows.

title: Coprime Divisors of Square Number are Square
theorem_text:
Let $r$ be a square number.
Let $r = s t$ where $s$ and $t$ are coprime.
Then both $s$ and $t$ are square.
proof_text:
Let $p$ be a prime factor of $s$.
Then for some $n \in \Z_{>0}$:
$p^{2 n} \divides s t$
where $\divides$ denotes the divisibility relation.
But we have that $s \perp t$ and so $p \nmid t$.
Thus $p^{2 n} \divides s$.
This holds for all prime factors of $s$.
Thus $s$ is the product of squares of primes.
Thus $s$ is square.
The same argument holds for $t$.
Hence the result.

title: Combination Theorem for Cauchy Sequences/Difference Rule
theorem_text: $\sequence {x_n - y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
proof_text:
From Multiple Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\sequence {-y_n} = \sequence {\paren {-1} y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
From Sum Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\sequence {x_n - y_n} = \sequence {x_n + \paren {-y_n} }$ is a Cauchy sequence.

title: Combination Theorem for Cauchy Sequences/Combined Sum Rule
theorem_text: $\sequence {a x_n + b y_n }$ is a Cauchy sequence.
proof_text:
From the Multiple Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\sequence {a x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence
$\sequence {b y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
The result now follows directly from the Sum Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\sequence {a x_n + b y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.

title: Residue Classes form Partition of Integers
theorem_text:
Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer.
Let $\Z_m$ be the set of residue classes modulo $m$:
$\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \dotsc, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$
Then $\Z_m$ forms a partition of $\Z$.
proof_text:
By definition of the set of residue classes modulo $m$, $\Z_m$ is the quotient set of congruence modulo $m$:
$\Z_m = \dfrac \Z {\mathcal R_m}$
where $\mathcal R_m$ is the congruence relation modulo $m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$:
$\mathcal R_m = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$
By the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, $\Z_m$ is a partition of $\Z$.

title: Structure Induced by Ring with Unity Operations is Ring with Unity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$.
Let $S$ be a set.
Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the structure on $R^S$ induced by $+'$ and $\circ'$.
Then $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring with unity whose unity is $f_{1_R}: S \to R$, defined by:
$\forall s \in S: \map {f_{1_R} } s = 1_R$
proof_text:
By Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring then $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring.
We have from Induced Structure Identity that the constant mapping $f_{1_R}: S \to R$ defined as:
$\forall x \in S: \map {f_{1_R} } x = 1_R$
is the identity for $\struct {R^S, \circ'}$.
The result follows by definition of ring with unity and unity of ring.

title: Cauchy Sequences form Ring with Unity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, +, \circ, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring.
Let $\struct {R^\N, +, \circ}$ be the ring of sequences over $R$ with unity $\tuple {1, 1, 1, \dotsc}$.
Let $\CC \subset R^\N$ be the set of Cauchy sequences on $R$.
Then:
$\struct {\CC, +, \circ}$ is a subring of $R^\N$ with unity $\tuple {1, 1, 1, \dotsc}$.
proof_text:
The Subring Test used to prove the result.
By Constant Rule for Cauchy sequences:
:the constant sequence $\tuple {1, 1, 1, \dotsc}$ is a Cauchy sequences.
Hence:
$\CC \neq \O$
Let $\sequence {x_n}, \sequence {y_n} \in \CC$.
By definition of pointwise addition:
$\sequence {x_n} + \paren {-\sequence {y_n}} = \sequence {x_n - y_n}$.
By Difference Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
$\sequence {x_n - y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
Hence:
$\sequence {x_n} + \paren {- \sequence {y_n}} \in CC$.
By definition of pointwise product:
$\sequence {x_n} \circ \sequence {y_n} = \sequence {x_n \circ y_n}$.
By Product Rule for Normed Division Ring Sequences:
:the sequence $\sequence {x_n \circ y_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
Hence:
$\sequence {x_n} \circ \sequence {y_n} \in \CC$.
By the Subring Test the result follows.

title: Structure Induced by Commutative Ring Operations is Commutative Ring
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring.
Let $S$ be a set.
Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the structure on $R^S$ induced by $+'$ and $\circ'$.
Then $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a commutative ring.
proof_text:
By Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring then $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring.
From Structure Induced by Commutative Operation is Commutative, so is the pointwise operation $\circ$ induces on $R^S$.
The result follows by definition of commutative ring.

title: Equivalence Relation on Power Set induced by Intersection with Subset/Cardinality of Set of Equivalence Classes
theorem_text:
Let $A$ be finite with $\card A = n$, where $\card {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes cardinality.
The cardinality of the set of $\alpha$-equivalence classes is given by:
$\card {\set {\eqclass X \alpha: X \in S} } = 2^n$
proof_text:
That $\alpha$ is an equivalence relation is proved in Equivalence Relation on Power Set induced by Intersection with Subset.
Let $U \subseteq A$.
Then $U$ is in its own $\alpha$-equivalence class.
Now suppose $U' \subseteq A$ such that $U \ne U'$.
From Intersection with Subset is Subset:
$U \cap A = U$
and:
$U' \cap A = U'$
So:
$U \ne U' \implies \eqclass U \alpha \ne \eqclass {U'} \alpha$
and so there are as many $\alpha$-equivalence classes as there are subsets of $A$.
That is:
$\card {\set {\eqclass X \alpha: X \in S} } = \powerset A$
